Race Between a Sheriff and Lynchers. BROOKVILLE, Fla., May 17.—This morning Alex. Jackson, a prominent negro politician, entered the room of Lucinda Berry, also colored, and shot her in the back, killing her instantly, and then fled to the swamps. There has been trouble between them for some time, the woman not long ago swearing out a peace warrant against him. A lynching party is after Jackson. The Sheriff, too, is unusually active this morning, and there will be a race between the lynchers and the Sheriff's posse, with the chances in favor of the lynchers. A Dinner in Honor of Melville W. Fuller.
CHICAGO, May 17.—A private dinner in honor of Melville W. Fuller, the President's nominee for Chief Justice, was given last evening at the Hotel Richelieu. The guests were thirty of the most distinguished citizens of Chicago, including men of all parties, among them Judge Walter Q. Gresham and Gen. George Crook. Mr. Fuller and other gentlemen responded to toasts, but informally.

Miscellaneous.

Stout, R. M. Gallaway, Jos. Harker, E. S. T. Kennedy, Samuel Thorne, Louis de Eebian, George W. Hall, and Lawrence Wells.

Lake City Saturday. Dr. W. R. Chalker attended the wounded man and pronounced his injuries dan zeros and probably fatal. He was taken to his home in Live Oak.

Columbia county farmers report tobacco cotton and corn just bounding right along since the rains b gan. The sugar cane crop, so we are inform al, is more promising so far than for many years. The sweet potato and rice crows are now being planted, and upon the whoe the crop prospect of Columbia county is above the average at this writing.

The Suwannee County Democratic Convention Saturday selected the following delegates to St. Augustine: Sam Martin, Dr. S. T. Overstreet, J. H. T. Bynum, J. R. Newton, R. F. Rogers, M. M. Knight, George Wolfe, S. G. Evans, J. J. Robinson, T. J. McIntosh, Dan McAlpin. The delegates go uninstructed for Governor and other officers.

A negro, who generally calls himself A. J. Jackson, and who is of a dark-brown complexion, about 6 feet high, weighs about 150 pounds, has smooth face, close-cut hair, dresses well, and usually carries a hickory stick, is wanted in Brooksville for the murder of Lucinda Berry, committed on May 14. Twenty-five dollars reward is offered for his arrest by N. B. Rhodes, of Brooksville.

Jackson county has elected the following delegates to the Democratic convention at St. Augustine: W. H. Milton, Sr., A. F. McCraary, J. L. Reddick, J. H. McKuin, H. T. Shirley, W. H. Milton, Jr., W. H. Dykes, L. Burmbrall, A. C. White, B. S. Camp, M. F. Boone, R. B. Stapleton, E. B. Erwin, Jesse W. Carter. The delegates are uninstructed, but favor Gen. Barnes for Governor and Judges Maxwell and Raney for the Supreme Court.

The convention of the Democracy of Nassau county met Saturday at Callahan to elect delegates to the State Democratic Convention. The delegation was uninstructed, though the almost unanimous sense of the convention was in favor of Maj. George R. Fairbanks, of Fernandina, for Governor. The following delegates were chosen: G. L. Baltzell, W. O. Jeffreys, W. F. V. Scott, J. Mizell, J. Google, John J. Upchurch, C. W. Hilliard, B. G. Dyall, N. A. Hicks.

At Lakeland, Saturday, the Democratic mass meeting for Polk county met to elect delegates to the Gubernatorial convention. Col. C. C. Wilson was elected chairman, and Hon. Eppes Tucker, secretary. Following are the delegates elected: C. C. Wilson, Frank Clark, Samuel T. Fletcher, J. T. Wilson, J. A. Fortner, R. C. Langford, S. L. Griffin, L. M. Ballurd, N. C. Bryan, T. W. Bryant, Eppes Tucker, L. L. Bristow and A. C. Franklin. They are uninstructed.

The Orange County Bar Association met Thursday. J. H. Lord, Leonard D. Browne and C. F. Akers were admitted to membership. The unfinished business of the election of new officers of the association was then taken up, and the following gentlemen were duly elected to fill the following offices for the ensuing year: E. M. Hammond, President; A. M. Thrasher, Vice President; M. Silver, Secretary; L. C. Massey, Treasurer; Directors—E. M. Hammond, E. R. Gunby, H. C. Harrison, J. L. Bryan, Andrew Johnson.

J. H. Clay, an industrious colored barber, who came to Bartow from Macon about a year ago, was shot dead by some unknown person at 10 o'clock Friday night. He was in the rear of the Bartow House when the shots were fired. Persons rooming in the building heard the sounds of a scuffle and Clay's cry, "Don't shoot," followed closely by three shots. When the persons reached him he was found to be dead, two shots having entered his head, the third passing through his heart. The authorities have no positive claw as to his murderer. Suspicion points to certain parties, and the Coroner's jury will closely investigate the matter. Clay was well liked, and public feeling is strong against his assassin.

Some person broke into the telegraph office at Gainesville, Friday night, by boring a hole through the back door. On Thursday, Dr. Porter, whose office is in the back part of the room, received $220 by express, and after counting the money, replaced it in the envelope and put it into a pigeon hole in his desk, where he let it remain until Friday evening, when he took the money and went to the United States land office and bought a piece of land. The person who broke into the building no doubt saw the doctor when he received the money, and watched him place it in the desk, as he bored open the left side of it, and left without molesting anything else in the building. The burglar was just one night too late.

Editor Pratt, of the Palatka News, thus laments the demolition of "that old stool": "The old office stool is no more. The average reader may think this insignificant, but in our estimation it deserves more than a passing notice. In the summer of 1866 a printer on the old Apalachicola Reporter went over to the Curtis House and 'borrowed' it. Owing to some cause or other it was never returned. When we 'folded our tent' for Palatka it accompanied us and for well nigh twenty years we have held it down. It stuck by us through all the trying ordals of our existence, and many printers—some far away, and some who have crossed over the river—have rested upon it while at the case. A big Kentuckian walked into the office the other night and sat upon it, and his weight being too heavy it went down with him. Although it can no longer serve us we shall preserve it. Peace to its pieces."

The County Executive Committee of the Democratic party of Marion county is called to meet in Ocala on Tuesday, June 5, at 11 o'clock in the morning.

Last Saturday morning Joe Wynn, while running the edging saw at G. P. Young's saw mill, at Starke, had all the fingers on his right hand completely severed.

The Baptist pastors of Apopka, Sanford and Orlando will participate in the ordination of Rev. J. A. Richardson on the second Sunday of next month in Apopka.

J. B. Speer & Sons, of Cresston, are among the successful shippers, having sent off over 700 crates of tomatoes, with more to follow. J. A. Asher has sent off about 100 crates, with more to follow.

Lumber is being delivered in Col. J. E. Alexander's grove, at Oviedo, for building a large orange packing house. As the crop on the trees is estimated to at least reach 10,000 boxes, he will have good use for the building.

There are rumors that the J., T. and K. W. railway will soon take active steps toward extending their line of road down the coast as far as New Smyrna. They lately have had an agent looking over the territory.

I. D. Gore, an old citizen of Volusia living near Bulow, was shot while at work in his clearing on Tuesday of last week. Four rifle balls entailed his body near the heart, and death followed almost instantly. There is no clue to his assassin.

George N. Dorr, of Heightsville, has an orange tree that was a sour stump only two years old, and Mr. Dorr budded it with a Mandarine bud in May, 1887. This tree had quite a number of blooms this spring, and is now holding five nice and fine oranges.

Complaint seems to be general in the interior of the State that the oranges are dropping off badly, some groves being reported as nearly bare of fruit. The Daytona hammock groves are holding their fruit, and the prospect is good for a large crop.

A jury was impaneled at Orlando Thursday to view and condemn the right of way and assess the damages for the Orlando and Winter Park railroad through the property of the water works company at Lake Highland. The damage assessed by the jury was $18.66.

The train which left Tampa at 3 o'clock Friday afternoon for Port Tampa, in charge of Conductor Coleman and Engineer Kinson, was derailed six miles from Tampa. The damage was slight, and no one was seriously injured. Fireman Davis was badly bruised on the side.

Tampa's new bridge is to be one-sixth of a mile long and 28 feet wide. It is to be completed by Sept. 20. A forfeit of $10 per day is to be paid by the contractors for each day the bridge remains unfinished after 110 days have elapsed from the date of the contract.

At Mount Tabor on May 16 a birthday dinner was given William Feagle, now 82 years of age, and who has been a resident of Columbia county since 1856. All his children were present, besides fifty grandchildren and two great-grand children, and all in good health.

Jeff Richardson, of Spring Garden, has successfully grafted the Texas pecan on the native hickory, and Mr. Fish, of the same place, has succeeded in grafting the chestnut into the scrub oak. These grafts are both growing finely, and will no doubt soon become thrifty bearing trees.

Cottages in Leesburg rent at 25 to 40 per cent on the cost of building them. Several which did not cost over $300 each to build, are now rented at $10 a month, or 40 per cent, on the cost of building. An office on Main street that did not cost over $100 has been renting for $12 a month.

The verdict brought in at Orlando Thursday by the jury in the suit of C. M. Heard vs. the city of Orlando, was for damages in the sum of $5,000. The case was on trial three days. The counsel for the defendant filed a motion for a new trial. The case will undoubtedly go to the Supreme Court.

At Lake Worth over 2,000 bushels of tomatoes were left to rot on the vines. About five vessels are out of the freight on that many bushels, and the cost of picking and packing is lost to the laborers here, and all on account of that unauthorized order to stop sending tomatoes to Jacksonville.

The old Green Cove Springs and Middleburg mail route will be resumed after July 1, next, and the Peoria route discontinued. The route now to be stopped proved very unsatisfactory to the people of Middleburg, and they, together with the people of Green Cove, will be thankful for the return to the old route.

Willacocoochee News: In writing for the News, write on one side of the paper, sleep over what you have written, strike out nine-tenths of the adjectives, stew down to news and strain; place what is left in the hull of a mustard seed, shake until you hear it rattle, then direct the same to the editor, in a legible hand.

Alexander Jackson, who shot and killed a woman by the name of Lucinda Berry at Brooksville last Wednesday, was captured at Ocala last Friday by the Florida Railway and Navigation operator and placed in jail. A party of lynchers and the Sheriff were after him, but failed to get the murderer. Both parties were colored.

A movement is on foot at Green Cove Springs, looking to the establishment of a "Fire Brigade," and to this end the Clay Guards are to be mustered into the new service, provided the necessary expenses can be met, of securing suitable uniforms, and the wherewithal with which to purchase an outfit of buckets, hooks and ladders.

R. R. Wynn killed a monster rattlesnake, a few days ago, within 130 yards of his residence, about seven miles south of Starke, having twelve rattles and a button and measuring 6 feet and 1 inch in length. This snake bit and killed Mr. Wynn's dog late in the evening previous to his capture, and when found next morning was lying "in coil" between two logs. The snake was very large in circumference and weighed about 150 pounds.

A strange negro brought a horse to G. D. Younglove's stable at Gainesville Friday, and attempted to sell him for $65. Mr. Younglove suspected that the house had been stolen, and went to hunt an officer. Marshal Davies was found, the negro lodged in jail and the horse placed in the stable; and the development of the facts showed that Sheriff Wienges had just a few hours before received a dispatch from Ocala, asking him to look out for a stolen horse. The description suited the animal the negro had, and he is held to answer.

Watermelons have been ripe at Brooksville for three or four weeks.

There are six colored candidates in the race for Sheriff of Volusia county.

The farmers of Huston are soaking their corn in coal tar before planting, to protect it from moles.

Capt. T. C. Butler, of Palatka, has shipped over 400,000 shingles from his mill in the last two weeks.

Dr. F. G. Williams, of Macleuny, is still very sick, but hopes are entertained for his speedy recovery.

High mass was celebrated Sunday for the first time in Orlando by Father Creed. The church was well filled and much interest manifested.

R. H. Puddy, from Kingsley, has bought fifteen acres of land near Lawley on which to build him a house and commence raising small fruits.

A negro man was run over and killed at the Lemon street depot at Palatka Saturday night. He was reported to be asleep on the track.

Dr. S. A. Foster, for many years a prominent citizen of Baker county, left Monday for Eastman, Ga., where he will enter the field of journalism.

At Maclenny John T. Stokes has purchased a half interest in the Florida Sentinal, and will in future devote his personal attention to the paper.

Several cattle belonging to a colored man in Palatka Heights were run over and killed, Sunday, on the Jacksonville, Tampa and Key West railroad.

At Sanford, H. Taylor, grocer, has formed a partnership with Benjamin F. Bowen, who comes from St. Augustine. The new firm will be known as Taylor & Bowen.

Shiffield, the negro who was arrested as accessory to the murder of Lucinda Berry at Brooksville, was examined Thursday. The evidence submitted by the State failed to establish any fact connecting Shiffield with the murder, and he was discharged.

A Palatka fisherman the other day baited his hook with a grub, gave it a toss, which landed it at the root of a tree jutting over the bank.

A greedy and fat old spider of the genus araneidae pounced on the grub and ran up the tree, carrying grub, hook, line and all.

A few days ago the presiding elder of the Methodist Episcopal church was at Lawley in consultation with the members of the church with reference to the construction of a new building. The elder thinks that the society ought to put up a church costing not less than $2,000.

The marshal of Orlando has summoned 382 men liable for street tax to appear and work or pay the tax. Of this number 178 have worked and 8 paid their tax, leaving 196 in arrears. The mayor has issued a notice to delinquents notifying them the ordinance will be enforced.

John Stroda, who was sentenced to the penitentiary for two years for shooting at Henry Harper at Brooksville with intent to kill, made threats against several parties before he left, but the two years will only end to see him behind the bars for a similar crime committed some time ago.

The Tampa Tribune says that a postoffice is badly needed in what is known as the Kicklighter and Alderman settlement, on the Little Manatee river. The nearest office is nearly eighteen miles distant, and, practically, might as well be twenty-five. This is quite a populous settlement. Thirty scholars attended the public school there the past term.

The Republican slate for Putnam county is about made up. The fight seems to be on the Sheriff, for which office the names of Capt. George Gay, James H. Shelley, J. H. Hibbard and A. V. Mount have been mentioned, but it is generally understood that the contest will narrow down to Gay and Shelley. The office of Circuit Clerk is between Messrs. Hind and Snow; Maj. Teasdale for County Treasurer; R. J. Broad, of Welaka, and Mr. Berkalman, of Manville, for the assembly, and Maj. Fowler for the Senate. So far no one has been named for Collector and Assessor.

H. Alden is adding 60,000 plants to his strawberry farm. Mr. Yates and Mr. Warvel will put in 120,000 plants. Fernandina was in a state of wild ferment all last week, and intense excitement raged among the colored population over the alleged appearance of a band of bold burglaries, who, in order to more effectually conceal themselves went about in gangs of six or more dressed in white. Stories of midnight robbery were rife, and every householder was upon the qui vire, or on the front veranda with a sho gun. A diligent search failed to elicit any authentic case of theft, nor could the singular rumor be traced to its source. The ex itement, while it lasted, was highly entertaining, people being gravely informed that these singular marauders, who went about in large gangs, clad in a uniform of white, were in the habit of killing people by pinching them on the arms, thus stopping the arterial circulation, and that death ensued without leaving any trace of violence; also that, enraged at the interference which a policeman naturally offered, they set upon and stripped him naked.

How a Sheriff Outdid Lynchers.

Amos Miller, a Negro, Assaults a White Lady in Maury County.

He is Captured After Several Days and Put in Jail.

A Mob Gathers, But the Sheriff Removes Him to Franklin.

The Assumed Dispensers of Justice Go to That Place, But There They are Doomed to Defeat, as the Prisoner is Removed.
How a Sheriff Outdid Lynchers.
NASHVILLE, Tenn., June 18. — Amos Miller, a negro, about twenty-one years of age, was arrested at Santa Fe, Maury county, last Thursday, upon the charge of criminal assault on Mrs. Scott, a white woman. The deed is said to have been committed Friday, a week ago, but the officials were unable to catch Miller until Friday night, when he was placed in the jail at Columbia. Saturday night, the sheriff learning that a mob was on its way to the jail, slipped the negro out and took him to Franklin, Tenn. About 6 o'clock last evening, Sheriff Russell, of Williamson, got information that a mob composed of seventy-five or 100 men were en route to Franklin with the intention of mobbing Miller, so he and the jailer took the prisoner out and secreted him in a wheat field about half a mile from town, where they remained until 3 o'clock in the morning, when they returned to the jail with their prisoner. Early this morning the jailer took Miller to Mallory's station, and there boarded a train and brought him to Nashville. A mob visited the jail at 8 o'clock last night, but dispersed after finding their prisoner gone.

TELEGRAMS TO THE STAR.
To Save a Prisoner from Lynching.
HARD WORK OF TENNESSEE OFFICERS IN TRYING TO
To Save a Prisoner from Lynching.
HARD WORK OF TENNESSEE OFFICERS IN INTRYING TO CIRCUMVENT A MOB.

NASHVILLE, TENN., June 21.—Amos Miller, colored, who was arrested at Santa Fe, Maury County, on the charge of having criminally assaulted Mrs. Scott, of that vicinity, was lodged in jail in this city yesterday to prevent his being lynched by a mob. Miller was first placed behind the bars in Columbia, but the sheriff learned that a mob was on the way to the jail and took the prisoner to Franklin. He received information that one hundred men were en route to Franklin with the intention of mobbing Miller, so he and the jailer took the prisoner out and secreted him in a wheat field about half a mile from town, where they remained until 8 o'clock in the morning, when they returned to the jail with their prisoner. Early yesterday morning the jailer took Miller to Mallory's Station and there boarded the train and brought him to Nashville. The mob entered Franklin about 8 o'clock Tuesday night and immediately went to the jail and demanded the prisoner. The turnkey opened the jail, and the mob visited every cell, but failing to find Miller, went out the Nashville turnpike to the first toll-gate, but learning there that the sheriff had not gone through, they returned to Franklin, and after waiting around the jail for two hours dispersed.

Took the Revolver for a Plaything.

CANONSBURG, PA., June 21.—A little boy named Williams, during the temporary absence of his parents, secured a revolver from a cloth pocket on the wall, and, being too young to know the dangerous nature of the weapon, placed it to his forehead and pulled the trigger. The ball took effect between the eyes. The child is in a critical condition.

He Dreamed of Garfield's Nomination.
AND NOW HE DREAMS THAT MCKINLEY WILL CARRY
OFF THE PRIZE AT CHICAGO.

PITTSBURG, June 21.—A special to the Post from Beaver Falls, Pa., says: This place can boast of the boss dreamer in the person of Jonathan Anderson, a well-known brewer. He has the wonderful facility of dreaming dreams that as a rule come true. Of late he has dreamed three times in succession that Major Wm. McKinley, of Ohio, had received the nomination at Chicago. Before the convention of 1880 Mr. Anderton dreamed that Garfield would be nominated. A few months ago he dreamed that his brewery was on fire. So realistic was the dream that he arose from bed and went to the brewery only to find it on fire.
amos-miller-franklin-1888-08-10.A7:
Amos Miller, Who Outraged Mrs. Scott, of Maury County,
Hanged in a Court-Room in the Presence of the Judge.
His Brother Witnesses the Death of His Brutal Kinsman.
The Story of His Crime Retold Almost Justifies This Disregard for the Law-How the Villain Accomplished His Purpose.
FRANKLIN, Tenn., Aug. 10. — Amos Miller, the negro who outraged Mrs. Scott in Maury county lately, was lynched here about 10:30 o'clock this morning. It was thought best by the officers of the court not to attempt to try him at the regular session of the court and it was accordingly arranged to have a special session for his trial. Miller was brought here this morning from Nashville, where he has been held for safe keeping and arraigned in court. The mob had promised the officers of the court that if Miller was given a trial at once they would make no demonstrations, but let the law take its course. It seems, however, that

THE MOB WAS ORGANIZED

and held itself in readiness for action when the leaders gave the signal. Very soon after the court convened the leaders understood that the attorneys for the defense, Messrs. House and Henderson, were preparing to make a motion for a change of venue, and sent word to that affect to the mob. The court was proceeding to take up the case, and the attorney-general had announced himself as ready for the State, when the defendant's council applied for a continuance and proceeded to write an affidavit. At once an organized body of about fifty men, well armed, advanced to the court-house, entered the court-room, seized the negro and

SWUNG HIM TO A BANISTER RAIL
in the building almost in the very presence of the judge and the officers of the court. An effort was made to prevail upon the lynchers to desist but they were determined not to countenance anything that had the appearance of delay, and summarily executed their conception of justice. No one was allowed to interfere. A brother of Miller was in the courthouse and witnessed the hanging, but made no demonstration. Mrs. Scott was present at the trial but upon being notified left a few moments before the mob came.

None of the mob were disguised, and when they had executed their mission quietly dispersed. Intense excitement prevails throughout the town and county, but the result is nothing more than was expected by many of the people familiar with the details of the crime.

THE CRIME
for which Miller was lynched was committed on the 10th of June. Mrs. Scott, the victim of the criminal assault, is a resident of Maury county. Miller, who was twenty-one years old, and had been employed on a farm near Hillsboro, visited the residence of Mrs. Scott and asked for something to eat, securing some bread and milk. Miller then proceeded some distance from the house and concealed himself in the bushes until he observed Mr. Scott, the husband of the woman, leaving his home. Returning to Mrs. Scott's Miller attacked her and accomplished his design. She stated that she first attempted to drive Miller away, but he refused to go; then she attempted to escape, whereupon he seized her until she became unconscious. Miller fled immediately after committing the crime, and although diligent search for him was made by Mr. Scott and many neighbors the negro evaded arrest for a week. He was then taken to jail in Columbia, where he admitted his guilt. It was subsequently learned that his intention was to outrage the person of Mrs. Scott's daughter, but finding she had left in company with her father, Miller then determined to force the mother to submit to him. Several attempts have been made since Miller's arrest to lynch him, but they proved futile until today.
amos-miller-franklin-1888-08-10.A8:
A Mob's Desperate Work.
NASHVILLE, Tenn., Aug. 11.—Amos Miller, colored, was hanged at Franklin by a mob for an outrage committed on Mrs. Scott, in Williamson county, June 15.

Soon after the commission of the crime Miller was brought to Nashville and jailed, to prevent mob violence, and taken to Franklin and arraigned. The attorneys moved for a change of venue.

A mob already collected got wind of this and immediately filed into the court room and hung Miller to the railing of the front porch of the court house.

The mob was not resisted and were unmasked. A number witnessed the hanging, but the coroner's jury returned a verdict of death by hanging by unknown parties. Miller's brother witnessed the hanging but made no demonstration.

Parliament will adjourn on Monday next until November 6.
Djelaedddin Pacha, Turkish minister of finance has been dismissed. Agod Pacha Kasassian has been appointed minister of the interior.

It is proposed that a fund be raised to defray the expenses that may be incurred by Irish members of Parliament in connection with the inquiry of the Parnell commission into the charges made against them by the London Times.
The offices of the Labor Exchange in Paris, were reopened yesterday, but the meeting hall remained closed.

The election in the West Derby division of Liverpool yesterday to fill the vacancy caused by the resignation of Lord Claud Hamilton, conservative, resulted in the return of Mr. William Henry Cross, the oldest son of Lord Cross, who is also a conservative.

The newspapers of Vienna, commenting on Lord Salisbury's speech at the lord mayor's banquet in London, on Wednesday, say they do not share his hope of the maintenance of peace. They consider his reference to Russia and Bulgaria as subtle irony.

Ten brigands, forming a portion of the Nellova band, have captured a Sofia photographer and another person. They are being pursued by troops.

The Holland Society of New York was received by the municipal authorities of Amsterdam in the town hall yesterday.

The steamship Trave, which was reported having arrived at Southampton at 10 p. m. on August 8, did not arrive there until 10 a. m. on August 9. Hence the statement that she made the passage from SandyHook to the Needles in 7 days 2 hours was erroneous.

It is believed that M. Goblet's circular regarding the occupation of Massowah is intended to close the discussion in a manner honorable to France. The cabinet's adherence to its views regarding capitulations does not apply to Massowah.

The Turkish government has borrowed from local banks 1,500,000 pounds at 64. The interest on the loan is fixed at 5 per cent., and is guaranteed by the new fisheries and silk taxes.

A conference between the chiefs and lending buckets of the Southern Ute tribe and the conference committee was held Thursday. Judge Smith addressed the Indians through an interpreter, showing them that because of the rapidity with which the country is being settled by the whites and the scarcity of game on the reservation, it would be to their advantage to sign the treaty for their removal to Utah. The Indians did not seem disposed to give their consent to removal.

Bearden, the negro who shot and fatally wounded officer Palmer, Wednesday, near Springfield, Mo., was captured yesterday, but not until his body had been filled with lead. He was placed in the Springfield jail, which is now surrounded by a mob of 300 men, who threaten to lynch the desperado. The negro is so badly wounded, however, that it is thought he will die.

Two little girls, one five and the other eight, were caught stealing handkerchiefs in a store in Brooklyn. Thursday. A number of stolen articles were found on them. They said their mother forced them to steal. The mother was arrested, and $250 worth of stolen goods were found in her apartments.

A colored girl named Maggie Jones, 18 years of age, who lived alone in the upper part of a house on the Black Stump road, Long Island, was found dead in her room yesterday morning. Her head was split open. It is supposed she was murdered by a white woman to whom she had given a night's lodging. The woman is under arrest.

The fruit men of the Delaware peninsula recently passed a "tramp protective" resolution, wishing to utilize that labor in handling the peach crop. This has resulted in a rush of tramps for that section. It is estimated that fully ten thousand are now on the peninsula, and more are pouring in. Over one hundred are in Dover jail.

The convention of recent Northern settlers in Louisiana met in New Orleans Tuesday and continued their session on Wednesday. Every Northern State was represented in the convention, and the general verdict was warm praise for their new home. Measures are to be taken to induce further immigration from the North.

The business failures occurring throughout the country during the last seven days number, for the United States 205, and for Canada 28, or a total of 233, as compared with 216 last week, and 221 the week previous. For the corresponding week of last year the failures numbered 180—151 in the United States and 29 in Canada.

William Simpson, jr., of the firm of William Simpson, Sons & Co., Philadelphia, has been missing since noon of Wednesday. He left his office at that hour with the expressed intention of joining his family in New York State and taking a few days' rest.

THE HOWE MURDER. How the Terrible News was Received in This City. A telegram announcing the murder of Mr.
in This City.

A telegram announcing the murder of Mr. and Mrs. Howe was received in Omaha yesterday morning, and was at once conveyed to the palatial residence of Charles H. Fowler, No. 1718 North Sixteenth street, by a mounted messenger, who gave it to Mrs. Fowler. She tore it open and read. Then placing her hands to her head, she uttered a piercing mound, and fell prostrate in the doorway. Her three children, none of whom have reached their majority, in life, were in the rear portion of the residence, and hearing their mother scream, rushed to the rescue, and though badly frightened, managed to convey her to a sofa in the parlor, after which aid was summoned. After lying in a semi-conscious condition for a short period, during which time she clung tightly to the ill-fated message, recovered her senses, and reread the tidings again, while scalding tears trickled down her cheeks. The victims of the reported tragedy were her aged father and mother. Her husband, C. H. Fowler, who is of the milling firm of Grant & Fowler, was sent for, and upon reading the dispatch immediately wired an answer stating that he and the family would start on the earliest, east-bound train. The telegram he sent was addressed to L. J. Hodge, who first imparted the information to the Fowler household, and who is also a son-in-law of the murdered Howes.

Mr. and Mrs. Fowler, accompanied by their three children, left on the 6:35 Rock Island train for the scene of the affair, yesterday evening.

Peter Howe, one of the victims, was a banker at Wenona, Ill., and conducted an extensive business under the firm name of Peter Howe & Sons. His wealth is rated at between $700,000 and $1,000,000. The Howes resided about one-half mile out of Wenona, which is a hamlet of about two thousand souls. The aged couple lived by themselves, and no house was located in the immediate locality. The husband was seventy-six years of age, and his wife had passed her seventieth milestone in life. The only occupant of the house, aside from the aged couple, was a domestic, of German parentage. The girl had been in the employ of the family for a considerable length of time.

Mr. Howe was in the habit of reaching the bank every morning in the year at the usual hour for banks to open for business. But a small amount of money was kept in the bank at any period, and in case the murder was committed for that purpose it must have been executed by somebody who had been misled as to the amount to be secured.

One theory is that the author of the crime is one Barnhart, who is said to be the stepfather of the servant girl employed in the Howe household. An Associated Press telegram to THE BEE stated that as soon as the suspicion of Barnhart's complicity in the murder had been thoroughly aroused. The Cowardly Perpetrator of a Dual Murder Commits Suicide Rather Than Be Taken Alive.

WENONA, Ill., Nov. 12.—This village is in a fever of excitement over a double murder, followed by the suicide of the assassin, this morning. The victims of the brutal assassination are Peter Howe, senior member of the banking firm of Howe & Son, of this place, and his wife, the former aged seventy-three years and the latter sixty-nine. They lived in a large two-story frame house, situated about half a mile from the business portion of the town. The only other occupant of the house was a domestic. At 6 o'clock this morning, as she came down stairs from her bedroom to begin her daily duties the light of a lamp which she carried fell through the open door of Mr. and Mrs. Howe's bedroom and revealed a ghastly sight. The walls and bedclothes were covered with blood, and lying on the coverlet was a car coupling-pin, to which adhered hair and clotted blood. She ran to communicate the terrible story to a Mr. Irwin, Mr. Howe's son-in-law. The latter at once suspected Charles Burkhart of committing the deed, and a watch was placed on the rooms where he resided with his wife, over a grocery store situated in the principal business block of the town. Burkhart was observed walking up and down the hallway, apparently in great agitation. It was not long until he discovered that sentinels had been posted outside, and he went into his bedroom, procured a razor and

CUT HIS THROAT, from ear to ear, and was a dead man inside of five minutes. His wife, who had been in the adjoining room, heard his dying moans. When she entered the room he requested her as best he could to "care for the baby." The cause of this terrible deed is attributed to a petty spite on the part of Burkhart. The domestic in the house of the murdered couple, Sarah Richardson, a handsome lass of nineteen and Burkhart's stepdaughter, was often importuned to come and live with him, but she refused to do so, and he thought the Howes were at the bottom of her objections. He therefore concluded to murder them. Some time during the early hours of this morning he left his apartments, procured a ladder and entered a second-story window, descending to the room where the fearful crime was committed. Nothing was taken from the room, Burkhart's only desire being murder. Peter Howe, the murdered man, had been a resident of Wenona for nearly thirty years, and had amassed a fortune of $250,000. He was very charitable, and possessed

A SPIRIT OF PHILANTHROPHY which led him, some time ago, to endow the Howe institute at New Iberia, La., and the Baptist institute at Memphis, Tenn., the latter being a college for the education of indigent persons of both races. The murdered wife is the sister of George Parks, the Magnolia, Ill., millionaire. Burkhart, the murderer, was a dissolute, drunken fellow, and very dangerous when under the influence of liquor. The citizens of Wenona emphatically express themselves to the effect that had not Burkhart committed suicide they would have lynched him. Sheriff Morrissey, of Ottawa, with three deputies, arrived on the scene at noon, apprehensive of difficulty of this kind, but the desperate man chose death in preference to being taken alive.

The coroner this evening obtained a statement from the domestic, Sarah Richardson. She said that her stepfather, Burkhardt, the murderer, came to the house last night, did his fiendish work down stairs, then came to her room, told what he had done, and, after an attempt to ravish her, left the house. She lay all night not daring to give the alarm lest he waylay and murder her. Apparently the assassin's motive, aside from revenge and liquor, was to enable his step-daughter to come into possession of a sum of money promised her by the old people, providing she would stay with them during their lifetime. It would seem that the murderer had a crazy idea with the girl once in possession of this money it would be an easy matter for him to secure it.
barnhart-wenona-1888-11.A8:
WHISKEY AND REVENGE.
THE TWO CAUSES OF A DOUBLE MURDER
A BANKER OF WENONA, ILL., AND HIS WIFE, KILLED BY A DRUNKEN RUFFIAN-ANGERED BECAUSE HE FAILED TO GET MONEY- CUTTING HIS OWN THROAT TO ESCAPE A MOB.
[BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.]
Hw. No. 12. The oldest son

Lasalle, Ill., Nov. 12.—The oldest and most prominent citizen of Wenona, Ill., was Peter Howe, the banker. For a score of years his bank has been a financial feature of Lasalle County. Mr. Howe was seventy-six years of age and lived with his aged wife and two servants in a house residence on the outskirts of the town. The banker's home is isolated, but Mr. Howe never exhibited any concern, though his friends often advised him to be careful in his journeys to and from the bank. The servants were a man for outdoor work, and a girl, Sarah Richardson, who attended to the domestic duties. The girl's family recently moved to Wenona, and consisted of a profligate stepfather, Charles J. Burkhart, an unhappy mother and several miserable children. About once a month her stepfather called at the house to get possession of the girl's wages. Mr. Howe ordered the fellow off the premises and instructed the girl not to give him a cent.

On Sunday Burkhart again put in an appearance. He was under the influence of liquor. He asked to see the girl and was told he could not see her. As her stepfather he claimed the right to see her. Mr. Howe denied the right and told him to go. Burkhart went away, but threatened to return and kill every one in the house. The old gentleman paid no attention to the threats and retired as usual. Mr. Howe and his wife slept in a large room on the first floor, adjoining the back parlor. Burkhart returned to the house about 1 o'clock this morning. He was armed with a coupling-pin that he picked up on the Central Illinois Railroad. He crawled into the house through a back window and soon found the door to the sleeping apartment of Mr. Howe and his wife. The door was unlocked and Burkhart made his way to the bedside. He beat the aged couple to death. He then returned to his rooms over a grocery store in Main-st.

The dead bodies of Mr. Howe and his wife were discovered by the girl Sarah, shortly after daylight. She gave the alarm and the whole town at once turned out to apprehend the murderer. Suspicion pointed to Burkhart and a rush was made for his rooms. He heard the mob coming and divining their object, seized a razor and stepping into the hall, cut his throat from ear to ear. When the first man entered he found Burkhart's body on the threshold. It was thought the girl might have been an accomplice and she was arrested. No evidence has been found that would implicate her. Nothing was taken from the banker's house and revenge seems to be the only motive for the crime.

—Burkhart's Guilt Clearly Proven.

WENONA, Ill., Nov. 14.—Banker Howe and his wife, the victims of Charles Burkhart, will be buried on Thursday. Developments at the coroner's inquest went far to prove that the drunken assassin committed the deed in the hope of securing $1,000 which it is said the banker promised to will to Sarah Richardson, Burkhart's step-daughter. It was also shown that the deed had been premeditated for some time, his actions while at home being of a suspicious kind, as testified to by his wife. Howe had feared Burkhart for some time, and had advanced his domestic's wages to avoid trouble with her quarrelsome step-father. It is thought here that Mrs. Burkhart and her daughter knew more about the murderer's schemes than they are willing to tell, and on that account much indignation is expressed. The body of the double murderer and suicide will be shipped to Chicago. It has been secured by the Hahnemann medical college, the dead man's relatives consenting to such a disposition of his remains. It is asserted on good authority that Burkhart was a mulatto, while his wife, who is a divorced woman, is white. He was of powerful physique, nearly six feet tall, and always bore a surly expression. His reputation was always bad in this vicinity, and he was thought capable of committing any crime. It was decided not to send Burkhart's remains to Chicago until to-day, when the cemetery association directors refused a burial permit under all circumstances. The triple tragedy is still the one thing discussed here, and it was, no doubt, well that Burkhart took his own life, for the enraged citizens would have made short work of him.
barnhart-wenona-1888-11.A11:
MURDESED FOR REVENGE.
A deed that, for ferocity and brutality, has no counterpart in the criminal history of central Illinois has turned the usually quiet, sedate and conventional village of Wenona and tranquil Marshall county into chaotic excitement. Banker Howe, the old patriarch pioneer of Wenona, and one of the first settlers of Marshall county, and his aged wife were murdered in a most brutal and cold blooded manner between ten o'clock on Saturday night, and five o'clock on Monday morning.

Banker Howe and his wife, one of them quite beyond three score and ten, lived alone in a small two-storied house near the fair grounds for many, many years. He had been the mainstay and paternal adviser of his little city from its infancy, when from log cabins of the prairie to Chicago or St. Louis was a journey of great consequence, requiring a couple of weeks in going and returning. As soon as the town became somewhat of a commercial center he established the Wenona Bank, in the business of which he became a familiar figure in the history of Marshall county, and warmly identified with the best elements of society. He was a plain, sagacious man, with none of the vices of many of his fellows, and although in his latter years possessed of nearly a half million dollars, preferred to end his days as he had begun them, in industry and frugality. Mingling little with the purely social circles of his little town; his love for the fireside and his sons, caused him to select a habitation removed from others, and though cosy and filled with every comfort, his home was nearly a mile from his nearest neighbor; but the pretty, well-kept home has ever been the admiration of passers by.

Thus living simply and homely, the household duties until a few weeks ago, being of a simple nature, were performed by Mrs. Howe, but her age, she being well along in the sixth decade, caused her to employ a young girl named Sarah Richardson to do the general housework.

Sarah was industrious and expended but little of her earnings. Her stepfather, a low, worthless fellow, knowing her disposition and suspecting that she might possess a few dollars, went to the banker's homestead on Saturday afternoon to demand it. He was intoxicated and abusive. Banker Howe and his wife, who were sitting in the parlor, hearing high words and the noise of a struggle in the kitchen, hurried out and finding Burkhart attempting to injure the girl, assisted her to put him out and bar the door. Rendered frantic at being baffled, he raved about the place for an hour or more, threatening the lives of the inmates, and at about dark went away. After the evening meal the usual Scriptural passages were read, and the old couple retired. Instead of going to Wenona immediately after supper as was her custom, the girl, fearing trouble from Burkhart, remained at the house until ten o'clock, and after searching the premises to see that he was not lurking about, retired.

She arose at five o'clock on Monday morning to begin the usual preparations for doing the week's washing, and while passing the door of the banker's bedroom saw blood on the mat. The door was ajar, and fearing to investigate, she left the house. As was usual with him, one of the banker's sons called in at about eight o'clock and finding everything still, went to his father's room, and, getting no response to his call stepped inside, and almost fainted at the sight which confronted him. On the bed, the banker and his wife, with heads crushed and bodies mutilated, were surrounded with blood soaked and blood bespattered clothing and furniture. Blood covered the walls; it had congested upon the ceiling; in was present upon the nice mat carpet in great blotches, and the door and window sill bore the imprint of gory fingers. A coupling pin, covered with blood and hair, lay on the floor. The banker and his wife had been murdered in their night clothes, fairly slaughtered in their sleep. The position of the bodies seemed to place Banker Howe as the first victim. He lay squarely upon his back, and, while sleeping, his brains had been beaten out with the instrument which lay upon the floor. His wife, who had apparently been awakened
barnhart-wenona-1888-11.A12:
by the struggles of her husband, seemed to have struggled for some moments for her life. She lay crosswise of the bed. A deep wound upon her breast, her clinched hands, and the tossed and wildly disarranged bed clothing, gave evidence of a battle for life. The murderer had then tarried to vent his spite upon the lifeless remains of his victims, by beating their heads into unrecognizable masses of blood and brains and flesh.

Almost crazed with grief and terror, the son ran wildly to the nearest habitation and gave the alarm. It spread from tongue to tongue, and the house and grounds were soon filled with excited men, demanding the murderer that he might be lynched upon the spot. The girl told about how her stepfather had stormed about the house on the Saturday previous, and threatened the life of the banker and his wife, and unhesitatingly declared him to be the murder. Footprints in the rain-softened earth beneath the window led out over the lawn to the highway. Leaving a guard over the dead, the farmers galloped madly to the village, and the news spreading quickly, business was immediately suspended, and a dilligent search was instituted for the murderer, who, until the announcement of the murder, had been walking the street smoking his pipe as though he had not harmed a dove. When it became apparent to him that escape was out of the question, hurried to his rooms over Gable's meat market. At about nine o'clock, being assured that he was in his rooms, the infuriated citizens, with Marshall Wingate at their head, rushed to the house and was met by Burkhart's wife who said he was killing himself. They rushed up stairs and found his body lying upon its back with the throat cut from ear to ear, and severed to the spinal column. He lay in a bath of blood, with a razor grasped tightly in his right hand, a deep gash upon his right cheek and a number of old blood stains upon his clothing, which coupled with his suicide confirmed the suspicion of his uilt and though circumstantial were substantial witnesses.

Peter Howe, the murdered banker, was born in Connecticut, and had just celebrated his seventy-sixth birth day. Mrs. Howe was also a native of the east, and was well advanced in the sixties. Two sons, who had latterly shouldered the weightier cares of business, were partners in the bank with their father. Banker Howe, respected and loved by his townsmen, and identified with all that has been of lasting benefit to Wenona, with his wife, are sincerely mourned.

Coroner Clendennin, accompanied by Sheriff Morrissey and two deputies, repaired at once to the scene of the murder, and an inquest was held in the sitting room of the Howe residence. The evidence given by the Richardson girl and Mrs. Burkhart was very meager, Mrs. Burkhart stating that her husband was at home all evening and had not left the house, while the girl swore that she heard nothing of a struggle nor any noise whatever. The jury rendered a verdict fastening the blame on no one. The inquest was very unsatisfactory to the coroner, who thought that the evidence of the girl and her mother was incomplete, and he reassembled the jury and held another inquest. He then succeeded in forcing the mother and daughter to confess the entire truth, which makes the entire matter as plain as daylight. The girl said that she was awakened by Burkhart who came to her bedside with bloody hands and told her that he had murdered the old folks, and that it was all on her account, and then outraged her person. Mrs. Berkhart testified that her husband came home at about eleven o'clock and said that he had murdered Banker Howe and his wife, and asked for a weapon to destroy himself with. He then suggested that they die together, and next morning, after finding that he was suspected, he committed suicide.

Burkhart, a worthless drunkard, has chested the gallows, a fate which he most richly deserved. He is first identified as residing in Streator, later, he served a term of confinement for robbery at Minonk, and had resided but a short time in Wenona. His reputation was that of one who was utterly debased.

Banker Howe and his wife were buried on Tuesday. Their funeral was the largest held in Marshall county for many years.

While they are in the neighborhood it is proposed to have a public meeting in Jollet, as a great number are desirous of hearing Mrs. Gouger again.

William Thomas, the convict in the Jollt prison who is serving a term for the murder of Farmer Allen, at Sandwich, about nine years ago, was pardoned last Wednesday. He received 17 years. After he had served five, a convict named Young confessed, in a dying condition, that he was the man who did the deed. He was taken out and given a life sentence for the deed, but Thomas has been kept ever since. Younge was sentenced till last Wednesday, when he was pardoned, having served ten years for the crime of another. The Hon. C. T. Scanlan, of Chicago, procured his pardon.

William Gonigal, Victor Voudenwalder, James Whitfield and John Deary, La Salle, were arrested and fined ten dollars and costs for stealing parts of machinery from the railroad companies and coal operators, and selling it to a man named Hill. Hill was fined twenty-five dollars for receiving stolen property. The thievings have been going on for some time, and the losers determined to call a halt.

Lou Smith, a tough character of Lacon, while out coon hunting the other night lay down to close to a log fire, and while asleep a well-burned log rolled off the fire upon his thigh, burning it to the bone. He will lose the use of the limb.

The La Salle ghost, or rather the ldliotic joker, who is attempting to frighten little children in the town of coal dust and red headed policemen, narrowly escaped shooting the other night. He or she met a couple of gentlemen who ran to look for a revolver, but it got away before they returned. So says the News-Herald. Isn't this just a little silly. How can one be in danger of shooting unless the assailant has a weapon handy? Pooh!

Conductor Mitehell, of the Santa Fe, well known in Streator, was killed at the Mississippi river bridge last week. He tell from the car he was standing on and fractured his skull.

The much desired coal shaft at Ladd is still in embryo. The attempt to use the freezing process through the quicksand has been abandoned, as the New York firm demanded $75,000 for making the attempt, and even then would not guarantee a success. A fourth attempt will not be made on a variation of the puddling timbering and the big shoe are now being made and work will commence about January 1st, and the engineers are confident of success.

Elgin having decided to do away with the tower electric light system, and procure cheaper and better light, refused to renew the contract with the company, and advertised for bids to furnish a complete system. The accepted bid, which gives 95 arc lamps for $11,500, is very low. This contemplates suspending the lamps from wires, at street intersections, doing away entirely with the tower system. It is a thoroughly reliable company.

Poverty Causes a Double Tragedy.
Poverty Causes a Double Tragedy.

PITTSBURG, Jan. 30. —The village of Snowden, in Jefferson Township, about ten miles south of this city, was the scene of a double tragedy about dusk last night. Shortly after 6 o'clock Christian Feick, formerly pit boss at Snowden's mines, killed his wife with a shotgun, and then committed suicide by shooting himself in the mouth with a bulldog revolver. The only witnesses to the terrible affair were the six children of the couple, the eldest of whom was but fourteen years of age and the youngest a six-months-old baby. Mrs. Feick died almost instantly and her husband expired in less than an hour. It is thought that Feick committed the deed while laboring under temporary insanity, the result of brooding over his poverty.

They Let an Insane Woman Die.

CHICAGO, Jan. 30.—Mrs. Margaret Sullivan, a middle-aged woman, came here from Idaho, Jan. 19, to visit her daughter. There was a social gathering at her daughter's house that night and in the midst of it Mrs. Sullivans walked out into the cold air scantily clad. She wandered around the streets for several hours, when a policeman found her and took her to the station. She could give no account of herself and was evidently crazy, but the police let her wander out into the snow again and she has not been heard of since. Her relatives here are well-to-do people, and now that they have given up Mrs. Sullivan for dead they propose to hold the police responsible for her death.

They Hanged the Wrong Man.

LOUISVILLE, Ky., Jan. 30.—The nine-year-old daughter of Samuel Carter, a well-to-do farmer of Rowan County, was assaulted on the morning of Jan. 21 by an unknown negro. Bob Yenders, of the neighborhood, was suspected and a number of farmers went to his cabin and hanged him to the beam above his door. Just as Yenders was in the throes of death word was brought that not he but John Hooper was guilty, and Yenders was cut down.

Accidentally Killed by His Son.

[SPECIAL TO THE WORLD.]

WATERVILLE, Me., Jan. 30.—Edward Wentworth, the father of a large family, was accidentally killed by his son last evening in a scuffle over a revolver with which Wentworth intended to murder his wife and daughter.

The Crain Resolution. WASHINGTON, Jan. 31.—The house selected committee on election of president, vice-president, and representatives in congress, has agreed to report favorably to the house the Crain resolution, proposing an amendment to the constitution, substituting the 31st day of December for the 4th of March, as the commencement and termination of the official term of members of the house of representatives, and providing that congress shall hold its annual meeting on the first Monday in January. A Double Wreck.
CHICAGO, Jan 31.—A freight train on the Lake Shore & Michigan Southern yesterday went through a bridge at Pine, Ind., twenty miles east of Chicago. Several men are reported killed. A second freight plunged down on the first wreck, killing several men at work there, and also the entire crew of the last train. Four are known to be dead, and many more are believed to be buried beneath the wreck. A part of the mass took fire and was consumed. Particulars have been suppressed.

Without Fuel and Freezing.

MORRIS, Minn., Jan. 31.—Owing to the blockade of a branch of the Northern Pacific road, over which most of the wood consumed here is brought, the supply of wood in all the yards here is completely exhausted, with no prospect of an early rescue. The rotary plow came as far as Cyrus, nine miles east, Friday, but then broke down and was taken to St. Paul for repairs. Since then work on this branch has been suspended, and will probably not be resumed until the rotary returns. At this time the people of Morris are in painful suspense as to the condition of the fuel market.

Made Insane by Poisoned Food. DUBLIN, Jan. 31.—The family of a farmer named Doyle, consisting of father, mother, an imbecile son and three daughters, inhabiting an isolated house near Killarney, became insane Sunday evening from the effects of eating poisonous food. During the night they fought one another like wild beasts, tearing their clothing and cutting their flesh horribly. The son was found dead in the pig sty yesterday morning, his body nearly naked and his face entirely eaten away by the pigs, while the others were discovered in a semi-nude state, still fighting, in the house. They were removed to an asylum, where they were pronounced incurably insane. The father, it is thought, will die from the effects of his injuries.

A Blow at "Cut Throat" Leases.
WILKESBARRE, Pa., Jan. 31.—The eviction cases of the Stout Coal company against a number of tenants who are on strike in the Lehigh region were decided by Judge Woodward yesterday in favor of the tenants. Their leases provide that in case of non-payment of rent the tenants were to confess judgment in an amicable suit of ejectment. The judge decided that a suit of ejectment is not an amicable action and that the tenants could not confess judgment in that way, therefore the writs of dispossession were null and void.

To Correct the Records.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 31.—Mr. Steele, of Indiana, has introduced a bill in the house authorizing and directing the secretary of war to so correct the military records as to remove the charge of desertion against those who did not honestly intend to desert. The bill specifies at length the proof which must be furnished to show that the soldier did not intentionally become a deserter.

A Hairbreadth Escape Indeed.
LOUISVILLE, Jan. 31. A letter from Rowan county says that Bob Yenders was hanged by a crowd of farmers on the 21st instant for the outrage of a 9-year-old girl. Yenders was nearly dead when word came to the mob that they had hanged the wrong man, and that John Hooper was guilty. Yenders was cut down in time to save his life and the lynchers are now looking for Hooper.

Nearing the End of Life.

NEW YORK, Jan. 31.—There was no material change yesterday in the condition of James Redpath, the well known journalist and lecturer. He was able to swallow a little food, but no hopes are entertained of his recovery, and he is liable to die at any moment. Mr. Redpath has been conscious since his stroke of paralysis, though it has deprived him of the power of speech.

Death of an Eminent Botanist.

BOSTON, Jan. 31.—Asa Gray, the eminent botanist, professor of botany at Harvard college for many years and author of numerous works, died of paralysis last night, at the age of 77 years. He had been ill for some time.

From $1,500,000 to $2,000,000 Gone Up in Smoke—Many Hairbreadth Escapes.
New York, Jan. 31.—New York was visited yesterday morning by one of the most disastrous conflagrations experienced in many years, and which destroyed property valued at from $1,500,000 to $2,000,000, situated on Broadway, between Spring and Prince streets. Four big business houses, with their contents, were completely destroyed, and three more seriously damaged. Thirty-two firms were burned out, one of which employed over 200 girls, who will be thrown out of work for some time.
The fire endangered the whole neighborhood. For hours torrents of water were poured on the burning buildings from twenty steam fire engines and two water towers. Besides the brave firemen who managed them, there were seven hook and ladder com-

panies called out with their trucks. Many brave deeds were performed, and there were numerous narrow escapes among the firemen, several of whom were injured, but fortunately no fatal casualties occurred, although three victims had to be removed to the hospital.

The scene of the fire was midway in the block between Spring and Prince streets, and extended clear through from Broadway to Mercer street. It is adjoining the site of Barnum's American Museum, which was burned on March 2, 1868. The origin of yesterday's conflagration is so far a mystery.

Twenty minutes after the fire was discovered there was a loud explosion somewhere in the middle of the building. Windows were rattled violently, and showers of glass rained down on the firemen who were dragging long lines of hose inside the building. This led to a third alarm being sounded, and for several hours the entire department was obliged to work steadily in subduing the flames, and there were many hairbreadth scapes. The first alarm sounded at 6:40 a.m., and by 1 o'clock all that was left of the four immense structures was a pile of debris heaped up in the basements, from which thick smoke ascended, and the fragments of masonry and iron work, which were strewn clear across Broadway.

During the progress of the fire six special calls had been sent, in addition to the ambulance calls, which the police had taken the responsibility of sounding.

Matters and Measures of National Interest and Importance.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 28.—For a long time there has been a demand for a fractional currency, that would take the place of the old "shimplasters," for convenience in mailing small amounts. Postal notes, which were expected to meet this demand, are not as popular as expected, and there is a sentiment in the banking and currency committee of the house that favors an issue of this kind of fractional currency. It is thought that a bill will be reported to the house providing for an issue of $20,000,000 of this currency, and it is likely to pass.

A MURDERER'S DANGER.
A Moorhead Mob In Search of Young Murphy.
THE JAIL IS SEARCHED.
But the Sherifi, Anticipating Trouble, Removed His Prisoner in a Hack.
Special to the Globe.
MOORHEAD, Minn.
MOORHEAD, Minn., Oct. 19, 3 a. m. — Shortly after midnight a mob of 400 men went to the county jail to lynch Murphy, who murdered Officer Poull last night. Sheriff Jensen, anticipating the mob's coming, took the murderer away in a hack. The committee appointed to search the jail failed to find him. The vicinity is being carefully searched, as Murphy cannot be taken far owing to his condition, as he is very seriously wounded. There has been intense excitement in this city and Fargo all day. The particulars of the tragedy are substantially as follows: There have been numerous robberies in Fargo of late, the last of which was a bold robbery at the Manitoba house. These caused the police to be alert. Murphy was strongly suspected, being the author of the last one. He came over to this city yesterday and, while getting his hair cut, said he was going to a dance at Erickson's hall in the evening. Officer Benson, of Fargo, was detailed to come over and capture him. Benson attended the dance in citizen's clothes, but Murphy suspected him and was on his guard. When Officer John Thompson, of this city, came up into the hall, Benson went up and asked him if he knew Murphy, at the same time pointing to him. Murphy saw the action and, drawing a revolver from his belt, which he wore.

UNDER HIS VEST,

stepped up to them and said: "You s— of a b—, I know what you want." He, at the point of his pistol, made them walk down stairs. When they reached the sidewalk, Benson, frightened badly, ran into a saloon door close by. Thompson, still covered by the revolver, was made to walk a few rods to the railroad track, when he was stopped and questioned as to what the Fargo policeman said. Before he could reply Officer Poull, having been informed of his brother officer's danger, came running up, and when twenty feet away Murphy turned on him and shot him through the heart. He reeled and fell off the sidewalk into the street, dying almost instantly. As soon as Murphy turned on Poull, Thompson drew his revolver and shot at the murderer, hitting him near the shoulderblade. Murphy returned the fire, shooting twice without hitting him, and then started to run. Thompson pursued him closely, and while running each exchanged three more shots, the plucky officer escaping, unhurt, while Murphy was hit twice. He fell down as the officer reached him, exclaiming: "I'll give up," then swooned away from loss of blood. He was taken into the depot close by, where he laid in an unconscious condition four hours. When he became conscious he was taken to the jail in a carriage, where he now lies in a critical condition. Poull's funeral occurs tomorrow, the city council having charge.

Murderer Murphy, of Moorhead, Lodged in Hennepin County Jail.
Murderer Murphy, of Moorhead, Lodged in Hennepin County Jail.
Special to the Globe.
MOORHEAD, Minn., Oct. 20.—Sheriff Jensen returned this morning from Minneapolis, where he took Murphy, the murderer of Policeman Poull, and lodged him in the Hennepin county jail. Thursday evening, a short time before the mob went up to the jail to lynch the murderer, Sheriff Jensen assisted by a deputy, took Murphy in a carriage and drove out in the country several miles, where he remained over night. Early next morning he drove to Tenney, a flag station on the Northern Pacific, six miles east of this city, where they boarded a train and rode in the baggage car to Minneapolis. Murphy will be kept in Minneapolis for safety until arraigned for trial before Judge Mills. Policeman Pouli was buried today, the funeral being largely attended.

General Master Workman Powderly and General Secretary Hayes have prepared for the members of the order of the Knights of Labor a statement as to T. B. Barry's expulsion from the order. The formal resolution of expulsion appears to have been unanimously adopted by the general executive board on Oct. 15 and was based upon charges that he had illegally drawn money from the treasury of the order and had been guilty of other irregularities during his membership.

Thomas Brown, the man who murdered Policeman Paull of Moorehead Mina, has been in and around Fargo for some time. He is known to be a professional crook, and is suspected to have been one of the burglars who robbed the Minnesota house and the Manitoba house a few nights ago. Policeman also think it was he who shot at William Dent, and it is reported that he was sent to the penitentiary four years ago, but for what crime cannot be ascertained. During the day there has been strong talk of lynching Brown, and if he should meet that fate it would surprise no one. A crowd of several hundred went out to the jail, carrying with them a railroad tie to batter down the doors, but the sheriff had anticipated their visit and removed the prisoner to some place of safety before their arrival.

HE HAS AN ALIAS.
Ben Bennett Charged With Complicity in the Murder of Policeman Poull.
Special to the Globe.
FARGO, Dak., Nov. 2.—Ben Bennett, alias James Kelley, was arrested to-day, suspected of being the pal of Brown, the murderer of Policeman Poull, of Moorhead. When first arrested he gave his name as James Kelly, but afterwards said his real name was Bennett. He had an empty revolver on his person, but it was loaded a few evenings ago when he attempted to shoot a man in a quarrel. Immediately after the shooting Bennett disappeared, but returned three days ago. The police have been looking for him since then. Since his arrest it is reported that he confessed to one man here that he had been associated with Brown, and that he wanted to do something to break the law so that he could be with his partner.

RIS, MINN., WEDNESDAY, NOVEMBER 28, 1888.
MINNESOTA NEWS NOTES
The Manitoba depot at Albany was burned, with all the contents. Loss, $3,000.

The bodies of the city poor buried on the Minneapolis work house farm, numbering some 250, will be transferred to a small piece of ground set aside for the purpose on the farm attached to the quarantine hospital.

Mrs. John Malesch, a widow residing near Freeport, was murdered by John Pfium, a half demented fellow who had been paying some attentions to her for the past six weeks. She had been to a dance, and Pfium became jealous and shot her while she was entering the house.

The board of education of the city of Cleveland filed papers at Duluth in an action to recover $19,219.13 from the estate of Thomas Axworthy, the defaulting city treasurer of Cleveland. Axworthy had invested in mining stock on the Vermillion range, and owned some valuable dock property at Duluth.

Governar McGill has appointed a board of four members which will represent Minnesota at the labor conference of the National Prison association, to be held at Albany, N. Y., next month. Those appointed are A. K. Doe, of Stillwater; John F. Norrish, of Hastings; Edwin Dunn, of Eyota, and H. H. Hart, of St. Paul.

The new Tileston flour mill, St. Cloud, is running.

Easterville and Marcus postoffices have been raised to the presidential class.

Vosburg and Hopka, the Faribault fire bugs, were sentenced to seven years each in the penitentiary.

During the past four months the Austin cheese factory has manufactured 24,000 pounds of fine cheese.

Work has been completed on the Duluth fish hatchery, and it will be put in operation about the 15th of next month.

At the last election women superintendent of schools were elected in Faribault, Fillmore, Kanabec and Mille Lacs counties.

Henry Beaser, clerk of the Indian agencies in the vicinity of Duluth, is investigating the reported starving condition of the Indians there.

Over $2,000 has been contributed in Winona for the fund for Louis Oleson, who lost both hands by the premature explosion of a cannon at the Republican jollification.

Brown, the Moorhead murderer, was taken to a place of safety Tuesday night, the sheriff fearing he would be lynched. His trial will come up at the January term of court.

Tommy Erb, an 8-year-old boy living at Scrambler, while leading a colt to water tied the haker to his waist, and the colt becoming frightened, ran away, dragging the boy to death.

Nine young ladies, mostly from St. Paul, renounced the world and joined the order of the Sisters of St. Joseph at St. Paul. The ceremonies took place in the chapel of the Academy of St. Joseph, and were conducted by Archbishop Ireland.

A general order suspending all ore trains until the opening of navigation in 1889 has gone into effect on the Duluth and Iron Range road. The mines will keep on producing all winter and will stack the ore ready for an early rush in the spring.

Minnesota's Prohibition vote was less than 15,000.

Anoka is moving towards electric lights and an electric street railway.

Work has been begun on a 550 barrel reservoir to help Wadena's water supply.

It is charged that Minneapolis police have to be "squared" to the extent of $300 before a pugilistic contest is permitted to go on.

Burglars went through three safes in as many business houses at Owatonna Thursday night. The amount of plunder secured was small.

R. S. Shepard, C. E. Reynolds and George O. Hawkins were the prize winners of the Pillsbury academy declamation contest at Owatonna.

A special train on the Wisconsin Central road, transporting the Boston Ideals from Milwaukee to Duluth, was wrecked near the latter place by an open switch. No one was injured.

The Mankato city council has appointed a committee to revise the city charter for submission to the coming legislature. A board of public works and two new wards will be asked for.

H. H. Scott, justice of the peace at Hinckley, shot and killed S. K. Irvin at that place. The quarrel arose over some trivial affair, and in the dispute Scott shot his opponent. The murderer immediately gave himself up to the officers.

An insane man named Hill, a passenger on the Omaha train, took possession of the telegraph office at Mankato, and was secured only after a hard struggle with the train men. He was on his way home from the Rochester asylum.

Moorhead wants a public library.

Ed and Willard Kitohell, cousins, were drowned while skating on the river at Montevideo.

Ludwig Mogrin, a farmer residing near Minneiska, had his neck broken by a fall from a straw stack.

The trustees of the state insane hospitals are looking over the building now in construction at Fergus Falls.

Rose, the 13-year-old daughter of John Topinsky, of Lake City, was sent to the reform school for entering the residence of Mrs. Gines and stealing various articles of value.

John Lindquist was killed in Stillwater by a runaway team. His brother Gust was seriously injured. The two men were walking on the street and did not see the team until too late to escape.

At St. Paul Judge Simons has issued a writ of mandamus to compel Insurance Commissioner Shandrew to issue a license to the National Mutual Indemnity association. Mr. Shandrew recently refused to grant them a license.

The Winona and Southwestern railway was formally opened Friday by an excursion over the first twenty miles of the road, tendered by President William Windom and other officials to about 200 business men and representatives of the press.

Two attempts have been made to set fire to the Gustavus Adolphus college at St. Peter. The first was made on Monday night, when a map was found on fire.

The young ladies of Anoka have organized a toboggan club.

HASTY ACTION.
A Negro Lynehed in Georgia Thought to Have Been of Unsound Mind.

ATLANTA, GA, May 7.—News has been received here of the lynching last night of Dan Sale, colored, near the village of Danbury by a party of twenty-five men. The negro was caught attempting to commit a nameless crime on Miss Smith, a school teacher of that place. He was taken before a justice of the peace, bound over and put in charge of the bailiff. Georgia Rapist Lynched.
ATLANTLA, Ga., May 9.—The lynching of Daniel Sales, a well known colored desperado, in Wilkes county, is reported. Near Danbury, in that county, there is a school, presented over by Miss Sallie Smith, a pretty young lady. On Saturday she went to the schoolhouse for some books, returning home through a road in the woods. She was startled by the cat-like tread of bare feet, and the next instant she was in the hands of Dan. Sales, who began to drag her into a clumb of woods. Her screams brought help, when her assailant dropped her and ran. Men scoured the woods all night, and toward morning found Sales near Petersburg. They brought him back to the scene of his attempted crime and had him fully identified. The officers started with him to the county jail. They were intercepted by a masked mob of about thirty men, who put a rope around the prisoner's neck and soon pulled him up into mid-air, where they left him hanging until morning.

LYNCHING THREATENED.
Delphi Excited Over a Possibility that Lynch Law May Once More Be Enforced.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal. DELPHI. Ind. April 28 - One y
DELPHI, Ind., April 28.—One week ago Ed Chamberlain, in a jealous rage, shot Ella Wattenberg, at Reynolds, White county. The young lady died last night and so intense was the feeling that the prisoner was taken from jail at midnight and removed to this city. There is great excitement here tonight, because of numerous rumors to the effect that a mob has been organized in White county, and that a move will be made on the jail before morning. What gives color to this report is the fact that the prisoner is rich, and his relatives have boasted that his money will acquit him. The young lady was a member of one of the most prominent families in White county. Seven months ago Amer Green was taken from the jail here and lynched, and the possibility of a recurrence of such a tragedy has caused great excitement. Every precaution has been made to guard the jail, and Sheriff Vangundy states that under no circumstance will he surrender the prisoner. If no assault is made on the jail to-night, Chamberlain will probably be removed to the penitentiary at Michigan City to-morrow, an order having been issued by the judge to this effect. The streets are crowded with people, and the feeling of anxiety is intense.

The Prisoner Removed to Lafayette.

Special to the Indianapolis Journal.
The Prisoner Removed to Lafayette. Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

DELPHI, Ind., April 28—Midnight.—The lynching of Chamberlain by an indignant organization from White county, has been averted. An hour ago Sheriff Van Gundy, with an armed posse, quietly spirited the prisoner out of the rear of the jail, placed him in a closed carriage, and drove rapidly toward Lafayette. Had he been kept here all night there certainly would have been an attempt to take him from the jail, as the authorities had positive information that an assault would be made. Relief is expressed on all sides.

LAFAYETTE, Ind., April 29.—Sheriff Nelson Vanguundy, of Carroll county, arrived here shortly after midnight with Edward Chamberlain, the murderer of Ida Wittenberg, of Reynolds. He removed him from Delphi jail, fearing a mob from Reynolds would lynch him. Chamberlain said he did not fear a mob.
ed-chamberlain-delphi-1888-04-28.A9:
Ida Wittenberg's Slayer.
LAFAYETTE, May 2.—Henry Chamberlain, father of Edward Chamberlain, in jail here for killing Ida Wittenberg, of Reynolds, was in the city. He says there is no danger of mob violence even in Reynolds, and wants to have a speedy trial of his son. The people there are quiet, he says, and are perfectly willing to let the law take its course. The Chamberlain and Wittenberg families were very intimate, their marriages occurring on the same day and year. The son is the youngest child of Mr. Chamberlain, and the dead girl was the youngest child of the Wittenbergs. Both families are prostrated over the unfortunate occurrence.

LAFAYETTE, May 3.—Sheriff Henderson, of White county, this afternoon removed Edward Chamberlain, who killed Ida Wittenberg, from the jail here, where he had been brought for safe keeping, to Monticello. Chamberlain is to have a preliminary hearing on Friday. The sheriff does not anticipate any trouble from a mob, though there is a strong feeling against the prisoner.
