ed-chamberlain-delphi-1888-04-28.A13:
ED. CHAMBERLAIN CAPTURED.
He is Suprised While Asleep at His Uncle's House—A Lynching Feared.

MONTICELLO, Ind., May 28.—Ed. Chamberlain, who murderously assaulted the sheriff Thursday night and escaped from jail, was captured Friday night at Uncle William Biddle's house, six miles southwest of his father's home. He was asleep on a sofa, when his cousin, Mary Biddle, notified Jacob Fisher, a neighbor, who is a member of the Horse Thief and Detective association. Fisher summoned a posse, composed of Arthur and Ralph Laurie, Charles Echert and Elias Ward. Chamberlain was surprised, bound hand and foot and lodged in jail here at daylight.

He refused to talk. The jail is guarded by deputy sheriffs. No one is allowed near it. Sheriff Henderson's condition is worse. Chamberlain does not want to be removed, and is utterly indifferent. There is intense excitement. Big crowds of men are coming on trains and by road. Lynch law generally discussed, and the general opinion is that he will be hung by a mob. Chamberlain's mother is not expected to live.

His father says: "I am through with him. They can fire a thousand bullets into him for all I care."

Catherson, the remaining tramp, has not yet been captured. The commissioners offered a reward of $800 for Chamberlain, and $200 for Catherson.

A MOB DETERRED BY THE MILITIA.
CHAMBERLAIN, THE INDIANA MURDERER, SAVED BY HIS GUARDS.
Wabash, Ind., May 27.—Monticello last night swarmed with men from White, Carroll and Tippe-canoe counties, expecting to witness the lynching of Chamberlain, the murderer of Ida Witterberger, who murderously assaulted Sheriff Henderson when he made his escape from jail on Thursday night. A band of four hundred armed lynchers came from Reynolds, where the girl lived, but they halted on the outskirts. The presence of the State militia about the jail had a wholesome effect upon the invaders, who had no desire to run up against Springfield rifles.

At midnight the Sheriff's condition changed for the worse and his life was despaired of. He has not once lost consciousness. He is held in the highest esteem, and many a White County man would risk his life for Sheriff Henderson. Chamberlain nervously paced his cell and refused to eat any supper. When captured he expressed a willingness to return to jail, being weary and footsore. His bravado had left him. He did not seem to realize that he had committed an offence in braining the Sheriff or in murdering the girl. His head gives evidence of deficient intellect, and a plea of insanity will doubtless be made if he is ever tried in any but Judge Lynch's court. Chamberlain advises all young men to murder their sweet-hearts if treated as he was.* The girl's crime was in discarding the worthless fellow.
ed-chamberlain-delphi-1888-04-28.A15:
They Killed the Sheriff.
Monticello, IND., May 25.—Ed. Chamberlain, Robert Catterson and Albert Benson, confined in the White county jail, made a murderous assault on Sheriff Henderson last night, crushing his skull so badly that he will die. They afterward made their escape. Catterson and Benson were tramps awaiting trial for highway robbery.

Chamberlain murdered his sweetheart Etta Wittenburg, at Reynolds, some time ago, and was awaiting trial on charge of murder. He narrowly escaped lynching, and will surely be lynched if caught. Henderson entered the jail to lock the prisoners in their cells, when Chamberlain felled him with an iron bar. The whole county is aroused and searching for Chamberlain, and his escape is almost impossible. Eight prisoners have escaped from this jail in the last two years.
ed-chamberlain-delphi-1888-04-28.A16:
CHAMBERLAIN SAFE IN JAIL.
MOB AND MILITIA AT MONTICELLO.
The Sheriff Growing Worse-In Case of His Death Soldiers Will be Overpowered and Chamberlain Lynched. Everything Quiet.
Monticello, May 26.—[Special.]—Cham. berlain was captured last evening at 9 p. m. at the home of his uncle, William Biddle, two miles from his father's home, while laying asleep upon the lounge. His captors were Jacob Fisher, Arthur and Ralph Lawrie and a man named Eggert. They were neighbors, and were informed of his presence by his cousin, Miss Mary Biddle. He was overpowered before being able to offer any resistance, securely bound and brought to Monticello at 3 o'clock this morning. The news of his capture spread over the country like wildfire, and by 9 o'clock the town was filled with people. While there were individual expressions in favor of lynching, the better sense of the people appeared to prevail, and no immediate danger seemed to threaten until the arrival of the 3 p. m. train from the south when, without notice, there filed therefrom a company of state militia from Delphi under command of Capt. Edward Gresham, which proceeded to and immediately surrounded the jail with a guard, relieving the civil officers. Upon investigation it was found that Judge Gould had telegraphed to Gov. Gray for a company of the state militia and that this company had come in response to the governor's order. The people feeling that there was no immediate danger and that the citizens with the assistance of the civil officers of White county were willing and able to prevent any outbreak on the part of a mob, became exasperated, and great excitement has prevailed ever since. Frequent threats of lynching have been indulged and all evening people from remote towns and parts of the country have been flocking in until 1,500 persons are now in town. The guard has been withdrawn from the outside and the company now stationed within the jail. While I write the soldiers are loading their guns preparatory to repelling any attack that may be made upon the jail. Judge Gould is receiving his share of censure for this apparent premature coming in of troops, especially from Delphi, the scene of the Amer Green lynching. The condition of Sheriff Henderson changed for the worse this evening and his life is now despaired of. The tramp Benson, recaptured yesterday morning, was sentenced this morning by Judge Gould to five years in the northern prison and was taken north at 3 p. m. today by Guard Ballinger, who was here in attendance upon his trial as a witness. The outlook now is that there will be no mob to-night, but should Sheriff Henderson die it is thought that his friends will make common cause with the friends of Ida Wittenberg, the murdered girl, and make short work of Chamberlain. Should any such crisis arise, the handful of militia now guarding the jail could not prevent a lynching. When interrogated after being captured Chamberlain stated upon escaping that he traveled all night in a south-western direction to a point five miles west of Brookston and twenty-one miles from Monticello. He then retraced his steps and arrived at his uncle's in the evening passing in sight of one of the pursuing parties. The town is still full of men but it is thought that all danger for the present is over. At 10 o'clock word came that a band of 100 men were a mile west of town preparing to attack the jail. THE SENTINEL correspondent investigated and found a crowd of about fifty, but they lacked organization and have since disbanded. There is a rumor that a mob is forming further west but it cannot be verified. Ajt. Gen. Koontz arrived on the midnight train and is now in the jail.

LOGANSPORT, Nov. 29.—The trial of Ed Chamberlain, the murderer of Miss Ida Wittenburg, of Reynolds, was begun in the Circuit Court here yesterday. The whole of the day was consumed in impaneling a jury, which was selected from a venire of fifty-two men. During all of the procedure in the case Chamberlain sat in court with an apparent vacant look and disinterested sort of demeanor. He is twenty-five years of age, about five feet and nine inches in height, and is a little fleshy. He weighs, perhaps, 155 pounds. He is dark complexioned and has a round but not intelligent face. His hair is a dark brown and closely cut, and a very dark, medium-sized mustache adorns his upper lip. Thanksgiving Day at Several Places.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

LA PORTE, Nov. 29.—The M. Rumely Company, of this city, arranged for Thanksgiving day in a novel and appropriate manner. At 4:30 o'clock, yesterday afternoon, all the employees were summoned into a large room of one of the warehouses, which had been tastefully decorated for the occasion, and each of the married men was presented with a turkey, while each unmarried employee received a box of choice cigars. It was a complete surprise, which will be long remembered by the men.

CRAWFORDSVILLE, Nov. 29. — To-day was generally observed as a day of thanks in this city. The services were conducted by Rev. R. J. Cunningham in Center Church. Music especially for this occasion was rendered by Miss Mary Thomson, Mrs. E. L. Thomas and Messrs. A. A. McCain and G. L. Hughes, with Mrs. A. B. Anderson as organist. This evening an entertainment was given at the A. M. E. Church, and was called a Japanese tea, with songs and drilling. At the Catholic Church special services were held at 8 A. M.

WINCHESTER, Nov. 29. — Union Thanksgiving services were held here to-day at the Presbyterian Church, Rev. Welch, of the M. E. Church, delivering the discourse. The day was quite generally observed as a day of true thanksgiving and prayer. At night the W. E. Miller Military Band gave a Thanksgiving ball at Gordon's Rink.

GREENSBURG, Nov. 29. — Services were held at the Christian Church to-day. The sermon was preached by Rev. Reynolds, of the Centenary M. E. Church, and assistance was rendered by all the other city pastors. Many family reunions were held, and the usual fine dinners served.

RICHMOND, Nov. 29. — This was a typical Thanksgiving in Richmond, given up to church services and feasting during the day and social exercises in the evening, including a home-talent public entertainment.

Ed Chamberlain Saves Marion County the Expense of an Execution.

INDIANAPOLIS, Ind., Dec. 3.—The murder trial of Ed Chamberlain at Logansport, was terminated this morning at 6 o'clock by the suicide of the defendant. The Chamberlain jury was impanneled last Thursday. By morning the jury had scarcely risen from breakfast when a messenger from the sheriff's office rushed in crying: "Chamberlrln has suicided." This news was a great relief to the twelve men. Since they disbanded they have talked freely, and are unanimous in saying that Chamberlain relieved them of a sad duty. The evidence was overwhelming, and the death penalty would surely have been inflicted. Chamberlain hanged himself with a strip of bed ticking. His crime was the murder of Ida Wittenburg, a young girl residing near Monticello, White county.

A HORRIBLE MURDER.
A Negro Boy Deliberately Shot and Killed by a Druken Man.
A Negro Boy Deliberately Shot and Killed by a Druken Man.
Special to the Gazette.
FCRT SMITH, ARK., April 13.—Yesterday afternoon Jo Hulsley and J. T. Hunt left this city in a wagon for their homes in the Choctaw nation. They were accompanied by a small boy, and had laid in a supply of whisky, of which they imbibed very freely. They grew boisterous, swinging their pistols over their heads and yelling. About four miles out they frightened a lot of children by threatening to shoot them. When about ten miles from town they were passing a house, on the porch of which were two negro women, and a boy about four years old. One of the men said "watch me kill the d—n thing," or words to that effect, and raising his pistol he fired at the child. The ball entered his back, passing entirely through the body, killing him. They then drove about two miles further on and camped by the roadside, and here at 2 o'clock they were found and arrested by Deputy Marshal J. B. Lee, who brought them in, and they are now in jail. The boy with them was allowed to go. They deny the killing; say it was done by a boy who was with them, who had decamped; but a close search by the officers failed to discover any traces of a fourth party. A pistol was found hidden by the road-side some distance from the camp. Hulsley is a son-in-law of the late Governor Jack McCurtain of the Choctaw nation, and is a man of excellent reputation among his people; yet the murder charged to him is one of the most horrible that ever occurred in the Indian Territory.

Guerrero broke the forty-eight-hour go-as-you-please record, at Providence, Thursday night, with 282 miles, 420 yards—seventy yards ahead of Noremac's record.

Capt. W. G. Rector shot his son-in-law, John W. Koehler, dead, at El Paso, Tex., for alleged seduction of Lee Rector, the eighteen-year-old unmarried daughter of Rector, and own sister of Koehler's wife.

City Marshal John Howard shot and killed E. L. Little, a colored preacher, at Conway, Ark., yesterday. The preacher had knocked the marshal down with a can of peaches, for some unexplained affront.

Twenty-five years ago, at Frankfort, N. Y., William B. Gates, of Chicago, and George W. Gates, of Oshkosh, Wis., brothers, were married. Thursday evening they celebrated their silver wedding at the same place, the clergyman who married them being in attendance.

The five-year-old daughter of Thomas Baker, living near Wellsville, Ohio, yesterday fell into a burning brush-pile. Mrs. Baker went to the child's assistance and both were fatally burned. Mr. Baker also received serious burns while extinguishing the flames on his wife's and child's clothing.

On Thursday night four men entered a switch shanty of the Wisconsin Central railroad at Wood street, Chicago, and took possession. The switch tender, Wm. Studner, endeavored to put them out, when they assaulted him with stones and clubs, inflicting fatal injuries. His assailants escaped.

Two boilers used by the Armistead Lumber Company, at Telahatchee, Miss., exploded yesterday killing two firemen. One was a white man named Perkins; the other, colored, and named Joe Hill. A young white man, named Deming, a son of the sawyer, was also killed. A laborer named Allen Lindsey had a leg badly crushed. The mill-house is a complete wreck. Both boilers were blown to pieces.

Joseph Mages, a well-to-do farmer of Estelle county, was found dead in an alley back of a boarding-house at Frankfort, Ky. He had evidently fallen from the window of his room and been so badly crushed as to be unable to call for help. Mages had come to Frankfort to sell araft of logs he had floating down the Kentucky river. It it supposed he was ill in the night and going to the window for air lost his balance.

Advices from the Indian Territory give an account of the cold-blooded murder of a four-year-old negro boy by two white men from Short Mountain. The men, J. R. Halsey and J. C. Hulist, were returning home from Fort Smith, drunk, and as they passed a cabin by the roadside one of them said, "Watch me kill that coon," whereupon he put a bullet through the child's breast. The men have been arrested, but disclaim the killing.

The developments in the Sergeant Sherman cigarette-picture case, at New Haven, Conn., show that the business has been carried on to a greater extent than was at first supposed. It has been learned that many girls have had their pictures taken by the signal officer. His studio was broken into by the police, yesterday, but it had been stripped of everything. The police are collecting what evidence they can to form a basis for arrests.

Willie Grady, six years old, accidentally shot and killed his sister Ella, three years old, Thursday morning, at his parents' home in Chicago. The little fellow, in company with his sister, went into a store-room to play, while there, Willie opened a bureau drawer and pulled out a pistol. While examining it the weapon fell from his hand to the floor and was discharged, the bullet taking effect in his sister's left breast, close to her neck. She died in half an hour.

Major W. Z. Leitner, Secretary of State of South Carolina, died suddenly of heart disease in Columbia.

Max Moller, of Tribune, Kan., has died of hydrophobia, contracted from a mad dog bite received two weeks ago.

William Polk, an insane colored convict in the Tennessee State Penitentiary, at Nashville, committed State suicide by biting his tongue off, thus bleeding to death.

The boom near Fremont, Wis., containing 15,000 feet of fire, has been carried away by the floods and the logs, and the logs are scattered over an area of two miles square, many of them reaching the lake.
A QUARREL over the ownership of a handkerchief resulted in a riot at Spooner, Wis., which culminated in a fusillade with revolvers. Twenty shots were fired, William O'Hearn was fatally wounded. The residence of D. A. Hoffman, a widower, who lived near Oak Ridge, Mo., with eleven children, was burned and three children perished in the flames. Hoffman died from his injuries, and three other children were fatally injured.

Two Indian policemen at Los Cruces, New Mexico, attempted to arrest Sacate, a Mescalera Apache, and his son, who were drunk and making trouble in the camp. CAPTAIN RUSCH, of the schooner Four Brothers, of Racine, was knocked overboard at Marshowoc, Wis., and drowned.

The Louisiana State election was held on Tuesday, and resulted in a Democratic majority of about 40,000. The Legislature is overwhelmingly Democratic in both branches, thus insuring the election of two Democratic United States Senators.

By having one of them here and the other there, the transactions were facilitated, as meeting half way they could swap the stock and take it to where it was not known. We mentioned some weeks ago that a mare and pony had been stolen from the rack at the Webb school one night, where the owners, Messrs. Webb and Garrett, were in attendance at an arithmetic class. Since that time a horse was stolen in this county from Mr. Moses Anson, and his brother, Mr. Amos Anson, set out in pursuit of the thief, whom he traced to Benton county. It seems that a mule was stolen about the same time from a blending rack at Higginsville, and Deputy Sheriff Jackson pursued Riley Wright into Benton county as the thief, he and Mr. Anson being there after two of the brothers about the same time. LYNCH LAW
Put into Practice Near the Kansas Line.
WALLACE, KAN., April 18.—A homesteader named Baker, of Bent county, Colorado, living near Burlington, was lynched last evening by an angry mob at Cheyenne Wells.

The details, as near as they can be gathered at this distance, are as follows:

Two land seekers, T. B. McConnell and John C. Morrison, from the Burlington and Missouri railroad in Nebraska, were driving across the country to Cheyenne Wells, in company with the stage driver.

In doing so they drove across some breaking belonging to a homesteader, and not retracing as ordered, they were fired upon with a shot-gun, and the two land seekers, sitting in the rear seat, were mortally wounded.

One has since died, and the other is expected to die at any moment.

The murderer was arrested and taken to Burlington.

Threats of lynching being freely indulged in, the prisoner was taken to Cheyenne Wells with the intention of taking him to Denver for safe keeping; but the mob took advantage, and hung him to the coal chute. It appears that his wife handed him the gun with which to do the shooting.

She is under arrest as an accessory, and threats have been made of lynching her also.

Newt. Vorce has been convicted of murder in the second degree.

The Salida alderman have appropriated $300 for advertising the city.

The Prohibitionists will hold their state convention on the 8th of May.

A party of thirty families from Iowa are on their way the San Luis Valley.

A rich gold find is reported from Beulah Springs, a few miles west of Pueblo.

The Colorado Coal and Iron Company will hereafter make steel nails instead of iron nails.

The Denver Street Railway Company intends converting some of their principal lines into cable roads.

The corner stone of a new and costly Presbyterian church was laid at Colorado Springs last week.

The Montezuma tunnel is nearly completed, and in a few days water will be turned into that great valley.

A piece of quartz containing fine gold was found near Manitou the other day, creating considerable excitement.

A Del Norte man has been awarded the contract for furnishing 200,000 pounds of potatoes to the Government at Santa Fe.

The six days walking match which took place in Denver last week was won by Hart, a colored man, who covered 473½ miles.

Franklin Baker, the murderer of two ranchmen near Burlington, was taken from the sheriff at Cheyenne Wells by a mob of infuriated men and hanged.

The trans-continental lines of railways have cut their rates from New York to Colorado points to meet the Panhandle figures. A lively railroad war is likely to be the result.

Seven saloon keepers of Durango have petitioned the city council to raise licenses to $1,000, each agreeing to take out a license at that figure. The rest of the whiskey dealers are in favor of a $200 license.

A HORRIBLE MURDER IN MADISON. We learn from several gentlemen
We learn from several gentlemen who were in the city yesterday from Madison county that Gaither Reese, of Spring Creek, was shot and instantly killed by Jerome Ruff and three other parties on Friday 23rd inst. It seems that some time since a slight difficulty occurred between Reese and Ruff, and on seeing the latter with three other friends armed with rifle guns approaching, Reese thought it best to prevent any difficulty sought to make his escape; and as soon as he made the effort to get out of danger the assailants opened fire, lodging several balls in Mr. Reese, one of them going in the back of his head and coming out of his forehead, causing death instantly. They were all arrested, but Ruff made his escape. One gave bail and the other two were placed in Marshall jail. Officers are out with warrants for Ruff who seemed to be the leader of the gang. The names of the other three men our informants were unable to learn. This has caused great excitement in that community where many of the best citizens of the county live.

THE FIRE DEPARTMENT.

The new quarters of the Ashville Fire Department have been materially improved. Instead of the old-time, old-fashioned lock and key doors, Mr. L. Swicegood has invented and placed in use an instantaneous device for opening these doors at a moment's notice. The device is Mr. Swicegood's patent, and is one of the most complete we have ever seen. Col. Sawyer and Capt. Fagg have complimented him highly upon the successful operation of his invention. The new quarters are larger and better arranged in every particular, and the addition of drop harness for the horses is all that is now needed to make the Asheville fire department one of the best in the State. As it is now it only requires one minute to harness the horses and get out of the hose house after the fire alarm has been sounded. The department deserves much credit for the faithful and efficient work it has done, in preserving from the ravages of fire the property of our people, without remuneration or hope of reward.
gather-reese-spring-creek-1888-04.A2:
THE MADISON MURDER.
An Outrageous Affair—Great Excitement Prevailing.
A correspondent at Spring Creek gives us the following concerning the horrible killing in that section:

"Gaither Reece was shot and killed near here (Spring Creek) on Friday. A capias had been issued from Haywood county for the arrest of Reece, and the latter fled to Madison. The capias was put in the hands of Jerome Ruff and Pink Kirkpatrick of Haywood to execute, and thinking they had a right to make the arrest in Madison county summoned Charles Rice and C. Coward, telling them they would be fined if they did not go. The party proceeded to Joe Plemons, where Reece was, who upon seeing and recognizing the party started to run, when two guns were discharged at him; a ball from one struck him in the back of the head killing him instantly. Kirkpatrick, Coward and Rice were arrested, had a hearing before Esq. Jasper Ebbs. Rice and Kirkpatrick were committed to Madison jail; Coward was held in the sum of $500 for his appearance at court. Ruff at once fled to Haywood county. There is great excitement in this section over the affair.

SPRING CREEK.

According to this statement a very gross outrage has been committed for which the guilty parties should be severely punished. It is time to put down the idea that many seem to have that an officer has a right to shoot a man down, who, guilty only of a misdemeanor, endeavors to escape. The law allows nothing of the kind.

It seems to be conceded that the peach crop in the mountains is a failure, all killed in the bud. The apple crop so far, is perfectly safe, only a few trees showing buds. This is our chief reliance for fruit; peaches, though grown in perfection, are a precarious crop, dependent upon weather contingences, cold snaps not being unusual even late in the Spring.

We are indebted to Mr. Harry Batterham for very beautiful specimens of skeleton leaves, of English growth. They appear to be of the poplar family. All the fleshy part of the leaf has disappeared under the action of the weather, leaving a skeleton net work of exquisite beauty and delicacy. THE SUPERIOR COURT.
The Case of Jerome Ruff and Others, for Murder, Continued, Etc.
The case of the State vs. Jerome Ruff, et als., charged with the killing of Gaither Reese, and removed from Madison to Buncombe for trial, was to have been commenced in our superior court yesterday morning. In view of this fact, Judge Boykin on Monday, ordered Sheriff Worley to summons a special venire of one hundred and fifty men, returnable yesterday morning to try the cause. It was thought that counsel for both sides, would be ready to go into trial yesterday morning, but when the case was called Solicitor Moody asked for a continuance upon the grounds that material witnesses in the matter were not present, and cannot be obtained. He claimed that they were in Tennessee, their wherebouts in that State to him unknown. The Solicitor's motion was resisted by the defendants counsel in a strong argument. Judge Boykin, however, allowed the Senator's motion, after argument by counsel of both sides, and the case was continued for trial until the next regular term of Buncombe Superior court. An order was also made, allowing the defendants to give bail in the sum of $2,000 each for their appearance for trial at the next court. The clerk was directed to issue capias ad testificandum for the State's witnesses in Tennessee. The defendants had not given bond last night, but it is understood that bail will be furnished to-day. The calendar for yesterday was disposed of by one o'clock, p. m., and the court adjourned for the day. Judge Boykin is an active, working business man, and under his skillful management of the public business there is avery fair prospect of the docket being cleared at this term, and both His Honor and the members of the bar seem determined to finish it up entirely.

About Adam and Evolution.
COLUMBIA, S. C., Oct. 18.—Rev. James Woodrow, D. D., although expelled from the faculty of the Columbia Theological Seminary, continues to fill the chairs of geology, botany, zoology and mineralogy in the University of South Carolina. The students of the Theological Seminary are cordially invited to attend lectures in any of the departments or schools of the University. After Dr. Woodrow's expulsion several of the theological students attended regularly his scientific lectures in the State University. This incensed the Seminary Faculty and Board of Directors, who, led by Drs. Girardeux and Mitck, determined to boycott the Professor. They at first admonished the students, and subsequently adopted a resolution forbidding them, under pain of expulsion, from attending any of Dr. Woodrow's lectures.

The report of the Committee on Seminary made to the State Synod yesterday, after reciting these facts, recommended the adoption by the Synod of a resolution, condemning the action by the Faculty and Board of Directors in the Premises. After a protracted and bitter debate the resolution was adopted by a vote of 78 to 45.

Another victory won in the Synod by the Woodrow party was in the election of two members of the Board of Directors of the Theological Seminary to fill vacancies caused by expiration of terms. Rev. J. G. Richards and Rev. N. J. Holmes, both avowed Woodrow men, were elected, that issue being made and assented to by the opposing factions of the Synod.

The Woodrow party in South Carolina is thus in the ascendancy again, but the battle in so far as it relates to Theological Seminary matters, will have to be re-opened and fought over again in the Synod of Georgia, Alabama and Florida, which, with the South Carolina Synod, conjointly control the Seminary. From present indications it would seem that the troublesome evolution question must inevitably cause a complete division of the Southern Presbyterian Church.

Woodrow again vindicated.—ATLANTA, Ga., Oct. 23.—The Augusta Presbytery closed its session in Madison yesterday. The notable feature was the election of Dr. Woodrow of South Carolina, as Moderator. He is in full fraternization with his Church.

Messrs. J. K. Morrison & Co., bought 1,000 Ashe county chickens and 1,000 lbs. of Ashe county butter. Since the first of January last, this firm has paid out more than $5,000 in cash for chickens and eggs for shipment. Pretty big business, isn't it?—Statesville Landmark.

MURDER IN PITT.—On last Saturday night, W. H. Branch and G. P. Frentress murdered Calvin Cox near Greenville, N. C. One of the weapons was a board with a nail in it, which penetrated the skull. All the parties are white men, and the difficulty arose out of some old teud. The murderers are in jail.

The Baptist State Convention will meet in Greensboro Nov. 14.

Rewards have been offered by the Governor for four murderers as follows: $125 for Robert Tucker, Jr., white, of Warren, for murder of Weldon Davis, colored, on the night of the 27th of September; $200 for Jerome Ruff, white, of Haywood county, for the murder of Gaither Reece in Madison county, on the 2d of March last; $125 for W. B. Adams, white, of Beaufort, for the murder of Joshua N. Cox; $75 for Arthur Barnes, white, of Alexander, for the murder of J. H. W. Robinett.

The N. C. Methodist Conference meets in Newbern on Nov. 28th.

AGRICULTURAL STATE SOCIETY.—At the meeting of the Agricultural Society, Mr W. G. Upchurch was unanimously re-elected president of the Society. Mr P. M. Wilson was re-elected secretary and treasurer. Short speeches were made by J. B. Batchelor, Esq., Col. Faison, Col. J. M. Heck, Maj. R. S. Tucker, Dr. K. P. Battle, Capt. S. B. Alexander and Col. J. F. Taylor. In addition to the vice-presidents from the judicial districts, the President of the Society was empowered to make the Presidents of the local Associations of the State Vice-Presidents.

DIED FROM A FINGER SCRATCH.—One of our honest and industrious citizens, Wm. C. Lattimore, died at his residence near Polkville, from blood poisoning from a scratch or blister on his little finger. About a month ago his finger, which had a blister or scratch on it, began to swell and caused much pain and confined him to his bed for over two weeks before his death. He died at the age of 56 years and leaves a wife and eight children.—Shelby Aurora.

NEW FIELDS OF LABOR.—Revs. J. T. Kendall and G. F. Smith of the North Carolina Conference, have been transferred, the former to the St. Louis and the latter to the Southwest Missouri Conference, and both will leave for their new fields of labor after the session of the N. C. Conference, which convenes on the 28th of November at Newbern.—Wilmington Review.

Mr Geo. Pierce, the Olin township weather prophet, prophesies three big snows for the winter; two before Christmas and one after.—Two bets upon the result of the presidential election—one of $100 and one of $50, both even money—have been made in Statesville.—Statesville Landmark

To show how the farmers are fighting the bagging trust it may be stated that at Weldon, usually a large market for bagging, only two yards of jute bagging have been sold this season, and that, too, for some other purpose than as a covering for cotton.—Grensboro Patriot.

We want the counties on a bee line from Newbern to Charlotte to unite and demand the building of the Newbern and Charlotte Air Line Road.—Newbern Journal.

AN OLD HAND AT THE BUSINESS.—Dr. W. D. Vieyard, representing himself as from Virglnia, otherwise known as Watson Cumbo, was arrested in this city on Saturday last, charged with horse-stealing in Davidson county. He was arraigned before Esquire Eccles, who bound him over in the sum of $500, in default of which he was committed to jail.—Grensboro Patriot.

The Baptist Association held at Glen Alpine Station last week was largely attended. The collections for all purposes amounted to something over four hundred dollars, which reflects credit upon the organization. They are also solid on the temperance question. They refuse to fellowship with several churches that persist in retaining members who make, drink and sell whiskey.—Morganton Star.

THE CASE OF MESSRS STAMPS AND PRIMROSE.—The case against Messrs E. R. Stamps and W. S. Primrose came up for hearing yesterday afternoon at five o'clock before U. S. Commissioner T. R. Purnell, and the defendants waiving a preliminary examination, were required to give bond in the sum of $300 each for their appearance at the next term of the U. S. Circuit Court which will convene in Raleigh on the last Monday of November. Before giving said bond, the following entry was made upon the records of the Court: "The defendants protesting their innocence, and that there is no probable cause against them, yet, to avoid the trouble and loss of time incident to a tedious preliminary examination of witnesses, waive said examination and enter into the bond as above."

The amount of the bond fixed by the U. S. Commissioner for their appearance at Court indicates that he does not attach any great importance to this proceeding, and that seems to be the sentiment in the community. Only the counsel, the defendants and the reporter were in attendance. The case did not seem to make a ripple. Mr Cross, who swore out the warrant, did not appear, nor was there any prosecuting attorney present representing him.—Raleigh Observer, Oct. 23.

ALABAMA CONVICTS KILLED.
Mutinous State Prisoners Shot By Deputy Sheriffs Near Birmingham.
Mutinous State Prisoners Shot By Deputy Sheriffs Near Birmingham. Special Dispatch to The Appeal.

BIRMINGHAM, Ala., March 24.—Several months ago the county commissioners of this county passed an order prohibiting the whipping of any convict except upon an order of the county engineer and warden, and in his presence. Ever since this the convicts have been so defiant of authority that the road contractors to whom they are leased could hardly get enough work out of them to pay expenses. A squad of twenty-five that J. M. Lovelace is working some four miles from the city, on the Woodlawn road, have been especially troublesome in that way. This morning they announced that they had decided not to work any more. Lovelace came to town and got two deputy sheriffs, who were directed by Probate Judge Porter and Sheriff Truss to suppress the mutiny one way or another and put the men back to work. When the officers arrived upon the scene the convicts retired into their shanty, announcing that any one who ever interfered with them would do it at his peril. The deputies, summoning a posse of citizens, tore a board from the side of the house and fired in among the rebels. Archie Stokes, colored, of the latter, thereupon ran out, with a pick in his hand, and made at one of them, but was met with a volley of pistol balls and gunshot, which killed him instantly. Henry Allen, another negro, was slightly wounded in the side by one of the first shots. The coroner's jury returned a verdict that the shooting was done in performance of duty.

Another had fallen off and exploded on the ground thirty feet below. CHESTERFIELD, March 23.—This section was visited by a severe rain and wind storm, with heavy thunder and lightning, on last Tuesday night. The prisoners in jail here, taking advantage of the night, broke jail, and all of them escaped. They had obtained a two-inch anger from some one on the outside, it is not known from who or how, and with this instrument bored two holes in the ceiling overhead and one in the gable. They then tied blankets together and let themselves down to the ground. Sheriff King has been in search of the missing birds for two days, but up to this morning had not captured any of them.

CHATTANOOGA, March 23.—Smithville, in this state, is suffering from an epidemic of measles. There are now over one hundred cases, and there have been fifty deaths in three weeks. Those who recover are marked for life.

BIRMINGHAM, ALA., March 25.—At Loveless convict camp, near the city yesterday morning, Archie Stokes, a negro convict, was shot and killed and Henry Allen, another convict, severely wounded. Loveless was working a squad of county convicts on the public roads. When ordered to work this morning Stokes and Allen refused to go and would not let the other convicts leave the barracks. They stood in the door armed with picks and defied the guards. Sheriff Truse was informed of the state of affairs and sent two deputies out to the camp. The officers tried to enter the barracks, but the two negroes still defied them. They opened fire on the two men and Stokes rushed at the officers with a pick in his hands, but was shot dead before he advanced far. Allen's wounds are not fatal.

Columbia, S. C., March 24.—Joseph Bell, a young son of Captain John Bell, had a narrow escape from death this morning. While flying a kite in the old field, used by Yellowstone Kit for his meetings, he stepped backward and was precipitated into a dry well. He fell headforemost, but during the fall his feet struck against a protruding portion of the wall, turning him completely over so that he landed on his feet. The well is about twenty feet deep. The little fellow was drawn up by a rope. He escaped without injury, being a little bruised and shaken up.

Washington, March 23.—A quiet fracas occurred in the room of the chief clerk of the patent office to-day. The parties were Mr. Bullock, of Tennessee, and James N. Lipscomb, of South Carolina. Several blows were exchanged, but the combatants were finally separated before any harm was done.

Lansing, Tenn., March 25.—Balaam Sims was frightened to death here yesterday. Several young men caught the boy, cut off his hair and threatened to kill him, when he became so alarmed that he died in a few hours.

DAVISBORO, GA., March 21.—Meagre news reached here to-day of a shooting affray, which occurred two or three days since in the lower end of this county. Two brothers, Henry and Purify Holmes, have for some years been conducting a large turpentine business together, and in an effort to dissolve and settle the firm's business, they disagreed and resorted to blows. In the fight, Henry, the smaller brother, shot Purify in the left side with a shotgun loaded with buckshot. A heavy silver watch caught a part of the load, and it is claimed this saved his life. The wound is regarded serious, but not necessarily fatal.

CONVICTS IN ARKANSAS MINES BEATEN
TO DEATH.
A Terrible Tale of the Dead. A Terrible Tale of t
St. Louis, March 12.—A report says that startling developments have just been brought to light at Coal Hill, one of the mining towns where the mines are worked by convict labor, near Fort Smith, Ark. Anegro convict, named Williams, was flogged to death and further inquiry developed the fact that Mose Harvey, a white man, aged thirty-five years, who had been kicked to death by a fellow convict, who had been egged on to the desperate deed by Warden Gafford, and it was learned that he was in the habit of making the prisoners fight. The body of Mark Rider was exhumed and the bruises and gashes on the body indicated a violent death. It was also developed that a prisoner by the name of Hummel was tied up to a post in the mines last summer and beaten to death.

As the investigation continues the more horrible details are revealed, and the citizens of Coal Hill are much excited and threaten to hang Grafford and tear down the prison barracks.

Arkansas Convicts Abused. LITTLE ROCK, Ark., March 13.—Investigation into the abuses of convict miners at Coal Hill, Ark., show that convicts have been beaten and flogged to death; that Warden Grafford has made a practice of making the men fight, and that in one case the warden caused a desperado to kick a fellow-convict to death. The people are greatly excited and threaten to lynch Grafford. Result of a Political Quarrel. ATLANTA, Ga., March 11.—A political quarrel in Clark County, Ga., between Sheriff George W. Allen and ex-Sheriff Davis Carter resulted in a murder and suicide. Allen shot Carter dead and then killed himself. Eleven Lives Lost at Sea.
LONDON, March 10.—The British bark Lanoma, from Launceston, Australia, for London, with a cargo of wool, has been wrecked near Weymouth. The captain and eleven of the crew were drowned.

TRENTON, Ga., March 12.—Tom Roof (colored), who assaulted Mrs. Morrison here Saturday, was taken from jail and lynched by a mob of women.

Threatened with Lynching.

RICHMOND, Va., March 13. — Mormon elders who have been making converts in small districts of Botetourt County have been notified to leave or be lynched.
j-a-clifford-grafford-coal-hill-1888-03-.A21:
PRISON REFORM NEEDED.
The following account of the cruel and horrible treatment of convicts at Coal Hill mining camp, proves what we have heretofore said, Arkansas needs prison reform and needs it badly, this from the Gazette:

On February 22 J. A. Gafford, the warden, had whipped Williams, who, being unable to do as much work as his partner (convicts are worked in pairs), had been punished and had run off and hid in the mines. He was found by the guard and brought out one morning at breakfast time. He was stripped naked and chained to the whipping post, and during the day 400 lashes were laid on his naked back, that night he was taken to the hospital chained hand and foot and died the next day. When the body was exhumed it was found in a pine box, filled with mud and water. It was wrapped in a piece of old blanket and the only garment was a fragment of a shirt. Every particle of fiesh had been whipped off of the back from the shoulders down. The right temple of the skull had been fractured with a pick axe or some other similar tool. On the right side just over the kidneys was a hole six inches square which had been kicked in there. The doctors said ten of the blows were enough to kill him. The physician, Dr. W. Hunt, had been informed by the steward that the man died of a congestive chill and signed a certificate to that effect without ever seeing the body. The coroner's jury rendered the following verdict: "We the jury find that Charles Williams came to his death from cruel treatment inflicted by J. A. Gafford, which consisted of whipping, violence and neglect. "Coroner Blythe immediately swore out a warrant for Gafford's arrest but it was found he had gone to Little Rock the day before. He telegraphed here, but the wretch had gone on to Memphis.

The guards testified that Gafford was very brutal and delighted in seeing the convicts fight. He would go off and get drunk and come to the stockade and make two of them fight until one or the other was so badly bruised he could fight no longer. There are now no less than thirty convicts in the camp who bear marks and bruises received in these forced encounters.

When the coroner and the jury came back to Coal Hill they heard that another negro had just died at the stockade through violence. After hesitating some time and squabbling over the matter, Waller permitted Mr. Blythe to go in, but it was found the negro had been buried. After another long squabble they induced Waller to have the body exhumed. The coroner's jury examined it and then examined a number of witnesses and brought out the fact that the negro's name was Mose Harvey and that he had been killed by another convict named Mat Bailey. Altogether there were forty distinct severe kicks and bruises, any one of which might have produced death. The head had been punched out of shape and was unrecognizable. The eyes had been burst from the sockets and hung down over the face, looking like a black pulp or some raw, spoiled beef. A more revolting sight than that presented by the remains could not be imagined. The man had been kicked and bruised on March 1st, and lay in the hospital and suffered until March 8—one week.

While Waller was on the stand in the Harvey case the question was asked him if some time last summer a convict had not been chained to the post and whipped to death. Waller replied: "I am not called here to tell about that: I am a witness in the present (Harvey) case, and refuse to answer any questions outside of the case proper." The reporter found, though, that last summer a warden whose name was Hudson had had a negro chained to the post and stripped. Hudson hit him 150 licks making the back raw and causing the negro to yell so that his shrieks were heard at Coal Hill, more than a mile away. When he had whipped that way he then took salt and water and threw upon the lacerated and bleeding back. He then left the negro standing in the hot sun while he went down town and attended to some business. He then came back after two hours and whipped the negro until he died, at least he was found dead chained to the post.

Max Elder a white man, died about a month ago. Mr. Blythe had the body exhumed. It was somewhat decomposed on account of the stuff in which it was buried, but it could be seen that he died from injuries inflicted by the prison authorities, or they had been instrumental in it at least. On the back were thirty-four gashes, in any one of which a man's two fingers could be placed. There were other bruises, but it was impossible to tell which one of them caused the man's death.

An Arkansas Mining Camp Obtains an Unenviable Criminal Notoriety.
An Arkansas Mining Camp Obtains an Unenviable Criminal Notoriety.

St. Louis, Mo., March 21.—A special says the people of Coal Hill, Ark., are worked up to a furor over the series of outrages that have given that peaceful mining camp a criminal notoriety that is disgusting, and there is promise of a double lynching very soon. Clifford, the penitentiary warden who so brutally served the prisoners under him, is in the hands of the Sheriff, and will be taken to Coal Hill jail at once. While awaiting for him the people clamor for George Crisp, who is now in Ozark jail, having been arrested yesterday by the Sheriff charged with criminal assault on the eight-year-old daughter of Rev. Mr. Huddleston of Coal Hill. Both prisoners are hourly expected at Coal Hill, and a hanging bee is very probable.

j-a-clifford-grafford-coal-hill-1888-03-.A28:
CRUELTY TO CONVICTS.
Shocking Details of the Arkansas Mines Expose.
Coal Hill, Ark., March 22.—Governor Hughes and the Penitentiary Board arrived this afternoon to further investigate the cruelty to convicts in the coal mines. They found that Warden Scott, who preceded the fugitive Safford, was even more cruel. He whipped as many as seventy-five men in one night, until the blood ran down in streams from their bodies. The place where the convicts were confined is so filthy that there is a sickening stench from it. The beds and blankets are dirty and covered with vermin. Yesterday a lot of shoes and clothing arrived and men were provided, who had gone barefooted all the winter. Physicians to-day examined a large number of convicts who Gafford had whipped and found their bodies almost solid sores. The men feared to complain, while Gafford was here for fear of being beaten again. Some time ago a convict ran off and hid in the mines and refused to come out, and Warden Scott ordered Tom Eaddes, the pit boss, to go down and shoot him. He did so. Things are changed now, but the details of the past acts are sickening and horrible.
j-a-clifford-grafford-coal-hill-1888-03-.A31:
In Danger of Being Lynched.
LITTLE ROCK, March 21.—Clifford, ex-Arkansas penitentiary warden, for brutality to prisoners, and George Crisp, for outraging the little daughter of Rev. Mr. Huddleston, of Coal Hill, Ark., are in jail at that place and in danger of being lynched.

ARKANSAS STATE NEWS.
A ball was given a few nights ago at the State Insane Asylum. Quite a number of people went out from Little Rock and had a good time.

The loss in the recent fire at Little Rock is much heavier than was first reported, aggregating nearly $100,000.

Marshal Taylor, of Texarkana, recently arrested a man supposed to have robbed passengers and mail on the stage between Warren and Kingsland. The marshal of Kingsland, who, accompanied by one of the robbed passengers, went to Texarkana, identified the man and took him to Kingsland, where he will be kept until the grand jury meets and decides his case.

Ed Ferguson, the Arkansas County murderer, has been convicted in the Jefferson Circuit Court and sentenced to ten years in the penitentiary.

The executive committee of the State Teachers' Association met at the office of the Secretary of State in Little Rock, a few days ago, and fixed the time for the next meeting for June 25, 26 and 27, 1889.

News has been received of the capture at Cumberland Gap, Tenn., of J. A. Gafford, a fugitive from justice since last March, and under indictment for murdering or being accessory to the murder of three convicts at Coal Hill mining camp, Johnson County, of which he was warden. A reward of $400 was offered for his arrest, and last summer he murdered a detective named Perdue, who had followed him into Florida. The brutalities to the convicts at Coal Hill furnished a great sensation at the time, and entered largely into the political canvass for State officers that followed. J. A. Hudson, another warden, accused of beating a convict to leath while chained to a post in the camp, was arrested a few days ago in Arkansas County, where he was passing under an assumed name. He was practicing medicine, and is now lodged in Johnson County jail.

The reported death of Bob Fitzgerald in the recent disastrous fire in Little Rock is denied by that gentleman himself, and that is pretty good evidence.

A charter for the Stuttgart & Arkansas Railroad Company was recently filed with the Secretary of State. The capital stock is $5,000,000, and the corporators are men with means. This line is to be built from Arkansas Post, on the Arkansas river, to Stuttgart. J. A. Durell, of Vermont, Ill., is the moving spirit in the enterprise.

Albert D. Weeks, sheriff of Vigo County, Ind., and the sheriff of Sullivan County, Ind., arrested at Newport, this State, a few days ago, the negro Borton Galloway, who shot into a crowd at Terre Haute, Ind., just before election, and killed a white woman. Galloway gave himself up and went back without a requisition. He was located at Newport by a letter he had written.

A very tony wedding tock place at Christ Church, in Little Rock, a few nights ago, the contracting parties being Mr. W. H. Ragland, a prominent cotton man, and Miss Margaret Urquhart, daughter of Colonel E. Urquhart, of the American Cotton-seed O.I. trust. There were half a dozen bridemaids and groomsmen, and each and every thing was on an elaborate scale.

J. H. Merriman was recently arrested and jailed at Little Rock, charged with representing himself to be an officer of the United States and with having obtained money under false pretenses. Merriman is a lawyer. He made his appearance about a year ago. Recently it was learned that for some time past he has been claiming he was a United States pension agent. A number of persons have paid him money in sums of one dollar to fifty dollars and upwards. Most of the dupes are negroes, but several white persons were also victimized.

Officers from Kentucky passed through Little Rock, a few days ago, having in charge ex-Warden J. A. Gafford, who in the early part of the year whipped three State convicts to death in the stockade at Coal Hill. On their return the next day they collected $400 reward for Gafford's delivery to the sheriff of Johnston County, $200 being paid by the State and $200 by the penitentiary lessees. Gafford is in wretched health, caused by exposure in the mountains of Kentucky while dodging the officers. There is a strong feeling against him at Coal Hill, but it is believed that he is safe from lynch law while in the custody of the officers in the Clarksville jail.

Joe C. Wise shot and, it is thought, fatally wounded Lee Corn, son of a prominent physician of Lonoke, at Little Rock a few days since. Wise and Corn had at one time been bosom friends, but both fell in love with pretty Miss Hattie Gordon, of Lonoke County. Then bad blood arose between the men. Wise succeeded in winning the girl, and was married to her about a month ago. Since then they have lived happily in Little Rock. Corn said he would kill Wise and the girl, too. He went to the city and picked a quarrel with Wise and received a pistol shot which lodged in his spine. It was thought he would die.

The organization has been completed of the Bank of Little Rock. This will be the strongest bank in the State, the capital being fixed at $500,000. Dr. C. J. Lincoln, wholesale druggist of Little Rock, was elected president, and Mr. C. B. Wilkinson, a Philadelphia capitalist, vice-president. It is understood that Mr. C. T. Walker, for years cashier of the German National Bank of Little Rock, and one of the best known financiers in the State, will accept the place of cashier. The

A Georgia Railroad Wreck. ATLANTA, Ga., Nov. 9.—An excursion train en route to the Macon fair, on the Americus, Preston & Lumpkin railroad, was wrecked at road's crossing on Wednesday morning. Two passenger coaches left the track and were overturned. Four person were killed and many others injured. The names of those killed are: Charles Scoville, George Tyson, Jr.; Henry Martin, colored, and John Van Over, colored. George Davis, "Pig" Paris, colored, and W. C. Simpleton, conductor, will probably die from their injuries. Criminal Saved By Officers.
VERSAILLES, Ky., Nov. 9.—A dastardly outrage was perpetrated here Wednesday. James Curby, a burly colored ruffian, committed a rape upon the six-year-old daughter of Silas Mitchell, colored. After perpetrating the outrage Curby fled the town, but was followed by an infuriated mob of colored citizens, who soon captured him and would have lynched him, but for the interference of the town authorities, who arrested and lodged him in jail. The colored people made threats of mobbing the jail. The child is not seriously injured.

Shooting Affray at Mt. Sterling.

MOUNT STERLING, Ky, Nov. 9—Arthur Owens, a white man, and a comrade became drunk and disorderly on the streets Tuesday night, and, when the officers attempted their arrest, they resisted, and in the fight Owens was shot by an unknown party. He will probably recover.

A Murderous Arkansas Incident.
PINE BLUFF, Ark. Sept. 3.—William Wall, a prominent citizen of Clarendon, and John Stayton, a negro, were killed in a street fight Saturday by John Dilliard, colored. Some one threw a club at Dilliard, when he drew a pistol and shot Wall. Then Wall shot at Polk Montgomery, but missing him killed Slayton, a spectator. Dilliard then shot Wall twice, killing him. Dilliard afterwards fired on the sheriff, while being arrested, but missed him.
jim-dillard-clarendon-1888-09-01.A2:
A RIOT IN MONROE.
A Negro Begins Shooting Into a Crowd- Several Fatally Shot.
HELENA, Ark., Sept. 3. — Politics in Monroe county, adjoining this, has been for several months at a fever heat. Two tickets, known as "the people's ticket" and "the fair divide," have been placed in the field, both sides bidding for the negro vote. Partisanship has run very high, and quite a number of fights, of no great seriousness, however, have been engaged in by the followers of the different tickets.

Last Saturday, however, the feeling that had hitherto existed culminated in a double tragedy, with two or three seriously wounded people to hear from, among whom is the sheriff of the county, who had attempted to quell the riot. It was learned from an eye-witness this morning the full particulars of the riot. The fair divide and the people's candidates were advertised to have a joint discussion at the courthouse in Clarendon, the county seat, on last Saturday afternoon. Long before the speaking began quite a crowd had congregated and quite a number of whom were rather drunk. Before the first speaker had concluded what he had to say, a negro named Jim Dillard, who was the flag-bearer of the Fair-divide party, became offensive to parties of the opposite party, and was struck by some of them. At that time a young white man named William Walls rushed in to strike Dillard, when Dillard pulled his pistol and fired point blank at Walls, striking him in the abdomen. Walls fell to his knees, and before striking the ground, fired his pistol at Dillard, shooting him once in the shoulder and once in the leg, and then fell back dead. A number of men, white and black, rushed in on Dillard to mob him. when Dillard's friends, with pistols, clubs and knives, prevented them from killing him on the spot.

At this juncture Sheriff Robinson attempted to quiet the mob and place Dillard under arrest, but Dillard turned on him and shot the sheriff in the hip causing him to fall to the ground. LIVELY POLITICS. An Arkansas Meeting Ends in a Riot- Two Men Killed and a Dozen Wounded.
HELENA, Ark., Sept. 3.—A political meeting at Clarendon on Saturday night broke up in a riot, in which two men were killed and a dozen wounded. While the speaking was in progress a rough named Dillard continually interrupted the speakers with insulting remarks. A young man named Walls finally struck Dillard and knocked him down. Dillard pulled a revolver and shot Walls through the abdomen. Walls fell to his knees, pulled his revolver, and shot Dillard twice, once in the shoulder and once in the leg, and then fell back dead. A mob rushed in on Dillard, but Dillard's friends gathered around him with clubs, pistols, and knives and endeavored to defend him. Sheriff Robinson tried to quiet the mob and place Dillard under arrest, but Dillard turned on him and shot him in the hip, felling him to the ground. This only served to infuriate the mob, and they rushed in on Dillard and beat him over the head, stabbed him, and pounded him with their revolvers, but did not succeed in killing him. In the mêlée a stray bullet killed a negro who was merely a spectator. Dillard was carried away by his friends, and the mob dispersed.

Compelled to Keep Out of Clarendon, Ark., for Fear of Lynching.
Compelled to Keep Out of Clarendon, Ark., for Fear of Lynching.

Special Dispatch to The Appeal.

LITTLE Rock, Ark., Sept. 5.—Jim Dillard, the negro desperado who killed another negro and white man and shot the sheriff of Monroe county, at Clarendon, Ark., last Saturday, was brought to this city a second time last night and placed in the county jail for safe keeping. Immediately after the shooting Saturday he was brought here by the deputy sheriff to avoid violence from an infuriated mob. A short time after he disappeared a mob of several hundred men searched the town of Clarendon for him, with the avowed purpose of swinging him up, notwithstanding he was already wounded in two places and somewhat bruised. Yesterday an officer carried him back to Clarendon, but the bitter feeling among the citizens had not abated and the officer was compelled to return with him to this city, last night, where he will be kept till the excitement subsides.

EARLY on the morning of the 2d the American House at West Superior, Wis., was burned and three guests lost their lives. The fire was started by a lamp explosion.

ADVICES of the 1st from Denver, Col., state that a fight had occurred between the Pitue and Ute Indians, during which over one hundred were killed.

On the 1st the wife of a Mr. Steinlee, at Delhi, O., drowned her two little children and herself. She had been demented for years.

For the week ended on the 1st the percentage of the base-ball clubs in the National League was as follows: New York, 643; Chicago, 558; Detroit, 535; Philadelphia, 525; Boston, 524; Pittsburgh, 471; Washington, 380; Indianapolis, 359.

American Association: St. Louis, 681; Philadelphia, 624; Cincinnati, 622; Brooklyn, 604; Cleveland, 409; Baltimore, 398; Louisville, 380; Kansas City, 311. On the 2d a fire started in a toy warehouse at Baltimore, Md., and an explosion of fire-works wrecked the building, the falling walls burying seven firemen, who were all killed. The fire destroyed every thing in the block, entailing a property loss of $1,500,000.

WILLIAM A. SWART, who conducted a private bank at Roseland, a Chicago suburb, disappeared on the 1st, taking with him nearly 350,000 belonging to depositors.

Congressional nominations were made on the 1st as follows: Eighteenth district, John Baker (Rep.) renominated; same district, James Wickline (Union Labor). Tennessee, Second district, S. G. Heiskell (Dem.). Wisconsin, Fourth district, Henry Smith (Labor) renominated. Indiana, Tenth district, W. H. H. Carter (Rep.).

A party of vigilantes in the public land strip in Colorado surrounded a band of seventeen horse-thieves on the 1st, and in the fight which occurred all of the thieves were killed and the vigilantes had three men killed and nine wounded.

On the 1st Samuel Bliss, a Chicago wholesale sirup dealer, failed for $150,000.

Near Delphi, Ind., Mr. and Mrs. Robert McClintock were struck by a train on the 1st while crossing the track, and both were killed.

On the 1st John Baker, a farm hand, threw a boy into a threshing machine near Guide Rock, Neb., and his enraged companions lynched him on the spot.

Near Booneville, Mo., a freight train jumped the track on the 1st, killing six laborers who had stepped aside to let the train pass.

Three laboring men were struck by a train at Hammond, Ind., on the 3d, and all were killed.

A boiler exploded on the 3d in the Perry stove works at South Pittsburg, Tenn., killing five men.

Justice Field of the Supreme Court of California was reading the decision in the celebrated Sharon divorce case on the 3d at San Francisco when Sarah Althea Hill jumped up in court and accused him of having been corrupted. The marshal who attempted to take her was knocked across the court-room by her present husband, Judge Terry. Both were finally arrested, and the Judge sentenced Terry to six months' imprisonment and his wife to thirty days in jail.

Nominations were made on the 3d as follows for Congress: Henry Stockbridge, Jr., by Fourth Maryland district Republicans; A. B. Montgomery (renominated) by Fourth Kentucky district Democrats; Anthony Joseph by Montana Democrats, and Mark Smith by Arizona Democrats.

On the 3d a circular was issued at Detroit to all G. A. R. posts of the country soliciting ten cents each from all veterans for the fund to be used to erect an equestrian statue in Washington to General John A. Logan.

Friends of opposing candidates who were conducting the campaign in Monroe County, Ark., came together on the 3d at Clarendon, and a general riot ensued in which three men were killed.

ALONZO SMITH, Henry Tanner and John Tanner, all colored, were taken from the jail at Oxford, N. C., on the 3d, and hanged by a crowd of masked men for murder.

In Cleveland, O., on the 3d a band of Anarchists displayed a red flag at a labor picnic, and refused to acknowledge the stars and stripes. The Anarchists were at once attacked and severely handled, and their flag torn to shreds.

At the State election in Arkansas on the 3d, Eagle (Dem.) was elected Governor by about 20,000 majority, and the Legislature would be Democratic in both branches.

Among the active list a few stocks were firm, however, and St. Paul for the first quarter: of an hour was pegged at 76%, after which it advanced with the rest of the list, which rallied, and in most cases regained the early losses, when the activity and movement ceased, the entire market settling down to duiliness and stagnation. The same stocks which were prominent in the dealings yesterday were again active to-day, Reading, Lackawanna, St. Paul, and Louisville and Nashville being most conspicuous. San Francisco preferred advanced sharply 1⅛ per cent on very small dealings, but with this exception the market remained devoid of feature until near 11 o'clock, when there was a renewal of the activity, and in the decline, in which St. Paul took the lead, the lowest prices of the hour was reached, and at 11 o'clock the market was fairly active but weak.

CHICAGO, March 8.—A dispatch from Wichita, Kan., says: Three men living in Indian Territory, Julius Quinn, Wm. Antwerp, and Jos. George, were burned out or a log cabin Sunday night and shot down by a mob of cowboys. The murdered men recently went to the western part of the territory and took up a site for a claim on Rabbit Ear Creek, which they expected to make entry upon when the territory is opened for settlement. The land they squatted upon was in the range of cattleman Geo. H. Delaney. Delaney tried many ways to get the squatters to leave the country, but failed. SHOT DOWN AS THEY RAN. Brutalities by the Rough Crowd About "No Man's Land."
"No Man's Land."

WICHITA, Kas., March 9.—A ghastly crime has just come to light through the arrival in this city from the Indian territory, of United States Marshal John Woods, in search of some criminals. A short time ago three men, Julius Quinn, Pedro Antwerp, and George Burns, went upon some land near the Cherokee strip, about a mile east of "No Man's Land," and built a hut, intending to remain until the opening of the territory to settlement. They were disliked by the men already there, and a few nights ago a gang of these toughs, headed by George Delaney, set fire to the hut. As the inmates ran from the burning building they were shot down by men concealed in the brush. The better class of settlers have already lynched two of the gang. The ringleader, Delaney, and a Mexican, came north.

No change was reported in the Burlington strike on the 5th. There was a gathering of Brotherhood officials at Chicago to discuss the situation. At Kansas City a strike took place lasting a few hours on the Rock Island under a mistaken impression that the road was handling Burlington business.

The Anarchist case has been docketed in the Supreme Court of Illinois again on a motion filed by Black & Solomon, counsel for Fielden, Schwab and Neebe. The motion asks for a correction of the record, which is alleged to recite the presence of the defendants in the court when the order in each of their cases was made, while they at the time were not present either in person or by attorney.

A law has been enacted by the Ohio Legislature requiring that convict made goods in other States shall be marked as such before being offered for sale in Ohio.

L. M. Hays, a switchman in the railroad yards at Albuquerque, N. M., recently had one of his thumbs mashed in coupling cars and was being taken to the hospital at Las Vegas when as the train reached Wallace he was awakened by the arrival of the southbound passenger train and probably imagining he was in the yards switching seized the conductor's lantern and jumped out in front of the passing train, which struck him and killed him instantly, his body being horribly mangled.

Two brakemen, Williams and Furguson, were fatally injured, and two engines and nineteen freight cars were totally wrecked in a collision on the Iowa Central railroad near Mason City recently. The dispatcher at Marshalltown was at fault, for getting the wild train that was running north from Marshalltown.

The Citizens' Bank block at Ligonier, Ind., and five adjoining brick buildings were burned with their contents the other day. Jacobs & Co., bankers, and Jacob Baum, groceries, were the heaviest losers. Total loss aggregates $70,000; insurance, $35,000.

CAPTAIN A. H. BOGARDUS, of Elkhart, Ill., the champion wing shot of the world, says he will not again compete for championship honors. Advancing years and domestic affliction are the reason.

The Standard Oil Company has commenced preliminary work for the building of an immense pipe line from Lima, O., to Chicago, a distance of over 200 miles, for the purpose of transporting oil, both crude and refined, to the Western metropolis.

GEORGE H. DELANEY, a stockman of Oklahoma, and some of his cowboys are reported to have murdered three squatters and a woman. A deputy United States marshal has been searching for Delaney. A report existed that citizens had caught two of the cowboys and lynched them.

D. R. BRIERLY & Co., traders on the Chicago regular and open boards of trade, have failed. Brierly had recently cut a wide swath on the big board as a plunger in corn.

It was reported at St. Louis on the 7th that the bitter rate war which had been waged between the Chicago & Alton and the Wabash Eastern roads had been settled and that prices would be advanced to nearly the rates which prevailed before the war began. The figures agreed upon between St. Louis and Chicago were: 38.28.18, 14 and 9 for the five classes, and $22.50 per car for live stock.

AFTER important evidence in rebuttal, the tally sheet trial at Columbus, O., on the 7th was brought to a stop by the non-appearance of Myers, who was wanted as a witness. The court issued an attachment for him. His disappearance created excitement bordering on a sensation.

A SHARP shock of earthquake was felt at Los Angeles, Cal., on the 7th, being the severest for eighteen years. No damage was done, but houses were badly shaken and people ran into the streets in fright.

A DISPATCH from Elko, Nev., of the 5th says that the east bound passenger train on the Central Pacific had been wrecked at Fenelon the previous night with fatal results. Cause, broken rail.

ROBERT L. CARUTHERS, the well-known base ball pitcher, was married in Chicago the other night to Miss Mamie Danks.

A CATTLE KING'S CRIME.
Squatters Killed and Their Houses Burned by Cowboys in Oklahoma.
by Cowboys in Oklahoma.

WICHITA, Kan., March 8.—Deputy United States Marshal Wood, who arrived yesterday from the west end of the Cherokee Strip looking for George H. Delaney, a cattle king of the Strip, states that three settlers named Albert Quinn, John Antwerp, and Thomas George, who had been living in No-Man's-Land for over a year, when the Oklahoma agitation commenced concluded they would get in readiness to move to Oklahoma proper when that country was opened and accordingly some weeks ago with their families moved as they supposed to the line of No-Man's-Land and erected huts not thinking they were in the Cherokee Strip.

A few days ago some cowboys came along and finding the huts on the land a quarter of a mile east of the line ordered them to move back to No-Man's-Land. They refused to act according to commands and the cowboys after some words left. Last Saturday Delaney, the cattleman interested in the case, came to the huts accompanied by a dozen cowboys and ordered the men and families to remove immediately. They refused to do so.

A shooting match followed, in which the three men, Mrs. Antwerp and one cowboy were killed. The two women left and five children were spared and went back into No-Man's-Land. The torch was applied to the huts and they were burned, together with the corpses of the offenders.

Woods claims that Delaney has been tracked to Wellington and Winfield, and he is now in this city. The police and denuties are all on the look out. Delaney is said to be quite wealthy, having been robbing the Indians for twenty years. He is said to be connected with a number of shooting scrapes and some almost as horrible as the last. He is said to be a very hard man and the deputy does not seem anxious to find him when placed at a disadvantage.

KANSAS CITY, March 8.—A Times
special
KANSAS CITY, March 8.—A Times special from Wichita, Kan., says Deputy Marshal Wood, who arrived here yesterday from the western part of the Cherokee strip, reports a horrible massacre in that country last Saturday. It seems that three settlers named Albert Quinn, John Antwerp and Thomas George were living in the eastern part of No-Man's-Land. At the time of the Oklahoma agitation they moved (as they thought) to a point a short distance west of the territory line, and built huts. Some time afterwards, some cow-boys ordered them off, saying they were in the territory, nearly a mile east of No Man's Land. They refused to move back, and on last Saturday Geo. Delaney, a aranchman of the Cherokee strip, rode up to the huts, accompanied by about a dozen of his cow-boys, and again ordered them off. They refused to do so, and a general shooting followed, in which the three settlers, Mrs. Antwerp and one cowboy were killed. The other two women and five children were spared and went back to No Man's Land. Marshal Wood says he has traced Delaney to Wellinston and Winfield, and he now thinks that Delaney is here. Delaney is a very tough character, having been in several shooting scrapes before.

The great Berlin cathedral, in which rests the body of the late German emperor, is to be kept open to the public from 8 o'clock in the morning until 10 in the evening. lewis-edwards-jessup-1888-10-14.A12:
LYNCHING IN GEORGIA.
How Colored Men Are Treated in the Empire State of the South.
ATLANTA, Ga., Oct. 17.—Recently the news came of the cruel lynching of a colored man in Jessup, Ga., by a mob of white Democrats. The facts show that this lynching was wholly indefensible. Under great provocation and in self-defense the colored porter of a hotel killed the landlord, over two years ago. A jury of white men was impaneled and a trial had, resulting, of course, in the conviction of the colored man, but even this white jury added to their verdict of guilty a "recommendation of mercy," the legal effect of which was to make the punishment imprisonment for life and not hanging. The white judge was so displeased with the verdict of guilty that he promptly set the verdict aside and granted the colored man a new trial. On the 15th instant the second trial was to take place, and knowing full well the evidence would compel a verdict of not guilty. a Democratic white mob proceeded to the jail and riddled the poor, defenseless colored man with bullets; and yet there is no terrorism in Georgia.

Only a short while ago the negroes in another county in this State petitioned the court to place a few of their names in the jury-box, and in Dodge county, Georgia, it was done. That night a masked white mob of Democrats rode to the house of the clerk of the court, seized the jury list and destroyed it. In Liberty county (a travesty on the name), the colored voters outnumber the whites by five to one, and ever since the war a colored man has been sent from Liberty county to the Legislature, but in the election the 3d inst., "Lecturer" Crawford, the name of the colored candidate, was defeated—l.a., counted out—and the Democrat declared elected. Crawford is the colored man who, as a member of the last Georgia Legislature, shortly after the passage of the "Glenn bill," making it a penal offense to co-educate the races, favored the passage of a law to pension ex-confederate disabled soldiers, saying: "My race will not get any benefit under this law." At the very next election the Democrats "count out" this magnanimous colored member, who had displayed such a very generous spirit towards the indigent soldiers in gray! General Harrison, in one of his excellent speeches, insisted that, whatever differences or inequalities there might exist in wealth, intelligence and education, yet before the law there should be absolute justice and equality; and this noble sentiment could be studied and practiced with effect in Georgia.
