TAYLOR, Texas, Oct. 16 —Joe Joiner, a negro, was lynched at Hulto, near here, yesterday. Joiner attempted an assault upon a 12 years old white girl, and was arrested by the sheriff. On the road to the jail a mob of masked men seized the prisoner and hanged him to a tree.

ST. ALBANS, Vt., Oct. 17.—Horace Ellsworth's house and barn in East Fletcher were burned yesterday with all the hay and grain in the barn. Some farm machinery was also destroyed. Although the two buildings were some distance apart they were both found on fire at the same time.

KNOXVILLE, Tenn., Oct. 13.—At Johnson City, 100 miles east of this city, 14 guests of Smith's hotel are reported to have been poisoned by something eaten at supper. Three have died and several others it is feared cannot recover. It is believed that the poison was administered intentionally by some one unfriendly to the proprietor.

JESSUP, Ga., Oct. 16.—In January, 1886, Robert J. Smith of this city was murdered by Lewis Edwards, colored, who was sentenced to life imprisonment. His attorney secured a new trial and the case was to have begun yesterday. Sunday night the sheriff brought Edwards here, and at 3 o'clock Monday morning a party of masked men entered the jail and shot him dead.

WILKES BARRE, Penn., Oct. 16.—Another terrible accident occurred on the Lehigh Valley Railroad this morning. A construction train was unloading ties at the Tamand siding, near Lost Creek, on the Pottsville branch, when a fast Pennsylvania freight came along and dashed into the construction cars. Of the 40 Hungarians who were at work unloading ties, 6 were killed outright, and 26 injured. A brakeman on the Pennsylvania train was killed outright. Twenty of the freight cars were wrecked. It was 3 hours before help could be procured and during that time the injured lost so much blood that it is feared many of them will die.

NEW YORK, Oct. 11.—There was another large fire this morning in Greenpoint, which will result in a damage of $200,000, besides the injuring of several brave firemen. From what can be learned the fire broke out early this morning on board the steamer Navis, which was lying at the wharf of Pennsylvania and Scranton Coal Co., at the foot of North Tenth St. The flames then extended to other vessels and although three alarms were sent out to which the firemen quickly responded, the fire spread with surprising rapidity, communicating from the vessels to the pier, and from there to shipping department and buildings of the Standard Oil Works. Three vessels and the steamer Navis were all partially burned. An explosion of an oil well severely burned 6 firemen, besides injuring some of them otherwise. There were about 5,000 barrels of oil burned.

QUINCY, Ill., Oct. 11.—A grand stand was erected here yesterday to accommodate 5,000 people who were to witness the display of fireworks, "The Bombardment of Alexandria." The amphitheatre was crowded with people, and probably not less than 6,000 were massed upon the seats. Scarcely had the first rocket been fired when the supports at the west end of the structure gave away, the 800 feet of seats sidled over and the vast multitude were hurled upon the ground and buried in the mass of lumber which fell upon them. The air was filled with the cries and moans of the injured, while the panic stricken sought escape from the debris. With the descent of the platform the electric lights, which were to light the grounds, but which were extinguished to aid the display, were incapacitated for service and the darkness of the scene added to its terrors. As the lights from the pyrotechnics lighted up the place the able bodied sought their friends, while the more humane began the work of aiding the injured. Some say that fully 500 people were hurt, and this is probably true, but 150 will doubtless include those who were injured at all seriously.

WILKESBARRE, Penn., Oct 11.—Throughout the night the depot was throughed by hundreds of persons suffering untold agony over the uncertainty, the railroad people refusing to give any information regarding the accident.

The throng was loud in its denunciation of the company for refusing this information and causing needless suffering. Many persons wanted to go to the scene of the disaster, and endeavored to charter a locomotive, but the favor could not be obtained. After waiting from 10 to 3 in the morning many persons took the south bound train, which passed here at 3:10, and went to the scene of the accident.

It was there learned that the third section of the excursion train had stood on the track a few hundred yards from Mud Run, waiting for sections ahead to get out of the way. A flagman some say, had been sent back with a lantern to guard the train from the rear. Suddenly the passengers on the platform saw a train approaching at a high rate of speed. Several saw the danger and jumped and escaped. There was a frightful crash and the engine plunged her full length into the train. The shock drove the rear car through the next one for two-thirds its length, and the second car was forced into the third. Not a single person escaped from the rear car. The second was crowded with maimed and bleeding bodies, and the third had but few passengers who escaped. When the steam and smoke cleared from the rear car its awful sights were revealed. The timbers were crushed and wrenched, while on all sides hung mangled bodies and limbs. The few bodies which were not mangled, were burned and scalded by the steam, and little remained in the car which bore human semblance.

When the shock of the crash had subsided, the uninjured began to do what could be done for their unfortunate companions. The St. Francis Pioneer Corps, who were on the train, plied with zeal the broad axes which were meant for holiday occasions. They were but little adapted to the work and were soon useless. To free the bodies in the rear car the train men attached a locomotive to the wrecked engine and started to pull it from the wreck. The first movement of the shattered wreck brought from the wounded such awful cries that friends ordered the engineer to desist on pain of his life. The few houses about the spot were thrown open to the suffering, and bonfires lighted to aid the work of relief.

The passengers give many different accounts of the probable cause of the accident, some attributing it to the negligence of the flag man in not going back with the red light, others saying the fourth section which ran into the third had no air brakes. The latest figures give the skilled at 55 and the injured at 40. The scenes at the depot when the trains with the dead and wounded were expected were heartrending in the extreme. Several hundred persons assembled, and it was pitiful to see the parents looking for their children. and husbands for their wives and friends for friends.

H. F. SICKLE Colonel commanding 2d sub-district, Geor
LYNCHED IN JAIL.
From the Jesup, Ga., Sentinel.
From the Jesup, Ga., Sentinel.

Louis Edwards was tried and convicted at the March term of Wayne superior court, 1887, for the murder of R. J. Smith. The jury recommended him to the mercy of the court, and Judge Atkinson sentenced him to imprisonment for life. His counsel, Messrs. E. D. Graham and S. W. Hitch subsequently made motion for a new trial, and it was granted. Last Sunday Sheriff J. D. Robinson went to Greston on the East Tennessee, Virginia and Georgia railway, where Edwards has been confined since March, 1887, to bring him back for a new trial. The sheriff returned with the prisoner on the 11:15 train Sunday night, and was met at the train by a guard he had arranged. The prisoner was quietly conveyed to the jail, and after cautioning the guard to be vigilant the sheriff went to the Jesup house and retired.

About 3 o'clock the guard was overpowed and the prisoner lynched. Below we give the evidence before the coroner's jury: Messrs. T. Reddish, T. J. Lundy, T. A. Floyd and J. A. Wheeler, who composed the guard, and Sheriff Robinson were sworn.

LUNDY'S STATEMENT.

"About 3 o'clock a party of men surprised and arrested us. With presented pistols they demanded hands up. We obeyed the command. They then demanded the jail keys. They were masked, and had rags over their heads. I did not know any of them. I was near the man who picked the keys from off the ground. Did not know how came them there. I was terribly excited. I did not recognize any voice. They captured our guns. A guard was left over us, while others went into the jail. The prisoner was killed, and the parties went away without saying anything else. We then sent for the sheriff."

"Did you know who had the keys?"
"No, sir; I was under the impression that the sheriff had them."

"How many men were there in the crowd?"
"I could not say; I saw ten or twelve."

"How were they armed?"
"With pistols."

"How were they disguised?"
"They had on oil cloth and rags over their faces."

THOMAS REDDISH'S STATEMENT.

"We were sitting around a fire outside the jail yard. The first thing that drew my attention was the growling of a dog. About this time six or seven men rushed upon us with drawn pistols, and commanded, 'Hand up and surrender.' They captured our arms and left us powerless, and we obeyed the command. Two of the men gathered Mr. Wheeler and began kicking him and demanding the keys. He told them that he knew nothing of the keys. One also caught hold of me and began jerking me around. Just at this moment they found the keys on the ground. I am not positive, but I think only three men went into the jail. As many as five stood guard over us, one pointing a pistol at my breast, and saying: 'If you move I'll kill you.' I said: 'I surrender, and don't shoot me.' I heard those who went into the jail. Heard a noise like breaking of the jail door, and thought it was. After the shooting, they came out and went away. I am confident there were eight or nine, and may have been more."

SHERIFF J. D. ROBINSON'S STATEMENT.

"I went to Greston after prisoner Sunday, and arrived back here Sunday night between 11 and 12 o'clock. I was met at the train by the guard. I took the prisoner to the jail at once. After placing him in jail I cautioned the guard to be vigilant, and went to the Jesup house and went to bed, but had I known there would be trouble I never would have left the jail, although tired and worn out. I dug a hole with my foot near a pine sapling, dropped the keys in there, and covered them up. I placed them there so if they were demanded of the guard none of them would have them."

"Who did you ask to meet you at the train?"

"I requested Reddish and Austin to meet me at the train."

"Was there much of a crowd at the depot upon the arrival of the train?"

"There were a good many, but I saw or head nothing unusual. As I dismounted from the car, some one said, 'Hulloa, Mr. Sheriff.' I made no reply, but went at once to the jail, and deposited the prisoner."

The following is the verdict of the jury:

We, the jury aforesaid, upon oath say that Louis Edwards, of said county, did on the 15th day of October, 1888, come to his death by a number of leaden balls being shot into his body by an unlawful mob, with malice aforethought, the said mob unknown to said jury.
lewis-edwards-jessup-1888-10-14.A18:
KILLED IN HIS CELL.
A Murderer in Georgia Shot by a Gang of Masked Men.
Masked men wreaked vengeance upon a murderer at Jessup, Ga. In January, 1886, Robert J. Smith, proprietor of the Sunny-Side House in that place, was shot and instantly killed by Lewis Edwards, a negro porter of the Commercial House. He narrowly escaped lynch law at that time. He was convicted of murder and sentenced to a life imprisonment. His attorney secured a new trial, and he was to have been put on the stand again. The jail guards were overpowered by a body of masked men, who took the keys, entered the prisoner's cell, and shot twelve bullets into his body.

LEWIS C. LANE KILLED.
SHOT DEAD WHILE UNDER ARREST AT QUITMAN.
A Savannah Traveling Man Commits an Assault Upon a Young Lady and is Slain on His Way to Jail by His Victim's Father—The Sheriff Trying to Save His Prisoner from Lynchers.

Lewis C. Lane, a well-known traveling man of this city, was shot and killed near Quitman last night.

A Quitman dispatch to the Morning News says that Lane was arrested at Quitman Sunday night on a charge of assaulting with intent to rape a young lady of that place. He was locked up, but the sheriff fearing that an attempt would be made last night to lynch him, started yesterday afternoon to take him to Thomasville for safe keeping.

KILLED BY THE GIRL'S FATHER.

He had gone about five miles out of town when they were overtaken by the young lady's father. A fight ensued, and Lane was shot and killed.

Lane's former home was Quitman, and his mother lives there now. The prominence of the parties and the character of the crime have caused intense excitement in Quitman, where Lane was well known.

THE VICTIM OF HIS ASSAULT.

The Morning News was unable to get full particulars of the affair from Quitman last night, but a Waycross special gives the following:

Lewis C. Lane committed an assault upon Miss Yerington at Quitman. While being transferred to Thomasville jail about 7:30 o'clock to-night to prevent being lynched, he was overtaken and shot by the girl's father.

Lane was well known in Savannah. He was a member of Post D of the Travelers' Protective association, and was popular among traveling men and well liked by everybody who knew him. He has lived in Savannah for four years and boarded while here at No. 156 State street. He left Savannah two weeks ago to go out on the road. Saturday night he went to Quitman to spend Sunday at his old home. He was about 26 years old and unmarried. His friends here were surprised at the report of his crime and his tragic death.
louis-lane-1888-07.A3:
LEWIS LANE'S BAD DEED.
THE STORY OF HIS ASSAULT ON
MISSOURI ARRINGTON.
The Sunday Evening Drive That Led to Lane's Death — The Girl's Story of the Assault — Saved by the Lightning's Flash—Arrington's Interview With Lane at His Mother's Home—The Pursuit of the Sheriff and the Shooting in the Woods.

Quitman is just getting over the excitement of the Lane sensation. A Quitman gentleman who was in the city yesterday said that while the affair is deeply regretted by the people there, public sentiment was against Lane. The coroner's jury even rendered a verdict of justifiable killing.

Lane's mother has been unconscious since the death of her son, and it is feared that she will not recover. Young Lane was buried in the Quitman cemetery Tuesday afternoon. Those who knew him well say that there was not a young man in Quitman who was thought more of than he, and his friends cannot account for the act which led to his death. Saturday afternoon when he arrived at Quitman he bought a quart of whiskey, but his friends who were with him just before he started out to drive with Missouri Arrington, said that he had not been drinking, and his companion in the dr ve corroborated the story. Mr. R. E. L. McFarlin of Quitman was in the city yesterday, and he gave a MORNING NEWS reporter the story of the crime.

THE GIRL'S STORY.

In her statement before the coroner's jury the girl said that when she and Lane had gone about a mile and a half out of the town he asked her to kiss him. She refused, and said that she would get out of the buggy and go home with some friends whom they had just passed. Lane would not allow her to get out and drove into a swamp by a by-road and repeated his request with some warmth. Again she refused, and this time attempted to jump out of the buggy. As she did so Lane caught her by the throat, tearing her dress from her neck. Placing one hand over her mouth he held her fast in the buggy.

SAVED BY THE LIGHTNING'S FLASH.

A shower was coming up, and just then a sharp flash of lightning frightened the horse, and the animal sprang forward, throwing Lane out of the buggy. The girl followed him and started home on foot, but her companion promised her that he would not insult her again, and finally persuaded her to
Lane out of the buggy. The girl followed him and started home on foot, but her companion promised her that he would not insult her again, and finally persuaded her to get into the buggy and drive back to town with him. On the way he told her that he would kill her if she told her father what had happened, and she replied that she would tell him or die. After taking her home, young Lane went to his own home to change his clothes, and said that he was going to leave town on the next train. He had not more than changed his clothing, when the father of the girl, accompanied by a friend, were hunting him with shotguns. They banged on the door at his mother's residence. She answered the call, and after finding out their errand begged them not to interfere with her son.

AT LANE'S HOME.

Mrs. Lane is an elderly woman and quite feeble. The enraged father told her that he had come to kill Lane, and he intended to do it. Just then young Lane came out of the house, but his mother threw herself between the men and her son and prevented his being killed on the spot. In a minute or two Lane stepped up to the girl's father and told him that he loved his daughter and would marry her if he would consent. What he had done in the afternoon, he said, was to test her virtue. It was reported that Arrington, after some talk, consented, but he afterward denied that he had ever thought of such a thing.

LANE'S ARREST.

The two men finally left. A warrant was issued for Lane charging him with an attempted felonious assault upon the girl. He was arrested, but gave bond and was released. On Monday morning he was re-arrested and was this time charged with having committed the assault and was sent to jail. His mother and relatives, fearing that something might befall him, urged Sheriff McNeill to take him to Thomasville. During the entire forenoon and the greater part of Monday afternoon the friends and relatives of Lane were preparing for his safe trip to Thomasville. Relays of horses were stationed at every six mile post between Quitman and Thomasville. Between 4 and 5 o'clock Lane was quietly taken from the Quitman jail and, guarded by an officer, rode rapidly down the road.

IN PURSUIT OF THE SHERIFF.

The father of the girl had been apprised in the meantime of Lane's departure, and with a friend and relative mounted a couple of horses and started out to hire a third horse. This they failed to do. The stable-
in the meantime of Lane's departure, and with a friend and relative mounted a couple of horses and started out to hire a third horse. This they failed to do. The stableman to whom they went refused to hire them the horses.

The pursuers flaunted their pistols in the air and said that they were going to have a horse. Going to a stall, they cut a rein in two and slinging on a bridle and saddle, mounted and galloped off in pursuit of the officers and young Lane. The men were armed to the teeth.

TRYING TO ELUDE PURSUIT.

The officers who were in charge of Lane, fearing that they might be pursued, left the public road and followed a trail some distance, hoping to elude their pursuers. After waiting some minutes without hearing or seeing anybody, the sheriff sent his deputy back to where they had turned out of the public road to see if they were followed. The deputy had not more than reached the turning off point when he was startled by the clatter of horses feet. Riding into the road he saw three armed men riding rapidly after them. When the men saw him they ordered the deputy to halt, and drawing their revolvers, forced him to tell them where the prisoner was. This done they rode together to the spot where the sheriff and young Lane were.

THE FATAL SHOT.

The enraged father dismounted and leveled his shotgun at Lane who turned to the sheriff for protection. Finding himself overpowered, the sheriff turned his back, and in an instant more young Lane was staggering behind him with a ghastly wound in his back.

"For God sake turn me, loose, Lane," said the sheriff, as he tried to get away from him. The men stood a moment, when Lane, then mortally wounded, drew a revolver and, taking deliberate aim over the sheriff's shoulder, fired at his assailant. His aim was not true, and the ball went wild. Exhausted from his wound, he fell to the ground. Arrington had not finished his work yet. He sprung the trigger, and before anybody could interfere, he had placed the gun to the young man's left ear and deliberately blew his head off.

louis-lane-1888-07.A4:
The Lane Homicide.

Editor Morning News: Three days ago the sad intelligence reached here of the untimely end of Louis C. Lane, a young man in the very prime of life, shot down and killed without a hearing, without process of law and while in custody of the sheriff of the county.

Can it be possible that human life can be taken without at least first seeing whether the laws of the country will not afford the agreed party justice? If so, what will prevent a man from killing another for an offense wrongfully charged against him? Lynch law must be stopped, and it behooves every citizen to see to it that a party or the parties who take the law into their own hands are properly dealt with. CITIZEN.

A Brother-in-Law of Arrington Warned to Leave the County.

QUITMAN, GA., Aug. 3.—M. H. Williams,
a brother-in-law of W. T. Arrington, the
man who killed Lewis Lane, received on
Wednesday of this week, through the Quit-
man postoffice, an anonymous letter signed
"Many Friends of Lane," telling him to
leave town in twenty-four hours, or he
wouldn't sleep well. Williams is ignorant

The general opinion here seems to be that

A CARD FROM LANE'S FRIENDS.

The Quitman Free Press, which came
out this afternoon, publishes the following:

QUITMAN, GA., Aug. 2, 1888.

To the Editor of the Quitman Free Press:
The relatives of L. C. Lane, deceased, having
been informed that on Wednesday last M. H.
Williams received an anonymous letter notifying
him to leave town in twenty-four hours, we
beg space in the columns of your valuable
paper to denounce in unmeasured terms said
letter and we further state that its author is not
a friend of Lane's, but is an ignominious enemy.

The excitement over the case was dying out, but the anonymous letter which Mr. Williams received has created a little ripple. Arrington and Henry Williams are still out of town. They are keeping out of the sheriff's way until the question of bond has been settled.

Their lawyers will argue an application for bond before Judge Hansell at Thomasville next Monday.

THOMASVILLE, GA., Aug. 6.—Judge Hansell, in chambers to-day, heard argument for bail in the case of Arrington and Williams, charged with the murder of Lewis Lane. Without going into the merits of the case, the Judge allowed bail in $5,000 each, which was promptly given, and the prisoners turned loose to appear at the next term of Brooks county superior court for trial. Both prisoners came to Thomasville and reported to Sheriff Hurst, who turned them over to the sheriff of Brooks county, whereupon they furnished bonds.

QUITMAN, GA., Dec. 8.—Brooks superior court begins to-morrow, and if all the cases on the docket are tried, it will prove an interesting term. The Arrington-Lane case will probably be tried. Andrew Patterson, the young negro boy, who was convicted and sentenced to hang at the last term of court, will have another trial next week.

Quitman is a little agitated just now over the question of a public school to be supported by taxation. If it is, a lively canvass will ensue, as its supporters and opposers are pretty evenly divided.

Quitman's cotton receipts are holding up remarkably well for so late in the season. There was an extra spurt this week and receipts are wonderful for the time of year.

George Preaches, the alleged murderer of Henry Fushee, the colored man found dead near Fort Clinch on Sunday of last week, was arrested at Callaghan Wednesday and taken to Fernandina. Thursday he had a preliminary trial before Judge H. S. Baker, before whom he made the statement, in which he said that James Horatio killed Fushee while the trio were walking along in single file. Judge Baker committed Preaches to jail to await his trial at the next term of Nassau Circuit Court. On Friday, February 17, as Henry returned home from a ride in the neighborhood, he gave his horse to a boy to unsaddle and feed, and attempting to walk in his door was shot down by unknown parties. His wife, who was sitting in the door, received part of the load intended for her husband and was killed instantly. Henry was seriously wounded, three buckshot taking effect in his body, but was not killed.

mack-henry-1888-02-11.A2:
LAKE CITY AS A CRITIC.
The Request for Dr. Kost's Resignation Excites Comment.
LAKE CITY ELA July 30 A district
The decision of the board of trustees of the college and experiment station, in the case of Dr. Kost, is the topic of conversation. Criticism of the board is freely indulged in. They declare in words that none of the charges were sustained, yet they say Kost has committed many serious indiscretions in speech and in acts which impair his usefulness at the station, and demand his resignation, which has the effect of finding him guilty of the charges, thus imposing upon him the most extreme penalty in their power. Kost either guilty or not guilty. If guilty, he should have been dismissed from the service; if not guilty, he should have been vindicated and retained in his position as director. But the demand for the resignation of Drs. Maxwell and Appell and Profs. Curtis and Ashmood is a rather curious one. The action of the trustees must have been based on the ground that the professors had been caught in bad company, for, as far as known, there were no charges against either of them. If they were elected by the board and held their positions by virtue of this election, it is difficult to understand why they were all requested to resign, unless they had shown themselves to be incompetent and unworthy. Yet they received the same penalty Kost received, which gives room for comment and criticism.

The impression here is that Dr. Maxwell not only made good his charges, with sufficient proofs, but presented his case in an able, manly way, so that the character of the college and the faculty, which was in great danger, by reason of the trouble with Dr. Kost, has been vindicated. The interest of the state and the good of the college required an immediate change in the directorship of the experiment station, which has been brought about by the timely interposition of Dr. Maxwell's course in the matter.

Prof. W. N. Phillips, a highly recommended gentleman of Chase City, Va., and a graduate of Richmond college, has been elected principal of the Peabody high school at this place, vice Prof. H. Merz, resigned.

Mack Henry (colored) was shot and killed by some unknown assassin near Ichetuchnee Friday. It was only about three months ago that his wife was shot and killed at the same place in the same clandestine manner. Efforts are being made to apprehend the guilty party.

OUTRAGE AND LYNCHING.
The Wife of a Farmer the Victim of a Black Brute.
The Wife of a Farmer the Victim of a Black Brute.

BLACKSHEAR, GA., Nov. 2. At 7 o'clock this morning a negro man, named Macum Marshall, entered the house of Mrs. Henry Howard, the wife of a respectable farmer, and, in the absence of her husband, forced her to submit to his demand. After accomplishing his purpose he fled to a swamp about a mile from the house, and there remained until captured by a posse of armed men, who avenged the wronged woman by lynching the criminal.

Captain Joshua Slocum of the wrecked bark Aquidneck, who is on his way in a thirty-foot canoe from Rio Grande del Sur to Washington, a distance of 4,500 miles, has been sighted off the South Carolina coast.

Lord Tennyson is seriously ill.

Germany will strengthen her fleet.

The Prussian Minister at the Vatican has been recalled.

The Czar and Czarina were injured in the recent accident.

mosier.A2:
[From The Safety Valve.]
Fred Post, the Dare-Devil Engineer.
"One of the best and withal the most daring engineers on the Union Pacific was, and still is, Fred Post of Cheyenne," said one of the Rocky Mountain delegates to the recent Convention of the Brotherhood in Chicago.

"When Post is on an engine he doesn't seem to know what fear is. He has had passenger engines dozens of times, but it wouldn't be long before he would make some reckless run, just for the deviltry of the thing, and then he would be sent back to a freight run again. It seems to be almost impossible for him to run on schedule time—he isn't happy unless he can let her out for every revolution there is in her. One of his flash runs was from Cheyenne to Greeley, Col., and over to Fort Collins, and then back again to Cheyenne. A special was made up in Cheyenne to go over to Fort Collins after a murderer named Moshier. Post was ordered to take 'old 400,' the fastest engine on the road, and a 'way-car' was attached for the party of officers. Among the passengers were Sheriff Sharpless, several deputy sheriffs, some newspaper men, a few prominent citizens, and Mr. Deuel, the Superintendent of the road. The train had the right of way, and everything was ordered on the side tracks until the special passed. You see, the case was an important one, and, as it resulted in one of the most famous lynchings ever known in the far West, is worth telling.

The man Moshier was a low-lived assassin who had shot several people. He was tramping over the lonely trail between Cheyenne and the Black Hills one day when he met a freighter, who picked him up and fed him, and let him ride to Cheyenne. The freighter also had a passenger in a young man who had lived near Fort Laramie, and who was on his way to his former home in Iowa. The outfit consisted of a big 'prairie schooner,' a trail wagon, and sixteen mules. When the end of the journey was reached the party camped on the prairie, about three miles from Cheyenne, and near the Government post of Fort Russell. The freighter intended to come into town early the next morning, load the wagons with goods for the Black Hills, and come back in the evening to the same camping ground. The mules were turned out to graze on the rich upland grass, and, as the night was threatening, all three men spread their blankets in one of the big wagons, which, like all freight wagons, was cavered with canvas, stretched over high bows. A man standing in the wagon couldn't touch the canvas top overhead, so they make a pretty comfortable prairie bedroom. During the night Moshier got up, and, taking an axe, struck the sleeping freighter a blow on the head. Supposing he had killed him, he next struck the passenger, fracturing his skull. But the
mosier.A3:
was, grappled with the murderer, took the axe away from him, and threw it out of the wagon. Moshier then shot the man three times. A soldier at the post going out on a duck hunt passed not far from the wagons and heard the shooting. Returning to the post he obtained assistance, and an investigation resulted in finding the bodies of the two men, but Moshier had fled. The freighter was unconscious, but the passenger, although mortally wounded, was able to make a dying statement to an Episcopal clergyman and to the Prosecuting Attorney. Unfortunately, he didn't know Moshier's name. He died that afternoon. It came out that the murderer intended to kill his benefactor and his fellow-passenger, dump their bodies into one of the wagons, hook up the mules, and drive off with the whole outfit. At night he would bury the bodies, build a big camp-fire over their graves to hide the spot, and take the wagons and mules to some part of the country where he could sell the outfit, which was worth about $3000.

"The people were indignant over the dastardly crime, and the other freighters were wild with anger. Big rewards were offered by the Territory and by private citizens, and hundreds of men galloped over the country in search of the murderer. Three days afterward, and much to the surprise of everybody, the freighter regained consciousness. He told who the murderer was, and then many people knew the man they were pursuing. Several days afterward he was captured by Sheriff Sweene, of Fort Collins, Colorado.

"The Sheriff of Cheyenne feared a lynching, and so the special train was secretly made up to go to Fort Collins, and get back before daylight. Engineer Post was in his element, for he was expected to make fast time. The section of the road between Greeley and Fort Collins was new and rough. The ties were laid on the dirt, without any rock ballast, and recent heavy rains had made the ground soft. The way Post ran 'old 400' was an example of his recklessness. I always believed he must have hung a weight on the safety valve. There were stationary seats on each side of the way-car, and a few common chairs sat on the floor. In one half of the car were bunks for the use of the train-men, and the Sheriff and the Superintendent laid down on these to sleep. Post had about regained his standing from his last escapade, and had a chance to distinguish himself in the presence of the Superintendent, but, instead of running with express speed, he turned her over for every stroke there was in her. 'Old 400' plunged into the night hissing and rolling like a demon and a maniac in one. The way-car rolled from side to side so violently that it was impossible to sit on the chairs. Every little while the wheels would strike the end of some rail that was not joined evenly, and the car would give a lurch which threatened to land it in the ditch. While the train was rushing to apparent destruction, Post left the engine and came back into the car a moment, as happy as a man could be. Somebody said something about being turned over, and Post understood it to be a request to 'turn her over.' That suited him, and, returning to the engine, he did 'turn her over.' Heavens! How the engine and its one car rocked and sawayed and lurched! Yet on, faster and faster, they flew over that dangerous track. To add to the excitement of the moment, the men in the car discovered that Post had never been over that branch before. Suddenly the car gave a heavy lurch and there was a sound like a 'thud' in the bunkroom. The Superintendent and the Sheriff had been thrown out of their bunks. The former made his way to the front platform, and, by yelling at the top of his voice, attracted Post's attention.

The rest of the run to Fort Collins was made slower, and when the train got there Post got a jacketing for making such a wild run. The trip gave him quite a reputation at Cheyenne, but he didn't get a passenger engine. Perhaps the railroad people had their own views about such a run as that.

"And Moshier? Oh, they got back to Cheyenne with him just at sunrise Sunday morning. That night seventy-five men marched to the jail like a company of soldiers, broke open the doors, and, in the presence of 2,000 people, hanged the murderer to a telegraph pole in the center of the city. Secretary Morgan, the Secretary of the Territory, and the Mayor of the city made speeches to to the mob, and pleaded with the avengers not to hang the man. The night was cloudless, and a vividly bright moon lit up the faces of the stern lynchers, gave a ghastly hue to the pallid face of the

Thos. Carroll, the officer who arrested Patterson, captured the prisoner at Lance creek, some time in 1885. Patterson escaped from him at Thorp's, on a horse belonging to the latter.

There was offered in evidence a British bulldog revolver taken from the prisoner at the time of his capture; also the Dyer house register, showing that Patterson was in this city July 4, 1884. Defense admitted that the signature was genuine.

Attorney Patterson asked Carroll if his prisoner was not afraid to come to Cheyenne on account of the recent lynching of Mosier. Ruled out.

A CRIMINAL.

Experienced men stoutly aver that the tramp was an old offender. He did not commit a murder simply to escape serving a sentence for petty larceny. He was doubtless wanted elsewhere and feared that the publicity of his trial would cause his detention to answer to a more serious charge than larceny. Then the cunning which he exhibited in changing his trousers and ridding himself of the conspicuous bundle was the action of a man who had been hunted before. He evidently realized that with his curious burden he would soon be recognized and arrested.

THE SIDNEY MEN.

Sheriff Hubanks of Cheyenne county, Neb., arrested a tramp at Sidney yesterday and telegraphed the fact and his man's description to this city. The suspect was six feet tall and spoke English without any accent. Of course it was a case of mistaken identity.

It is said that a Union Pacific brakeman believes he ejected the murderer from a box car near Sidney. If it was the man he escaped and continued eastward.

THE PUBLIC'S THEORY.

Last evening a quite plausible theory was in general circulation. It was to the effect that the man had been captured and placed in the guard house at Fort Russell for safe keeping. The fact that Mosier was taken from custody of Sheriff Sharpless and lynched gave color to this rumor, but there was nothing in it.

TALK OF LYNCHING.

As intimated yesterday morning there is a strong movement on foot to lynch the murderer in the event of his capture. A man who claims to have been present assures THE LEADER that a number of determined men met in a barn in the west end last night and organized a vigilance committee for the express purpose of lynching Vannice's murderer. If the man is captured before the excitement subsides he will surely be hanged at once.

THE FLIGHT.

At present it looks as though the murderer at once set out for the main line of the Union Pacific and boarded a freight for either the east or west, probably the latter. Frank Stanton, who came in from Silver Crown yesterday morning thinks he met the man, and probably did. It is more than likely that the fellow, knowing nothing of the country, at once made for the railway. He might even have come to Cheyenne and boarded a train here. The flight by railway is the popular theory, but there are shrewd men who believe that the murderer is wandering about the country north of Cheyenne. At any rate that region will be thoroughly searched.

THE FUNERAL.

The remains of Mr. Vannice will be interred from the Presbyterian church at 2 o'clock Sunday afternoon. Rev. D. L. Rader, assisted by Revs. Geo. C. Rafter and A. W. Williams, will conduct the services, with the Masonic lodge and A. O. U. W. in charge of all.

THE OLDEST DAUGHTER.

Miss E. E. Vannice, eldest daughter of deceased, was in Laramie at the time of the tragedy, but came at once to comfort her mother and assist in caring for the little ones. She was, of course, horrified to learn of her father's terrible and sudden death. It is learned that Mr. Vannice was insured for $2,000 with the A. O. U. W.

A LITTLE RACE WAR IN TEXAS. Caused by Angry Citizens Hanging the Black Murderer of a White Man.
BRAZORIA, Tex., Oct 18.—The negroes of Brazoria and Fort Beid counties, who outnumber the whites three to one, threaten a general massacre of the whites on account of a lynching that occurred yesterday. Tuesday night Isaac Van Dorn was assassinated by Nat Nathaniel, a negro. Van Dorn was engineer on a plantation Between 10 and 12 o'clock on Monday Nat Nathaniel and two or three other negroes of the neighborhood came to the place and announced their intention to whip a negro boy. Van Dorn objected and ordered them off. The negroes made threats and left. That night Van Dorn was drawing the fire from the furnace when he was shot by the negro, the buckshot striking him in the face and breast, killing him instantly. He fell with his face in the fire. Early Tuesday morning citizens from the surrounding country captured the murderer in Wharton. His captors started with him to the Brazoria jail, but when five miles from Brazoria they were surrounded by infuriated citizens, who wrested the prisoner from them and hanged him.

STATE NEWS.
Items and Comments Culled From State Exchanges.
The cotton crop around the Dodd City section is 25 per cent short of what it was last year.

The corner stone of a new Catholic church was laid at Fort Worth on Sunday with imposing ceremony in the presence of 800 people.

Estacado has been blessed with a fine rain which will do immense good. Crops are looking well and grain is fine. A great many cattle of late are being shipped.

Lucie Greer killed Lizzie Burnes at a festival at Corregon on Saturday night by stabbing her to the heart. The woman died almost instantly. Both parties are colored.

Over 600,000 pounds of wool have been marketed in San Angelo this fall, all of which has found a ready sale at good figures. As many as six buyers have been there at one time, and all the staple is sold as fast as hauled.

Tuesday night Pablo Perez, a ranchero at Brownsville, was asleep in the yard of his son's residence near the court house, when some sneak thief stole $95 in American gold and a watch from him. The thieves also took his clothes and hung them in a neighbor's kitchen.

Wild geese crossed the city last night in many triangular droves, flying low and uttering many of their melancholy plaints. This is considered a sign of weather. Perhaps it is. The question remains however, what sort of weather will follow? It is certain that the geese do not know and do not care much. They "stride the blast, horsed upon the sightless couriers of the air," and make for the nearest corn field like a fly-up-the-creek hunting a fresh minnow hole.—Waco Day.

A number of charitably inclined ladies of Galveston held a meeting Wednesday forenoon, at Eaton chapel, to take action looking to the establishment in that city of a home for indigent old ladies. Temporary organization was effected, and each lady present was appointed a committee of one to solicit subscriptions. It is desired that all who can do so will contribute a certain amount each month. Another meeting will be held at Eaton chapel in November, when permanent organization will be effected.

High toned colored society of Galveston is violently disturbed. Prof. C. J. Waring, principal of the Central colored public school, has skipped the town in disgrace, while one of his subordinate female teachers will soon assume maternal duties without the sanction of marriage vows. Waring stood high among his race, was well educated and a teacher of marked ability, was religiously inclined and was preparing to enter the ministry; but, yielding to unholy passion, is now a fugitive from justice. The school board at a recent meeting declared his place and that of his victim vacant, and elected successors, while charges of the most serious character have been lodged against Waring.

G. A. Levi, of Victoria, who was appointed representative elector vice Hon. E. D. Lynn, received a telegram Tuesday from Chairman N. Webb Finley, of the state democratic executive committee, saying that F. B. Earnest, of Cotulla, who was nominated as Mr. Lynn's alternate, claimed the electorship. Levi, after consulting with Lynn, wired his resignation to Chairman Finley Wednesday morning, but received a telegram in response that his resignation was too late, as the official list of electors had been published. It is said by those who claim to be posted on the question that alternate electors are nominated to serve in case the elector for any reason is unable to cast his vote after election, and that they have no status or right of succession before election.

The lieutenant colonel in command of the post at Piedras Negras received instructions Wednesday from his government to take the evidence in the matter of the attempted abduction of a Mexican deserter from the Texas side by Lieutenant Cabrera, of the Mexican army, and three soldiers, which occurred last May. The attempt to capture the deserter was frustrated by the brave and prompt action of the officers in Eagle Pass, but resulted in the death of one of the Mexican soldiers and the serious wounding of Deputy Sheriff Shad White. This affair created great excitement throughout the two republics at the time, and Captain Munoz, the instigator of the business, and Lieutenant Cabrera, were tried and sent to the penitentiary. Shad White made a claim on the Mexican government, through the United States department of state, for the sum of $20,000 in recompense for his injuries, and it is supposed that this retaking of the evidence, which was all taken before by a commission of the Mexican government, has a bearing on this last issue.

It is predicted that one of the first things the receivers of the Missouri, Kansas and Texas road will do is to complete the Taylor, Bastrop and Houston road to the latter city.

A Wednesday's special from Brazoria says: On Monday night, October 8, Mr. Isaac Vandorn, an estimable young man in this county, was assassinated by a negro named Nat Thaniel. Mr. Vandorn was acting as engineer on his step-father's (B. T. Rowe's) plantation. Between 10 and 12 o'clock of that day Nat Thaniel and two or three other negroes of the neighborhood came on the place and announced their intention to whip a negro boy. About 8 o'clock that night Mr. Vandorn was drawing the fire from the furnace when he was shot by the negro, who was concealed behind a cord of wood which stood near the furnace, the buckshot striking him in the face and breast, killing him instantly, and he fell with his face in the fire.

ANOTHER HOMICIDE.
[Farmerville Gazette.]
Sunday morning news reached town to the effect that Mr. Luther Hayes, a white man about 35 years of age, was shot and killed at Marion last Saturday evening by a negro named Nathan Broadnax. The particulars of this deplorable affair as we learn them are these: It seems that the negro owed Mr. Luther Hayes the sum of $10, and the latter demanded a settlement. This brought about a dispute, during which the negro became very insulting and finally picked up a plank to strike Mr. Hayes; but at this juncture another negro stepped forward and suatched the board from the hands of the assailant, whereupon the latter ran to the rear of Mr. Roark's store and seizing a shot gun loaded with squirrel shot discharged the contents into Mr. Hayes' side from a distance of about 20 feet. After living about six hours the wounded man expired.

The deed was committed under the eye of a number of persons who started out in pursuit of the murderer, but he made his escape. He is about 5 feet 7 inches high, weighs about 150 pounds, has long white teeth in front, is black and about 20 years old. He is still being pursued and we hope that the posse will be successful in effecting his capture.

The deceased leaves a wife and four children to mourn his loss.

In addition to the above, Mr. W. F. Millsaps, who returned home from Farmerville Thursday, says there is considerable excitement in the parish and that further trouble is apprehended. On Monday a party of men who had gone in pursuit of the murderer captured a negro who was implicated in the murder in some way and hung him, afterwards riddling his body with bullets. A posse is still in pursuit of the principal murderer, he having so far eluded them. Deputy Sheriff McGuire received a telegram Thursday, asking him to send assistance to the posse on the Island, it having been thought that the murderer had made his way to this parish. Two deputies were sent but they returned Thursday evening, having failed to meet the posse or gain any clue as to the whereabouts of the murderer. Mr. Millsaps informed the Telegraph that there was a colony of some 300 negroes near Marion who are in the habit of giving much trouble and the opinion prevails that several of their leaders will be killed before the excitement abates. The rumor on the streets here that a deputy sheriff had been killed in attempting to arrest the murderer seems to be without foundation.

BLOOD IN ALABAMA.
A Couple of Senational Murders.
Which Are Brutal Enough to Make the Blood Curdle-A Poorhouse Tragedy.
EUFAULA, Ala., May 16.—[Special.]—At the county poor house, twenty-five miles distant from this place, occurred one of the most horrible murders of which this section has any record. Among the inmates of the poor house were Simon Long and London Walker, both colored, and the latter said to be over one hundred years old. Both have been occupants of the poor house a number of years, and on Sunday night they fell out about a light wood splinter used for lighting their pipes.

Blind Simon, who is said to have a terrible temper, while Walker was asleep, attracted by his breathing approached his bed with an ax, and dealt a murderous blow at him, but falling short of his intent the ax handle broke, and the noise awakening Balker, who surmised what it meant, he got under his bed, but determined on his destruction the blind negro secured another ax, and assaulting Walker, who was too old and feeble to offer resistance or to attempt to escape, he was literally butchered, his head being crushed, and his body chopped to pieces. Blind Simon was arrested, and is now in Clayton jail.

ANOTHER BLOODY STORY.

EUFAULA, Ala., May 16.—[Special.]—News from Abbeville, forty miles below here, today, gives an account of a murder committed on Abbeville creek Saturday. On the day before, Levi Bruner and Raiford Washington, colored, went on a camp fish, and Saturday Levi returned and reported that he and Washington had been assaulted by two men, one white, with revolvers, and while he escaped, he feared that his companion had been killed.

Sunday morning a party went in search of Raiford, who had not appeared, with Levi as the guide. On reaching the point where the two had been fishing blood was found on the ground, while near the water's edge the sand had been scooped up and thrown into the creek, and while dragging the creek opposite where the blood was found a cudgel weighing eight pounds was found, also a broken musket. No tracks were to be found except those of Levi and Washington, and further search discovering the body of the murdered man in the creek, and evidence all pointing to Levi, he was arrested and held.

Another Alabama Tragedy.

DAVISVILLE, Ala., May 14.—[Special.]—Pickens Pendergrass, of this place, was shot and instantly killed by Summer Little, a negro, near Heflin, between sundown and dark Saturday evening. Alfred Newell, his father-in-law, who is implicated in the affair, has been captured and landed in Edwardsville jail. Little is still at large. About forty armed citizens have been scouring the country since the murder, bent on lynching the murderer. The particulars of the affair, as nigh as can be obtained, is as follows:

Saturday Mr. Pendergrass, the victim, accompanied by his brother-in-law, John Smith, and Will Holmes, left here on the afternoon train for Heflin, returning afoot to avoid some high trestles on the railroad. Between here and there they decided to come by a trailway through the mountains, which is nearer. A few miles out from Heflin, in the mountains, they lost their way and went to the negro Summer Little cabins for direction. The negroes, it is thought, regarded the men as suspicious characters, being in an isolated region where it is believed that illicit business is going on among the negroes, and instead of giving the asked for directions the negroes were insulting to the men. This provoked Mr. Pendergrass, and he being slightly intoxicated, used some very plain language, after which the men were lost, as they were started off in the wrong direction from home towards Edmondville. The negroes were very indignant at the language used by Mr. Pendergrass; they armed themselves, one with a double-barrel shot gun and the other with a rifle followed after the three men who were unarmed and overtook them about a half-mile from their house. Alf Newell, who had the shot-gun, made an attack on Pendergrass; as he leveled the gun Holmes grabbed it. Little, who was in the rear of Newell, holding the rifle in one hand, reached around and fired at Pendergrass, the ball taking effect in his neck having struck a small hickory sapling first carried with a piece of the bark, making an ugly wound and killing him instantly. The negro then bid defiance to Smith and Holmes, who were powerless to do anything.

The excitement runs high. There is no doubt but Little will be mobbed if captured, and the people here are determined to find him if possible.

HARDLY SEE HIS WAY CLEAR IN IT.
From the Albany Times.
JUSTICE RUSS bottom ACKNOWLEDGES THAT HE CAN HARDLY SEE HIS WAY CLEAR IN IT.

From the Albany Times.

Our esteemed friend, Justice Russbottom, has sent us a short recital of a case on which he is adjudicating, and which contains some interesting particulars and perplexities of the law that even more learned disciples of jurisprudence may be pleased to consider.

One Jonas Bench, a reputable young gentleman of the dude characteristics from the metropolis, was paying clandestine attention to Miss Malvina Clutterbuck, the beautiful daughter of one of Greene County's most substantial farmers, and in the course of a delicate coquettting match at the Clutterbuck gate on Thursday night, Mr. Bench being outside on the roadway and Miss Clutterbuck being inside, a bull tossed Mr. Bench over the fence, where Mr. Clutterbuck kicked him. The case before Justice Russbottom consists of a complaint against Farmer Clutterbuck for assault, a demand for a process by which the ownership of the bull may be ascertained in order that a suit for damages may be instituted by Mr. Bench, and a counter charge of trespass against Mr. Bench by Mr. Clutterbuck, because of the young gentleman's entrance upon his grounds at the time the bull tossed him. The learned justice admits that the case somewhat puzzles him.

As to the assault by Farmer Clutterbuck, the justice has given to the young man an informal opinion that a city beau must expect to take his life in his hands when he goes clandestinely courting a mountain girl, and he's but a recruit lover who resorts to the courts for redress for any bodily inconvenience arising from his own love-making. He cites all the traditional precedents in romance and history to show that the lover who succeeds is the only lover with whom the world or law or society will have the slightest sympathy, and that in the case of Mr. Bench it were better that he bandaged his wounds in silence and sat for days in arduity than that he should expose himself to contempt and ruin by a suit. He thought that if the young man should cease his visits to Miss Clutterbuck, and proceed no further in his process relative to the owner of the bull, the case against him of forcible entry into Mr. Clutterbuck's grounds might be compromised. The justice is waiting to hear the young gentleman's reply before proceeding to extremities.

"As to the bull matter," writes the justice, "I am constitutionally bound (in my view of duty and according to a literal construction, for I am a literal construction democrat) not to take any action at all, owing to personal interest in the result of the case. The fact is, it's my bull, and he'll wait till—for a long time, before I decide in my own case against myself."

The subject is very complex, but we think on general principles the justice is right on some points, and pretty nearly right on others.

RALEIGH, N. C., May 7—At Carthage, Moore County, Saturday evening, a young man, named McNeill, shot Miss Ida Poe, seriously wounding her. Jealousy is supposed to have been the cause of the shooting. A LADY SHOT.
Jealousy Drives a Young Man to a Desperate Deed-Threats of Lynching.
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]
N. C. May 7 - Much excerite

of Lynching.

[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]

RALEIGH, N. C., May 7.—Much excitement was caused here this morning by news that Miss Ida Poe, a well-known young lady who resides at Fayetteville, had been shot at Carthage and seriously wounded. Miss Poe has a brother in the express office here who left this morning for Carthage. A special this afternoon gives the details of the affair: Miss Poe was visiting her brother-in-law, who keeps a hotel at Carthage. A young man named Robert L. McNeill, son of A. H. McNeill, clerk of Moore County Superior Court, had formerly been an admirer of Miss Poe, and it is said they had been engaged. Saturday night young McNeill went to Shaw's Hotel and asked H. A. Foote to say that he would like to see Miss Poe. Miss Poe was in the parlor with a young man and told Foote she declined to see McNeill. In a moment some one knocked at the parlor door. Miss Poe, thinking it was Foote, opened the door and saw McNeill. The latter said something to her in a low tone, and then shot her without taking the pistol from his pocket. The ball passed through her thigh, passing near a large artery. McNeill at once fled, throwing his pistol to a man named Jones, and shouting, "I shot Miss Ida; but I did it accidentally." A scene of intense excitement followed. A large party of mounted men, well armed, was made up and searched Saturday night and yesterday for McNeill with the avowed intention of lynching him. McNeill is a man of bad character, and stands charged with killing a negro. He ran away and was absent for a year or more. A true bill was found against him. He returned a few weeks ago and gave bail. Jealousy was the cause of his shooting Miss Poe. The indignation against McNeill is high.

Early yesterday morning vigilants went through the house of McNeill's father in desperate search of Bob McNeill. The would-be murderer can cross Drowning creek at only three fords, and all these are guarded. It is suspected that he will try to escape to Texas, as he did after he killed the negro two years ago. It is learned to-night he had made a threat that he would kill Miss Poe and would then kill Dr. Durant.

annual session of the North Carolina Medical Society began this morning at Williams's Hall, Fayetteville—Dr. T. D. Haigh, of Fayetteville, presiding, and Dr. Julian E. Baker, of Tarboro', secretary. Near Davidson College lightning struck the warehouse of John Caldwell and burned it with its contents, causing a loss of $1,200.

The municipal election at Durham yesterday was quite exciting. There were three tickets in the field, headed by John F. Freeland, W. J. Christian, and Thomas C. Oakley respectively for mayor. Oakley was the labor candidate, but many of his pledged friends deserted him and voted for Christian, who was elected.

The people of Monroe are greatly excited by the brutal murder of Policeman John Pearce by a negro named Bill Weddington. There was a row at a negro festival, and Pearce arrested the leader in the disturbance and started to the guard-house with him. A mob of negroes gathered and decided that they would rescue the negro who was under arrest. Weddington with a heavy iron bar in his hand was in the rear of Pearce. Frank Thomas, another negro, armed with a bludgeon, cried out, "Kill him!" Whereupon Weddington with one stroke crushed the skull of Pearce, who soon died, never having regained consciousness. Weddington was arrested at once, and Thomas, who had fled to Charlotte, was also captured. Both are in jail at Monroe. Thomas was tried for murder two years ago and got off. Pearce leaves a wife and four children.

It has been found that there are not enough legal signatures to the petition for the local-option election at Charlotte, and the county commissioners have withdrawn the order for the election.

The Federal Court began to-day at Asheville—Judge Dick presiding.

Reports to the Department of Agriculture from Durham and Orange counties state that the wheat and oats crops are being ruined by the prolonged and unusual drought. The same report says the tobacco-plants look well, and that large crops will be planted.

Mr. Hasten Poe, whose sister, Miss Ida Poe, was shot at Carthage by Robert L. McNeill, returned here to-day. He reports that her wound is not at present regarded as dangerous. No tidings of McNeill can be heard. This morning before daylight the town of Carthage, and particularly the house of McNeill's father, was strongly guarded, if having been rumored that McNeill was back in town in hiding. Search for him continued all last night, with the avowed intention of lynching. There is a belief this afternoon that he has after all gone safely away, and is now in Texas or on his way there for refuge.

North Carolina is rather coming towards the front in the matter of lynching. There has not been a legal execution this year, yet there have been five persons lynched. On the 27th of January Matthew Blouat, John Blount, and Patterson Spruill (all colored) were disposed of at Plymouth by his Honor Judge Lynch, and the same judge had another victim at Washington March 12th in the person of a white man, who boasted that he was the assassin of General Bryan Grimes. The last victim at this date is Frazier, who was disposed of at Washington last Saturday night for the murder of Cox. Of the persons sentenced legally to be hanged there have been the following, the commutations being in every case save one to life imprisonment: Charles F. Jones, Newberne; Lucien Rowe, Durham; James Thomas, Hendersonville; Allen McCarter, Statesville, and Daniel Biggs, Wilmington.

The Wake county Grape-Growers' Association met to-day and beard reports. It is discovered that vineyards west of the city and in this township were not hurt by the frosts of late April, while vineyards east of the city have suffered much damage.

Rev. Dr. C. H. Strickland, of Nashville, Tenn., was this evening called to the pastorate of the First Baptist church of this city. He is a very able man and will receive a $3,000 salary.

Captain E. R. Stamps, president of the Board of Directors of the penitentiary, and Mr. W. J. Hieks, warden of that institution, are now in the Blue-Ridge country inspecting the convict quarters in that section. The penitentiary is greatly cramped for funds and may have to remove from railways some of the convicts whose labor has been furnished free.

Major John Gatling, once so prominent as a lawyer, and who died yesterday morning, was buried this afternoon from Christ church, Rev. Dr. M. M. Marshall conducting the services.

The unfortunate white woman who drowned herself some days ago in Robeson county was a native of Robeson county. She ran away from her husband some months ago, and the greater part of the time wandered here and there.

There has been some dispute as to whether the names of the signers of the petition for a local-option election in Barton's-Creek township, Wake county, were or were not those of bona-fide voters, and so the county commissioners have been considering the matter.

The pea crop in the Goldsboro' section is about all picked. It has been quite remunerative. Next week the land now in peas will be planted in corn or cotton.

The Cape-Fear and Yadkin-Valley railroad make a fine showing in the matter of net earnings for the year ended April 30th. They were $31,188 in excess of those during the previous year.

A great revival is in progress in the Baptist church at Fayetteville. There have been many converts.

It is rather noticeable that the Democratic Convention of Cumberland county did not instruct its delegates as to the man they should support for Governor.

Mrs. Rebecca Long's house, in Richmond county, was burned a night or two ago, causing a loss of $1,500, with no insurance. Raleigh is well represented at the session of the Grand Lodge of Independent Order Odd-Fellows, which met at Greensboro' this morning in the hall of Buena Vista lodge. Grand Representatives Charles M. Busbee and C. B. Edwards are present. Captain W. A. Bobbitt, of Oxford, is grand master.

There were elections yesterday at several towns. At Shelby the Democrats were successful and W. L. Damson was reelected mayor. At Newberne the "Coalition party" carried the day. This is the "Reform party," composed of Democrats and the better class of Republicans which figured so extensively in the campaign of 1886. At Goldsboro' the Democrats were again winners, electing eight of the nine aldermen. At Greensboro' John A. Barringer was elected mayor.

Great fires have raged through the forests in Caldwell and Watauga counties, in a district covering some fifty or sixty square miles. The damage is immense. A great deal of the timber burned is chestnut.

ALEXANDRIA.
robert-j-mcneil-carthage-1888-05-08.A7:
BLAINE CHEERED
AT A REPUBLICAN CONVENTION IN NORTH CAROLINA.
General Observance of Memorial-Day--Miss
Poe's Assailant Heard From--
Personal Notes.
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]
N. G. May 10 - The Republic
RALEIGH, N. C., May 10.—The Republican Convention of the Ninth congressional district met at Asheville to-day. J. W. Bowman was made chairman. Resolutions were unanimously adopted denouncing Cleveland's Administration and favoring the Blair bill. Delegates were elected to the National Convention. All are for Blaine and have no second choice. Every mention of Blaine's name was enthusiastically cheered. W. H. Malone was endorsed for Associate Justice of the Supreme Court. There was no expression of opinion as to Governor or congressman.

Memorial-day was observed to-day at a great number of places in this State—among them Charlotte, Statesville, Greensboro', Fayetteville, Raleigh, Goldsboro', Tarboro', Newberne, Wilmington, and Washington. At the latter place the celebration was extensive, and many thousand people were present. A monument to the Confederate dead was unveiled. It stands in "Confederate Park," beside the river, and is imposing. It is erected by the Ladies' Memorial Association. There was a handsome parade and an address by Hon. D. G. Fowle, of this city, who is a native of Beaufort county. General William Gaston Lewis was chief marshal.

At Newberne there were public exercises at the theatre, at which General Robert Ransom delivered an address on the battle of Fredericksburg, December 13, 1862. After war is there was a procession.

In this city the Granville Grays, Captain W. A. Bobbitt, from Oxford, were participants in the exercises of the day. The visitors were given most hospitable entertainment by the Governor's Guard. This afternoon there was a large assemblage of people at Metropolitan Hall to hear ex-Congressman Risen T. Bennett, of Wadesboro', deliver an address on the life and services of General Junius C. Daniel. Colonel Thomas S. Kenan was chief marshal. There was a parade of the military and the fire department, with many ex-Confederates mounted. Colonel F. H. Cameron was in command of the troops. Much rain fell to-day in all this section of the State, and relieved further danger of the drought, which had already done damage. The rains interfered somewhat with the exercises by preventing the closing exercises at the cemetery.

There was a well-arranged observance of the day at Wilmington, with an imposing parade. Mr. Preston Cumming was chief marshal. After prayer by the chaplain, Rev. Robert Strange, the orator of the day, Mr. Herbert McClammy delivered an address.

The Evangelist Pearson attracts great audiences nightly at Asbeville. People from all that section are attracted by his really wonderful preaching.

The Democrats in a number of counties have given Mr. Cleveland a very hearty endorsement. The fact may be plainly stated that he will get North Carolina's full strength. Some counties have given Governor Scales's administration endorsements. Among these counties is Jones, where it was intimated that there might be some hostility to the Governor on account of his action in the matter of the Atlantic and North Carolina railroad.

It is claimed by some Knights of Labor here that John Nichols, who is the candidate for renomination, and is a Republican who got in two years ago by means of the Knights of Labor vote, must not count on carrying this district again, because he will not get the solid vote of that order, which has also fallen off in numbers, it is said.

There will be a pretty lively contest for the Democratic nomination for Congress in the Third district. Ex-Congressman Wharton J. Green will give Congressman McClainney a tilt.

It was learned to-day that Bob McNeill, the desperate young man who shot Miss Ida Poe at Carthage Saturday evening, was seen yesterday near Darlington, S. C. Telegrams were at once sent to the authorities of towns in that section.

In this county the Democratic primaries were held yesterday. The city went solid for Fowle for Governor. In some townships the delegates go instructed for Alexander. This is done by the Farmer's Alliance, which is strong in this county.
Curtis H. Brogden, of Wayne, is making earnest efforts to secure the Republican nomination for Governor. But that, as was stated weeks ago, goes to Dockery, for whom county after county is instructing its delegates. The Republicans hope that Dockery's membership in the Farmers' Alliance will be a source of strength to him.
The flies have done much damage to unprotected tobacco-plants in Vance county; but it is believed that after all there will be a sufficiency of plants in that section.
The receiver of the State National Bank of this city expects that in the next sixty days a dividend will be declared, but he has no idea as to its amount. He finds the bank's books in a greatly tangled condition.
robert-j-mcneil-carthage-1888-05-08.A8:
Murder and Lynching. Another horrible affair has happened in our State. It was a double tragedy. Mr. Joshua Cox, living at Blount Creek about 16 miles from Washington, was shot and killed by Thomas Frazier last Saturday night. Frazier attempted to escape but was captured and lodged in jail. That night, a crowd of masked men, took the law into their own hands, went to the jail, brought Frazier out, and riddled him with bullets. There were two other men, Wm. B. Adams and John M. Newton, implicated with Frazier in the murder, but they made their escape. They have been declared outlaws and it is thought that they are hiding around in the swamps near Washington. Disgraceful.
Moore county comes to the front with a most unpleasant affair. Bob McNeill, a young man of a family of good standing in the county, called, last Saturday night, at Shaw's Hotel in Carthage. He asked to see Miss Ida Poe, a young lady stopping there, but she refused to see him. He then went to the parlor, and knocked. Miss Poe, who was in the parlor, not thinking it was McNeill, opened the door; when she did, McNeill caught and closed the door behind her. He then asked, "Why have you gone back on me?" "I have not," she replied. McNeill then drew a pistol, pointed it towards her and fired, the ball penetrating her thigh. He immediately ran out, got into a buggy and made his escape.

Miss Poe is a young lady of pleasing manners and belongs to a family of the highest standing. She is a sister of Mr. Hastings Poe, of Raleigh. The wound though very painful is not very serious.

Every effort is being made to capture the jealous rascal. The CHRONICLE hopes that the attempts will be successful and that the law will punish him to its fullest extent.

GENERAL NEWS ITEMS.
—W. A. Potts, who murdered Paul Lincke, has been sentenced to be hanged July 13th.

—Gen. Phil. H. Sheridan still lives, but his condition is more critical than when we last reported.

—John Gowgne, a printer, published at London, in 1443, the earliest English treatise on book-keeping.

—Two thousand tons of steel will be used in the construction of the new American war ship "Maine,"

—Gov. Hill, of New York, has signed a bill abolishing executions by hanging and substituting therefor death by electricity.

—The Press Association of North Carolina will meet at Morehead city July 18th. A full quorum will doubtless be present.

—It has been estimated that during growth Indian corn draws thirty-six times its own weight of water from the soil.

—Dr. Worth, ex-State Treasurer, who is 78 years of age, has so far recovered from his recent critical illness, as to be able to walk about.
—Books with leaves of vellum were invented by Attalus, King of Peorgamus, about 198 B. C., at which time books were in volumes or rolls.

—Get twenty-five cents' worth of unslacked lime and scatter it about your premises in the damp and much shaded places. Don't delay the matter.

—The News says if Kernersville needs anything it is a town hall. There is positively no public place for entertainments or gatherings of the citizens.

—A company has been organized with $100,000,000 of capital to carry out the scheme of the late Lieut. Maury, U. S. N., for opening the Amazon to the trade of the world

—The Pee Dee House in Rockingham, advertising for a good cook and a smart porter, says a good "loaf-er" is preferred for cook. Here's a chance for one of our lamp-post supports.

—President S. B. Alexander requests that all communications be addressed to him at Charlotte, N. C. He is receiving many letters which were mailed to Raleigh and other points.

—Gov. Martin of Kansas has pardoned a man who killed his wife several years ago while under the influence of liquor, on condition that he will forever abstain from the use of intoxicating drinks.

—The Electrical Review says that the lightning rod is a relic of superstition, and that the day will come when a lightning-rod on a house will be regarded in the same light as a horseshoe over a door.

—Perhaps his preference may not be considered as worth a great deal in the eyes of the people of the United States, still it is announced that Bob Ingersol endorses Judge Gresham for President.

—The Democratic Convention at St. Louis nominated Grover Cleveland, of New York, the present incumbent, for President of the United States, and Allen G. Thurman, of Ohio, for Vice President.

—The Fayetteville Journal says that Bob McNeill, who shot Mias Ida Poe, in a hotel at Carthage a few weeks ago was arrested in Fayetteville. He was put under a $400 for his appearance at court.

—Thirteen hundred and fifty bales of cotton, valued at $65,000, was destroyed by fire at Columbia, S. C., on Tuesday afternoon last. It was set on fire by a spark from a passing engine. Not a bale was saved.

—The Elizabeth City Economist says "the storm of liberty is better than the calm of despotism, but the halcyon days of peace, prosperity and free but calm discussion of public men and measures, is better than either."

—Winston is preparing for a grand, rip-roarious, whooping, old-time-Fourth-of-July celebration. Excursion trains will be run from several of the neighboring towns, and a great day of hilarious relaxation is anticipated.

—The government has decided to establish a pigeon message service in connection with the signal office at Key West, Fla. The purpose is to bring the adjacent islands, especially the Bahamas into connection with Key West.

LYNCHING IN ALABAMA.
Two Hundred Armed Men Took a Negro Assassin Out of Jail and Hanged Him.

MONTGOMERY, Ala., March 30. — Judge Lynch got in his work at Hayneville, Lowndes county, last night, and avenged one of the most dastardly, cold-blooded murders in the criminal history of the State. At midnight about two hundred armed and masked men rode into the town, went to the county jail and demanded possession of Theo Calloway, the negro who murdered Mr. Mitchell Gresham, near Sandy Ridge, in Lowndes county, a few days ago. They forced the jailer to surrender the keys to the jail, and then they went to the cell where the murderer was sleeping, took him out and hanged him to the limb of a tree in front of the Court House. His body was riddled with bullets and left dangling in the air until to-day, when it was turned over to his parents, who had gone to Hayneville to be present at the preliminary trial, which was set for to-day. It was taken back to Sandy Ridge for burial. The lynchers, having completed their work, rode out of town and disappeared as quietly as they had come. Nothing is known as to their identity, except that they were friends of the murdered man.

Gresham and the negro had a dispute about a rubber coat one day last week. Gresham and his brother met the negro in the public road with a shot gun. Gresham asked him what he was going to do with the gun, and he said: "I will show you." He then levelled the gun and fired. The charge blew the back part of the young man's head off, causing instant death.
