NEWS CONDENSED.
George White, who killed Frank Conway, at Richmond, was given one year in the penitentiary.

Theodore Calloway, a murderer, was taken from the jail at Hayneyville, Ala., and hanged by a mob of 200.

Judge S. G. Sharp is now treasurer of Kentucky, his nomination having been confirmed by the Senate.

David Jennings, of Lyons, N. Y., claims to have discovered perpetual motion after a search of 21 years.

Troubles never come singly. The C. B. & Q. lost its shops and contents at Aurora, Ill., valued at $175,000.

President Cleveland and Secretary of the Navy Whitney attended Ex-Gov. Dorsheimer's funeral at New York.

It is stated as a fact that a couple at Cisco, Texas, aged 80 and 65 years, have recently become the parent of a boy.

The 41st annual conclave of the Grand Commandery Knights Templar will be held at Maysville, on May 9th and 10th.

An explosion occurred in the Rich Hill, Mo., coal mines killing 25 persons and entombing alive 15 others, who were afterwards rescued.

A woman at Brooklyn has just given birth to triplets, two girls and a boy, whose combined weights were 36 pounds; all living and doing well.

The Kentucky State Music Teachers' Convention will be held at Covington July 11-13. Prof. Bristow, of that city, will furnish all information.

Tammany Hall and the New York county democracy will go to the St. Louis convention 10,000 strong and will spend about $100,000 in doing so.

The receiver announces that depositors in the defunct Metropolitan National Bank of Cincinnati will get a dividend of 100 per cent. on the dollar.

Commonwealth's Attorney Bronston says he will resign in June, as he is tired of prosecuting men. They say he has the Congressional bee in his bonnet.

Four times has the White House been draped in mourning since President Cleveland became its occupant for Grant, for Hendricks, for Arthur and for Waite.

The Somerset Banking Company has purchased the Kindrick Corner Building for $4,000 and will have it fitted up immediately for banking purposes. [Reporter.

Barry Painter, of Monocacy, Pa., and Charles Wilkerson, of Sullivan, Missouri, roomed together, blew out the gas together and died together at Reading, Pa., Thursday night.

Sentence was passed on B. F. Hopkins, late assistant cashier of the Fidelity Bank, of Cincinnati, Saturday. He got seven years and ten months in the Ohio penitentiary.

August Krakow shot his wife dead after she had fatally poisoned their 12 children and then blew his own brains out, and the unusual sight of 14 corpses in one house was presented.

John R. De Camp, ex-vice president of the Metropolitan Bank, was surrendered by his bondsman, Captain Alexander Montgomery, and was committed to jail and will soon be on his way to join Harper.

Cornelison, the murderer of Judge Reid, has sworn out a writ of habeas corpus before Common Pleas Judge Scott. The fellow's punishment was light enough, but he takes it about as hard as any one ever did.

—J. V. Gillespie and wife, of Chillecothe, Mo., locked themselves in a room and engaged in a quarrel. Gillespie was shot three times and his wife's throat was cut almost from ear to ear. Both are thought to be fatally injured.

—President Ingalls, of the Chesapeake & Ohio road, states that the offices of the company will not be removed to Cincinnati, but be kept in Richmond and Gen. Wickham will have control. The new company will be worked in harmony with the Big Four road.

—Charles E. Cross, President, and Samuel C. White, Cashier of the National Bank of Releigh, N. C., were arrested at Toronto, Canada, on information telegraphed from Releigh charging them with forgery. Inside of the lining of Cross' coat were found $0,459 and in White's $15,352. Of this amount $600 was in unsigned currency bills.

—An 18-old-girl committed suicide at Marshalltown, Iowa, after writing this note: "No more will I have to struggle

to be true. There is one who will know why this is done. Bury me in a plain white cashmere dress, filled nicely with a box plait in the back. Fix my bangs pretty. Sing 'Shall we gather at the river?' and 'Yield not to temptation' at the funeral." The inquest failed to disclose any motive for the suicide. The ruling passion to look "pretty" was strong even in death.

LANCASTER, GARRARD COUNTY.

Bro. Yancey baptized Miss Eubanks Sunday afternoon in Dix river.

The oldest inhabitant is bound to confess he never saw a fairer Easter than Sunday. It was a glorious day.

The fishing season is here, and one can hear nothing but fish talk. There are as many Izaak Waltons as Nimrods in Lancaster.

At the rate the grass is growing this, Monday morning, the pastures will do to turn on the cows within two weeks. Bless the sun!

Miss Bessie Wherritt came up from Sister Catherine's on Wednesday and spent a few days with her father and mother. She returned yesterday.

Engleman & Farris have a horse, which on being hitched to a buggy about feeding time positively refused to budge, until he got his supper. A sensible horse, that.

Alex Dunn, of Danville, passed thro' Lancaster Sunday afternoon, with his son, Robert, of Richmond, who is quite ill of pneumonia. He was taking Bob home, where he can be properly cared for.

There hasn't been a marriage licence issued by our county clerk since March 15. This don't look like the young men's fancies are turned to thoughts of love. Not this spring—times are too hard.

Notwithstanding the fact that local option is in effect at Lancaster, it is evident whisky is being sold in the town. The officers were after some parties yesterday, but it seems hard to catch the violators of the law. The boys will have their bitters.

Miss Margaret Stuart died Friday. Her remains were taken back to her Iowa home by Mr. J. B. Johnston Saturday. It will be a sad home-coming to her mother, as she is an only child. Her father was with her when she died. He left on Friday night to break the news to his wife.

There isn't a finer stream for fish in Kentucky than Dix river. And if the good people would just quit seining it, the river would soon be full of fish. As it now is, the sportsman had about as well fish in a tub as Dix river. True now and then a nice jumper is caught, but it requires a world of patience and no end of labor to accomplish this feat.

Uncle George Beazley informs me that from to-day, Monday, until Friday, is the time to plant potatoes, radishes, beets, &c., as the moon is dark and the sign in the knees and feet. After that time the sign goes to the head and you may plant beans, peas &c. The man who fails to watch the sign had as well not plant, he will raise nothing if he does. That is the reason so many people have no gardens.

A RACE WAR IN ALABAMA. Negroes of Lowndes County Seeking to Avenge a Lynching. MONTGOMERY, ALA. May 4. 10 P.M. - A
Negroes of Lowndes County Seeking to Avenge a Lynching.

MONTGOMERY, ALA., May 4, 10 P. M.—A special to the Advertiser reports a bad condition of affairs in Lowndes county, growing out of the recent lynching of a murderer by a white mob. The negroes have been threatening vengeance, it seems, and to-day the Sheriff with a posse went to Sandy Ridge, and arrested fifteen negroes. On the way back to Hayneville, the county seat, the posse encountered a mob of armed negroes. A conflict ensued and two white men were wounded and several negroes killed. After several volleys the negroes dispersed. They are reported to be assembling again in large numbers and the sheriff has telegraphed to the governor for troops. Four companies from Montgomery are now leaving for the scene, including an artillery and cavalry company.

DEPARTURE OF THE MILITARY.

MONTGOMERY, ALA., May 4, 11:30 P. M.—The Grays, Blues, and Mounted Rifles, the latter with their horses, left for Lowndes county at 11:30 o'clock to-night. It was decided not to to take the artillery. In the conflict this afternoon, Deputy Sheriffs Rice, Meriwether and D. Cook (white) were wounded, and two negroes were probably killed. It is reported that the negroes are arming and collecting in large numbers. Ever since the lynching of Calloway in March, the negroes have been threatening vengeance. In attempting to arrest one of them a few days ago he resisted, and the sheriff wounded him. This infuriated the negroes, and precipitated the conflict to-day.

NUBS OF NEWS.
A party of log drivers in Baraga county, Mich., attempted to thaw some dynamite over a cook stove in their shanty. The result was a terrific explosion which killed three men.

Philadelphia had two hangings on Tuesday. One of the persons executed was David Vincent, who killed a sailor, and the other was Robert G. Hall, an actor, who killed Lillian Rivers (his mistress), the wife of James W. Rivers, last June.

The governor of Alabama asked the sheriff of Lowndes county for an account of a recent lynching of a negro, and the sheriff replied practically that his excellency might mind his own business. The sheriff and his posse then had a fight with a party of negroes, and the former sent to the governor for troops.

A package of $41,000 in national bank bills was sent last Saturday by express from New York to Washington for delivery at the treasury department. Upon being opened the package was found to contain only blank brown paper. It is believed the money was stolen before the package left New York, and not in transit.

St. Paul's cathedral at Buffalo, N. Y., was almost entirely destroyed by fire yesterday morning, owing to an explosion of natural gas. At least a dozen other explosions occurred at different points throughout the city. Four firemen were badly hurt in Pierce's Hotel by an explosion which occurred while they were putting out a fire.

W. C. Chamberlain, of Texas, has returned from Paris, where he went to be treated for a wolf bite by Pasteur, perfectly well. Another man bitten by the same wolf has since died of hydrophobia. Mr. Chamberlain felt the first symptoms of the disease before arriving in Paris. Pasteur feared it was too late, but the treatment proved efficacious.

The firm of Nicholson, Frost & Co., dealers in glassware at Boston, who recently failed, have discovered that they have been robbed of at least $10,000 by their bookkeeper. The peculations, which were not confined to the ledger accounts, have extended over several years. The firm has also lost several thousand dollars by dishonest salesmen.

Four Hundred Mexican Bandits in Rio Grande City Demanding the Blood of a Government Inspector.
Four Hundred Mexican Bandits in Rio Grande City Demanding the Blood of a Government Inspector.

BROWNSVILLE, Tex., Sept. 24.—Rio Grande City is in the hands of an armed Mexican mob of 400 men, of the lowest class of bandits and smugglers.

The county officers, Americans and foreigners, are barricaded in their houses. The trouble arose over the shooting of Cateriono E. Garza, editor of The Comercio Mexicano, a Mexican paper published at Corpus Christi, by United States Inspector of Customs Seebree.

Garza was shot in the stomach and mortally wounded. Seebree mounted a horse and fled so Ringold barracks. He was pursued by mounted Mexicans, shooting at him. Col. Clendenning, in command of three companies of troops, put Seebree in the guard house.

A mob of 200 Mexicans demanded him. Clendenning refused and ordered the mob out of the fort under penalty of death. The wires were cut at midnight, and no further news is obtainable.

The trouble originated over the killing of Blackmailer Reesendey some months ago by Seebree. Garza libeled Sebree in his newspaper. Seebree brought a criminal suit and had Garza arrested. His political friends rallied to his support. His party declares that no American can hold office in Starr county.
victor-sebree-rio-grande-city-1888-09.A5:
ON THE BORDER.
[Copyright, 1888, by the California Associated Press.]
Quiet Temporarily Restored at Rio Grande City, Texas.
[Copyright, 1888, by the California Associated Press.]

Rio Grande City (Tex.), September 24th. Catrino Garzia, shot on Friday last by Victor Sebrese, is still living. The surgeon at Fort Ringgold says the ball struck no fatal part. Sebrese, who was pursued, was shot at by Mexican friends of Garzia, but he reached Fort Ringgold safely and surrendered to the commanding officer, Colonel Clendenning.

The Mexicans made a demand upon the military for Sebrese, but Colonel Clendenning refused to deliver him, and warned them that any attempt to take him by force would draw the fire of the Galling guns and the entire command on them.

In order to prevent any communication between Fort Ringgold and the department headquarters, the Mexicans tore down the telegraph wires between this place and Fort Ringgold. The possible recovery of Garzia has had the effect of restoring order.

IN THE HANDS OF A MOB.
[Copyright, 1888, by the California Associated Press.]

AUSTIN (Tex.), September 24th. — Reports from Rio Grande City state that the place for the last twenty-four hours has been in the possession of an armed Mexican mob. Governor Ross has received a number of telegrams stating that anarchy reigns, and demanding the presence of troops.

CONFLICIING STATEMENTS.

Governor Ross has ordered the entire Ranger force in Texas to proceed with all possible haste to the scene, as a massacre of Texas citizens is feared. The Mexicans number ten to one of the white citizens in that section, and there is no telling to what excesses they will resort.

It is believed that a general massacre of citizens will take place before midnight unless the United States troops from Fort Ringgold come to the rescue.
victor-sebree-rio-grande-city-1888-09.A14:
The following letter, received by the governor yesterday, explains the troubles and gives the origin of the emute at Rio Grande City:

RIO GRANDE CITY,
September 22, 1888.

"On May 14, 1888, W. W. Sheely, sheriff of this, (Starr) county, made a complaint before Judge J. C. Russell, judge of the district court, against Abraham Recendez, charging him with having, some time before, robbed

MR. MANUEL GUERRA,

a merchant of this county, of $500. Recendez was arrested on May 16, and while being taken to jail resisted his guards and was killed by Victor Sebree, who had been summoned by Mr. Shely to assist one A. Dillard, a state ranger, detailed by the sergeant in command of the Rangers here to assist Mr. Shely. The killing, though justifiable, created

GREAT EXCITEMENT

among the Mexican population of the county, and a deep feeling of resentment against the Americans generally, and particularly against Messrs. Sebree, Dillard and Shely. Some time before that date a political club was formed here under the management of and head of Augustine de la Pena and Silnerio de la Pena, his son, This club, or faction, had already openly announced their intention of opposing Mr. Shely because of his suppose complicity in the lynching of four men some time before. Two of these four men were acknowledged participants in the kidnapping and robbery of $1,500 from one Juan Garcia Burrera some time ago. Mr. Shely had arrested them, and while on his way to town they were taken from him by an

ARMED BODY

of men and hung. The other two men were prisoners in the jail of Carmego, Mex., and, when seen on this side, were hanging in the government reservation. As to them, it is currently reported that the Mexican officials hung them on the Mexican side and afterwards transferred them to the United States reservation. This Pena club took up all of the killings, laid them at the door of Sheriff Shely and made political capital of them by exciting the Mexicans to oppose the Americans. Their conduct has brought on what may well be termed a race war. Among other efforts used to

FIRE THE MINDS

of the Mexicans, the Penas employed one Catarino E. Garza, the editor of a newspaper published in Corpus Christi in Spanish, to write incendiary articles and to lecture and speak to the Mexicans. Garza did this thoroughly and used his paper especially to make attacks on Mr. Sebree, calling him an assassin, a coward, etc., etc., and defying him to meet him. Garza made two trips here previous to the last one, and in both cases exerted himself to further the political schemes of the Penas. Several days ago he returned here for the avowed purpose of stumping the county, bringing with him a man named Lopez, as his companion, and, as it now seems, to

SHOOT ANYONE

who should attempt to call him to account.

Yesterday evening Mr. Sebree, accompanied by Mr. T. B. Norris, started to ride down the river to a ranch, three or four miles distant. Garza and Lopez were seated on the main street, and Sebree and Norris rode by. Sebree alighted from his horse, handing the reins to Norris, and walked to where Garza was sitting. He asked Garza if he

WANTED TO FIGHT,

making no attempt to use his pistol nor threatening to do so. Hardly had he spoken to Garza when Lopez, standing a few feet from him, opened fire on Sebree with a pistol. Garza made no reply beyond drawing a pistol and firing at Sebree. After Lopez fired Sebree drew his pistol and he and Garza fired about the same time. Lopez and Garza continued to fire on Sebree and he returned their fire. They did not wound him but he (Sebree) shot Garza in the abdomen

MORTALLY WOUNDING

him, and Lopez in the leg inflicting a flesh wound. This fresh shooting caused intense excitement. A mob at once formed, armed themselves and, about one hundred strong, openly announced their intention of

LYNCHING SEBREE,

And started for his room with that object. Meantime, however, he and Mr. Dillard had taken refuge in Camp Ringgold. This mob paraded the streets all night, and was increased from the country, threatening vengeance and demanding that the sheriff, county judge and justice of the peace deliver Sebree to them. This, of course, was refused, as does the commanding officer of Fort Ringgold, and the mob is virtually in possession of the town now. They have cut the

GOVERNMENT TELEGRAPH

line. The civil authorities cannot control the mob, though the sheriff is doing what he can, assisted by the few Americans here and a portion of the respectable Mexicans. The mob is composed entirely of Mexicans.

YOUR UNCLE SAMUEL.

Last night the governor received the following which explains itself:

SAN ANTONIO, Tex.,
September 25, 1888.

Gov. L. S. Ross, Austin:

I send you the following correspondence with reference to Rio Grande City:

SAN ANTONIO, Tex.
victor-sebree-rio-grande-city-1888-09.A15:
EXCITING EMEUTE.
Dusky Sons of the Montezumas On the Rampage.
Rio Grande City in the Hands of a Furious Mob.
Sebree, of Rio Grande city, had a difficulty with two Mexicans, one of whom was Editor Garza, of Corpus Christi, in which Garza was killed and his friend wounded. After the difficulty Sebree mounted his horse and made a break for Ringgold barracks, pursued by mounted Mexicans, firing on him. He got into the reservation and was put in the guard house. A mob of about 200 armed men went into the garrison and demanded of the commander, Colonel Clendenin, to give him up to them, which request was promptly refused and they were ordered out of the reservation. The greatest disorder prevailed, and the whole town was last night delivered over to mob violence. The telegraph office was besieged and no attempt to deliver messages was made, as it was believed that the messenger boy would be killed. An attempt was made during the evening to send a fraudulent telegram, purporting to be from Judge Kelsey to Austin, but it was discovered and its delivery prevented.

It having been intimated that the Starr county authorities would call on Sheriff Brito for aid, he made preparations to charter a special train from the Matamoras railroad and go to their assistance with fifty men.

The rioters are composed of the lowest class of Mexicans, among whom are many noted smugglers and bandits. Their party are adherents of the revolutionary Mexican chief Martinez and his gang, and are the same who started a society in Starr county pledged to run every American out of office in that section.

Fears are expressed by many in Rio Grande for the safety of American and foreign residents and families in that section.

Colonel Clendenin is in command of Ringgold barracks, has three companies of troops, a force of about 130 men, under his command, and it is to be hoped that, being cut off from communication with Washington by telegraph, he may assume the responsibility of protecting lives and property in the city.

The mob cut the telegraph wires, and only the brief telegram which appeared in Sunday's STATESMAN reached the governor Saturday.

The following telegrams were received by the governor Sunday and yesterday, and they speak for themselves:

BROWNSVILLE, September 23, 1888.

Governor Ross, Austin:

I have reliable information that the civil authorities at Rio Grande city are powerless against mob. Please telegraph request to United States military authorities to protect the citizens there until state troops can reach the place.

BROWNSVILLE, September 23, 1888.

L. S. Ross, governor:

I am requested to wire you immediately requesting that you send a company of state rangers to Rio Grande City with all possible dispatch. The people and officers there cannot communicate with you, as the wires are down, supposed to have been cut by the mob to prevent communication. From all that we can learn here I am satisfied that the aid they ask is very much needed, and should be sent at the earliest possible moment, or it may be too late. Cannot the United States troops stationed there at Fort Ringgold be ordered by wire to protect the people and aid in enforcing law and order until the rangers arrive?

DAVIS RANCH, VIA CAMARGO AND BROWNSVILLE, September 23, 1888.

Gov. L. S. Ross, Austin:

Street affray yesterday between two Mexicans and one American. Both Mexicans wounded, one seriously. Mexicans greatly incensed and demanding delivery to them of the American. Riot as yet prevented by placing the American under the protection of the commanding officer at Fort Ringgold. More than 100 Mexicans under arms demanding of me to place the American in jail. If I comply he will be lynched, as I am powerless to get a posse to protect him. If I don't place him in jail my life is threatened. I am temporizing, but can't do so much longer. If rangers are not sent at once I fear that they will arrive too late. Commanding officer at Fort Ringgold can't protect town without orders from war department. Wire president to authorize use of United States troops until rangers arrive. W. W. SHEELY.

DAVIS RANCH, (VIA CAMARGO AND BROWNSVILLE.) September 23, 1888.

Governor Ross, Austin:

Two Mexicans wounded, one mortally, in a street fight yesterday by Customs Officer Sebree. Large parties of armed Mexicans are parading the streets, demanding vengeance. A riot has been prevented so far by placing Sebrees under the protection of the commander of Fort Ringgold. They are demanding his being placed in jail, no doubt in order to murder him. Very few Americans here. Sheriff powerless, and his life in danger. Commanding officer at Ringgold is powerless to send troops to protect the town without orders from the war department. Wire the president for such orders and send a company of rangers at once. Have sent you full particulars by letter.

The names of some of the senders of the above dispatches are withheld.

The governor yesterday wired the following answers:

AUSTIN, September 24.

To Sheriff Brito, Brownsville:

Summon a posse of good men, and go to Rio Grande City, to aid the sheriff of Starr county, to restore order and the supremacy of the law at all hazards. Other contiguous sheriffs have the same orders. Expenses will be paid by the state.

L. S. Ross, Governor.

AUSTIN, September 24, 1888.

To J. B. Wells, Brownsville:

Troops are being sent as rapidly as possible. It is expected that Jones' company of rangers will reach there to-night.

L. S. Ross, Governor.

AUSTIN, September 24, 1888.

To J. J. Cocke, Brownsville:

All available troops ordered and on the way.

L. S. Ross, Governor.

AUSTIN, September 23, 1888.

W. W. Sheley, Sheriff Starr County:

All the avalaible troops are ordered to your assistance and the sheriffs of adjacent counties are directed to proceed with a posse without delay to aid you in restoring order. Don't place Sebree in jail till he can be protected from mob violence. Captain Jones will probably reach you Monday night.

L. S. Ross, Governor.

The governor also sent the following:

AUSTIN, September 24.

To Captain Clendenin, Ringgold Barracks;

I learn from the Express that you have protected Sebree from mob violence. Accept my thanks. State troops will arrive shortly to preserve order. L. S. Ross, Governor of Texas.

THE ASSISTANCE.

As stated in Sunday's STATESMAN, Captain Jones and his company of rangers were ordered to Rio Grande city Saturday night, and it is probable they reached the scene of the emuete last night.

Sunday, on receipt of Sheriff Sheely's dispatch, Lieutenant Brooks, stationed in Kerr county with his rangers, were ordered to join Jones with all dispatch, and will probably affect a juncture to-day at noon.

THE MOB STILL HOLDING RIO GRANDE CITY.

Rio Grande City, Tex., Sept. 26 (Special).—The mob still holds the town and there is a bitter feeling. The rangers arrived last night. Garza is resting comfortably and the doctors think that he will probably recover. Lopez, who was with Garza at the time of the affray, was also wounded by Sebree. The latter, with County Attorney Herd and Deputy Sheriff Millard, is in the garrison. The dispatches sent out from other points, giving the alleged cause of the riot, have not given the facts. The trouble arose from the killing of Recendez, a Mexican arrested for robbery, who was killed, while resisting the guards, by Sebree. A political club, the Penas, had already been formed to oppose the re-election of Sheriff Sheley on account of his supposed complicity in the lynching of four men, two of whom were acknowledged participant's in the
victor-sebree-rio-grande-city-1888-09.A19:
Sebree's Examination.
RIO GRANDE, Texas, September 28. — Victor Sebree, who shot Editor Garza in this city, was brought from the military garrison before County Judge Kelsey, at 10 o'clock to day. He waived examination and his bond was fixed at $2,500. He was committed in default of bail, to Brownsville jail. As this jail is not considered a safe place for Sebree, Sheriff Brito, of Cameron, now here, will take Sebree with him on his return to Cameron. All is quiet. Garza's condition is critical.
victor-sebree-rio-grande-city-1888-09.A21:
IN THE HANDS OF A MORAL.
Rio Grande City Invaded by Armed Mexicans.
FIGHTING ON THE TEXAS BORDER.
The Trouble Occasioned by the Killing of a Mexican Editor by a United States Revenue Officer-A General Massacre Feared.
AUSTIN, Tex., Sept. 25.—The most alarming telegrams continued to pour in on Gov. Ross, informing him that there is war, bloody and fierce, now raging on the Texas frontier and that Rio Grande City has been for the past 24 hours in possession of an armed Mexican mob.

All the telegrams thus received have come either from John P. Kelsey, county judge of Starr County, or the sheriff, and each succeeding one is more startling and sensational than the other. They all demand troops immediately and convey the impression in plain words that rampant anarchy runs riot on the border and that the lives of American citizens in that section are in imminent danger.

This extraordinary and sensational state of affairs had its origin in the fatal encounter which took place in Rio Grande City last Saturday between Catrino E. Garza, editor of El Comercio Mexicano, and United States Revenue Officer Victor Zebre. In the fight Zebre shot and killed Garza, who was very popular all along the Rio Grande, and as a result the Mexicans rose in revolt and endeavored to lynch Zebre. The Texas officials, however, saved him for the time being from the fury of the mob and wired Gov. Ross as follows:

Great riot is raging here. Armed men are parading the streets. Send State Rangers or call United States troops at Fort Ringold.

This dispatch was followed by another from B. T. W. Kenedy, member of the Legislature, as follows:

Send all the available troops you can and at once. Armed Mexicans are in control of the city and the county.

Last night and all this day similar messages of consternation keep coming,
the last one reading as follows:
A fight has just taken place between two Mexicans and one American; one Mexican killed. The Mexicans now demand the American to be delivered to them. Riot prevented by placing the American under arrest.
Another telegram reads:
Over 150 armed Mexicans are attempting to lynch Zebre. Send Rangers at once. The riot still continues.

Rio Grande City is eighty miles from the nearest railroad station and it is extremely difficult to reach it. Gov. Ross has, notwithstanding, ordered the entire ranger force of Texas to proceed with all possible haste to the scene of the battle, as the massacre of Texas citizens is feared. The Mexicans number ten to one of the white citizens in that section, and there is no telling to what excesses they will resort, especially as they have no difficulty in escaping to Mexico if it suits them. Gov. Ross has also telegraphed all the sheriffs of all the counties on the border or contiguous to it to proceed by forced marches to the troubled district and take armed posses along with them. He has likewise telegraphed the San Antonio Rifles, the Belknap Rifles and the famous Houston Light Guard to hold themselves in readiness to march at a moment's notice.

It is believed that there will be a general massacre of Texas citizens unless the United States troops from Fort Ringold come to the rescue.

The event is likely to lead to international complications, and should a massacre occur, swift and wholesale retribution is certain to follow. To-night Gov. Ross says the situation is extremely grave, and the absence of advices for several hours gives rise to the worst fears.
victor-sebree-rio-grande-city-1888-09.A25:
South and West.
VICTOR SEBREE, a United States Revenue officer shot and killed Catrino E. Garza, a Mexican editor, at Rio Grande City, Texas. He was placed in jail and the Mexicans attempted to lynch him. The sheriff placed him under the protection of the United States garrison at Fort Ringgold and Governor Ross sent several troops of Rangers to quell the disturbance.

ANTONY CARNEY, of Chicago, fatally shot his wife and then committed suicide while drunk.

MRS. EVA GATELY, a widow, with her two children, was killed by a train at Versailles, Ky.

THE "Lone Highwayman," who has for the last two years been a terror to travelers in the vicinity of Kerrville, Texas, has been killed. He was shot with a needle gun by Mrs. Lizzie Hay, at her home on the head waters of Rio Sabinal, Bandera County.

THE Georgia cotton crop has been damaged nineteen per cent, and the corn crop thirteen per cent.

TOWN MARSHAL WOOLWINE, of Jellico, Tenn., attempted to arrest William Lyons, Both drew revolvers and fired and both were instantly killed. E. A. Delfunian, a third party, was fatally injured.

LOVEZA AMADOR, captain of the Contras Guards of Mexico, and Granciuna Cantu, a State ranger, settled a long standing difficulty at San Felipe de Sabinas, Texas, by a pistol fight, in which both were killed.

H. S. Ives and George H. Stayner, the famous Wall street operators in railway securities, were acquitted of embezzlement and larceny at Cincinnati.

FIFTY men were buried by a cave, in while digging a trench at Little Rock, Ark. Three were taken out dead.

FIVE convicts, leased to the Missouri Pacific Railway Company, made a break for liberty while working near Dallas, Texas, under an armed guard. He fired upon them, killing John Davis and Chris Wells. Two swam Trinity River and escaped.

DESPERADO BILL WHITELY, for years a terror to Texas, was killed by a deputy United States Marshal at Floresville, Texas.

GENERAL STANLEY, commanding United States troops in Texas, has issued an order to the Fort Ringgold officers, telling them to use the United States regulars in enforcing order at Rio Grande City, where the Mexicans have been threatening to murder the Americans.

Some cattle were being transferred across the Missouri river in a flatboat at Glasgow, Mo., when they stamped and the boat was swamped. There were seven men on board, and three were drowned.

A "CORNER" in September wheat at Chicago forced its price up to $1.25 a bushel.

The Northern Pacific Railroad has negotiated a sale of 700,000 acres of its land-grant in Dakota.

GOVERNOR GUY marched to the Chickasaw Capitol at Tishomingo, Indian Territory, with an armed force and took his seat by force. Guy was legally elected Governor, but was counted out by the Byrd party, and Byrd took the seat as Governor. Governor Guy quietly went to gather some of his party and took the Capitol and the Byrd party by surprise.
victor-sebree-rio-grande-city-1888-09.A28:
STATE NEWS.
There is not a vacant store in Rusk.
There have been abundant rains at Del Rio; grass is fine.
Quarantine has been raised in Texas against the state of Georgia.
Railroad talk puts politics in the shade at Sweetwater.
A little over 800 bales of cotton have been received to date at Navasota. Business is booming.
The anniversary celebration of the Schuetzen Verein, Teutonia, was held at Victoria on Thursday.
Work is soon to be started on the Texas extension of the Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific.
The boot and shoe establishment of Morer & Son, of Waco, is closed by attachment.
Catori Garza and Jose Lopez, the parties engaged in the fight with Sebree and Abel Garza, have been arrested in Rio Grande.
An old gentleman, aged 80 years, yesterday shot himself through the head, causing instant death, in Houston.

The capitol furnishing board of Austin have issued a volumnious folio of specifications for furnishing the new capitol.

A difficulty arose at the City Planning mill, Nacogdoches, between O. J. Garner, owner of the mill, and F. W. Powell, lessee, in which Garner received a bullet in his left arm.

A gentleman in Decatur from McLennan county, identifies Bob and Dan Campbell as two of the men that robbed him of about $1700.

Sufficient money has been raised by the Humane society, Dallas, to permit the organization to employ an agent for the prosecution of offenses against animals.
One of the largest and latest improved water drills and 1000 feet of pipe are ordered to El Paso, for the effort to secure artesian water on the Mesa northwest of the city.

E. M. Norton, who operates a mill and cotton gin at Cottonwood, had his arm caught in the machinery and cut and sawed so badly that amputation will probably be necessary.

J. A. Johnson, at McKinney, charged with perperating four forgeries, has waived examination and required to give bail in the sum of $1,000.

Prof. J. T. Johnson, of Vernon, charged with committing aggravated assault and battery on Joe Creager, one of his scholars, is discharged with the verdict of not guilty.

The Fannin county alliance have met again in Bonham for the purpose of giving the jute bagging another black eye.

A cowboy named Bird Casaway, hunting cattle in Hall county, overhauled a bear. lassoed him, tightened his lariat to strangling point, and jumping from his horse, cut the beast's throat. Bruin weighed over 500 pounds.

Gov. Ross has a telegram from the Board of Health at Galveston, as follows: "The Board of Health raises no objection to the admission of any clean vessel coming from an non-infected port regardless of latitude, provided she be subject to inspection."

Fire broke out in Waco on Austin avenue, between Sixth and Seventh streets, and entirely consumed the buildings and stocks of the following parties: G. W. McLaughlin, grocery; E. J. Smith, grocery; Richard Webb, meat market; G. H. Massey, paints and oils.
Miss Maddern's Lithograph's do not resemble her very closely. She is prettier than they represent her.

Frank Mayo, who will be remembered as playing David Crockett here, has just recovered from a serious illness occasioned by contact with poison oak while resting at Canton, Pa.

Gracie Emmett, the piquant actress who supported T. J. Farron, when he was here, is now playing in the new success, "Beacon Lights."

The Pennant Winners.

A Policeman Shot by a Hobber.
Sr. Louis, Oct. 26.—A Post-Despatch special from Jackson, Tenn., says: Last night Walter Howard, a negro porter for the Southern Express Co., shot and seriously wounded Policeman J. E. Owens, who was attempting to arrest the negro. Howard had robbed the express office and was making his escape. He is at large, but will be pursued until caught, having only a slight start.
walter-howard-jackson-1888-10-29.A8:
SOUTHERN GLEANINGS.
brother-in-law, John Gordon, had a shooting affray, in which Gordon was seriously and Richard Draper fatally wounded.

It took sixteen men, fourteen dogs and nine charges of buckshot to kill a bear in Madison County, Ga., a few days ago. Four of the dogs were killed and three wounded. The chase lasted for twelve hours.

B. Sterling, a young white man living on his plantation on Deer Creek, near Greenville, Miss., had some words with one of the negro hands of the place a few days ago. It seems that the latter was around with a double-barreled shotgun ready to open fire on the white man, but Sterling was the quickest in procuring his shooting iron, and shot the negro in the stomach; inflicting probably a fatal wound.

A young woman named Salie Clements was found about four miles from Owensboro, Ky., a few nights ago, in a ditch. She was speechless and insensible, and bore marks of having been brutally treated. After a time she was restored to consciousness, but could give no account of herself or of how she came to be in the condition in which she was found. She soon lapsed into insensibility again, and could not be aroused. She was taken to Owensboro in this pecarious condition, and it was thought she would die.

E. L. Carter accidentally shot and killed Clarence Beall in Americus, Ga., a few days ago.

The skeleton of a union soldier was found recently under the flooring of the hotel kitchen at Dinwiddie Court-House, Va. Close to the skeleton was a musket and canteen.

Near Holleville, Ga., a few days since, William Sullivan shot and instantly killed John Wilson. The tragedy grew out of a disputed land line. Both men were wealthy farmers.

In a row at a circus at Mount Vernon, Ky., a few days ago, William Parker was fatally cut and James Jones shot.

Police Lieutenant Warren, of Columbus, Ga., a faithful and efficient officer, has resigned rather than submit to an investigation of the charge that he had negro blood his veins.

Wm. Strickland, the white man who was stabbed seven times, in Wake County, N. C., by Iola Hicks, a colored woman, several days ago, died of his injuries. The woman is under arrest.

The subject of a penal colony or farm on which to work State convicts is now being agitated in Alabama. It is put forth as a grand scheme for the reform of the present convict system.

At Spartanburg, S. C., a few days ago, R. Senn and Helen Boland, both white, were sentenced to be hanged on December 14 for the murder of Mrs. Senn two years ago.

The Memphis & Charleston and the Louisville & Nashville railroads are preparing to locate extensive yards and build shops at Sheffield, Ala., at an early date.

George Mude, an employee of the Georgia Marble Works at Atlanta, Ga., committed suicide a few days since by blowing his brains out with a pistol. No cause is known for the act.

Jim Rice, the seventeen-year-old boy who stole a horse and cart from a man living on the McKenzie place, near Helana, Ark., was arrested at Brinkley, and taken back and placed in jail.

John Bolton, a colored man, residing in Montgomery, Ky., was hunting a few days ago when he fell from a cliff, breaking his back and receiving other injuries that resulted in his death.

Walter Howard, a negro, robbed the express office at Jackson, Tenn, a few days ago. He made an effort to escape on a freight train. Policeman J. E. Owen was shot through the leg by the scoundrel while trying to arrest him. The negro escaped.

While Joseph Whitaker, colored, was absent from his home in Blackshear, Ga., a few days ago, his house caught fire and was burned. His four children made ineffectual attempts to escape and their bodies were found in the ruins. It is said the fire was started by an enemy of Whitaker.

A sensation has been created at Knoxville, Tenn., by the announcement that J. A. Swan, late treasurer of Knoxville County, was short about $25,000 upon a final settlement with his successor. He is now absent somewhere in the West.

The body of an unknown man was found in the woods near Hartford, Ky., a few days since. There were no marks of violence on the body, and from surrounding circumstances it was evident that he had committed suicide by taking poison. There were no papers on his body by which he could be identified, and no one in the neighborhood had ever seen him before.

By order of the board of trustees, the public schools in Bowling Green, Ky., have been closed on account of the prevalence of diphtheria and measles among the students. There have been forty cases of measles reported and about twenty-five of diphtheria, and six or eight deaths from the latter cause.

The steamer Phil Armour, running in the Vicksburg and Greenville trade, struck a snag at Wilson chute, forty miles above Vicksburg, Miss., a few nights ago, and sunk in eighteen feet of water. No lives were lost, and the books and papers and a portion of the freight were saved. It was thought the steamer would be a total loss.

A terrible tragedy occurred at Lumpkin, Ga., a few nights ago. A party of bloods were painting the town. One of the number, E. L. Carter, began firing his revolver. One shot struck Clarence Beall in the back, killing him at once. Carter was so overwhelmed that he enleavored to kill himself. A coroner's jury returned a verdict of killing by accident.

The United States District Court at Nashville, Tenn., has indicted Henry T. Wilson for counterfeiting. The indictment was found at the instance of United States Detective Bauer, who recently succeeded in having Wilson sentenced to five years' imprisonment. Wilson is one of the most expert counterfeiters that ever operated in Kentucky and Tennessee.
Jackson, Miss., is all right again.
There has been recently placed in position at Sparta, Ga., the handsome monument which the friends of Bishop Pierce have erected to his memory. It stands over the grave of the deceased Bishop in the old Sparta cemetery, within ear-shot

wash-attaway-sulphur-springs-1888-07.A2:
White Man Murdered.
SULPHUR SPRINGS, July 17.—Sheriff Ferguson got a telegram yesterday afternoon from Carroll's prairie in this county, stating that Marion Gamblin had been killed by a negro and the bloodhounds were wanted. The hounds were sent at once. Late in the afternoon a negro named Wash Attaway came to town on a mule and told how he had knocked Gamblin down with a club. While he was talking the sheriff came along and took him off to jail. Some time ago Marion Gamblin sold a mule to the negro and was to recieve his pay for it in the fall, but Attaway did not have good crop prospects, and his security refused to stand good for the amount any longer. Gamblin went to the nearest house, about four miles from Carroll's prairie, Monday to take possession of the mule. A bitter quarrel between the two was carried on in the presence of Belton Wilson and three negro women. Gamblin started to lead the mule out of the yard, when the negro took his stand at the bars, and flourishing a pole, threatened to strike Gamblin if he attempted to pass. Gamblin dropped the rein and took hold of the pole. Attaway jerked it away from him and struck him a powerfull blow on the head, felling him senseless to the ground. Wilson attempted to help Gamblin, but was prevented by Attaway's wife. Attaway made at Wilson and Wilson ran for help, and when he returned with some neighbors he found Gamblin dead. He had been struck twice on the head and on the arm, which was crushed. In his back was a deep wound made by a knife. When Attaway had finished his victim he mounted the mule and rode to his brother's. His brother advised him to come to Sulphur Spring and make complaint against Gamblin for trespassing. He did so and found sheriff waiting for him. Gamblin was about 25 years old and was very highly esteemed in his community. He leaves a wife and two children. The citizens of Carroll's prairie are very indignant, and if Attaway had been found in the neighborhood yesterday he would have probably died.

Extending her Boundaries.

DALLAS, July 17.—The election in North Dallas to-day to decide the question of annexation resulted in a victory for annexation by a small majority. This adds 3,000 people, 3,000 acres area and $2,000,000 taxable values to the city of Dallas.

A Water Scheme.

FORT WORTH, July 17.—The platting for the Hurst lake survey for the Dallas water supply company is completed. The artesian well that supplies this lake flows a six inch stream, and the survey shows the actual distance is 138,000 feet, with a total fall of 76.6 feet. The Trinity is crossed near Ogle Ford, where it is about twenty-five feet from the highest bank to the bottom of the bed of the river. This line can be shortened four miles by crossing the big bend in the river south of Hurricane swamp. Estimates of the cost of the pipping and laying the line will be made and then it will be decided if further steps are to be taken. The object, if carried out, is to pipe the water to Dallas and sell to wagons which will distribute it to consumers.

LYNCHING A NEGRO.
He Brutally Murdered a Planter in the Presence of His Family.
YAZOO CITY, MISS., Nov. 19.—A week ago Wilson Arnold (colored) came here and surrendered himself to the sheriff, stating that, in self-defense, he had shot and killed Capt. Robert Johnson, one of the most prominent citizens of the county, at his home near Satartia. This morning a large number of Johnson's friends went to the jail and took Arnold, saying that they intended to avenge the death of their friend and neighbor. Since their departure nothing has been heard from them, but it is reasonably certain that Arnold has paid the debt for his fearful crime.

CAUSE OF THE CRIME.

The particulars of the murder are as follows: Capt. Johnson had had some words with Arnold, but nothing of a serious nature. Arnold armed himself with a large-sized derringer pistol, walked up to Johnson, who was under the influence of liquor, and threw him to the ground, at the same time placing his pistol to Johnson's left temple and fired, causing instant death. Arnold then took an unloaded gun from Johnson and beat his head into a bloody mass.

VAIN PLEAS FOR HIS LIFE.

Arnold's wife and two brothers were witnesses to the tragedy, and pleaded for Johnson's life, but Arnold threatened to kill them if they opened their mouths. These facts were given to a citizens' meeting near the scene by Arnold's wife and other witnesses. In the posse to take Arnold there were many colored people, who said that the killing of their old master was brutal, and that his slayer ought to be lynched.

HARRINGTON CHARGED WITH CONTEMPT.
to the Parnell Commission.

[BY CABLE TO THE PRESS NEWS ASSOCIATION.]

LONDON, Nov. 20.—In the Parnell Commission to-day Sir Henry James, the Attorney-General, charged Edward Harrington, member of the House of Commons for Kerry, with contempt of Court.

The Attorney-General produced a copy of the Kerry Sentinel, of which Mr. Harrington is editor, and read from it an article criticising the conduct of the Commission.

This, he declared, constituted the contempt, and for it Mr. Harrington, who had been allowed to appear as counsel for himself before this Court, was responsible, if not the actual writer of the article in question.

Mr. Harrington treated the whole matter with jaunty indifference. It was arranged that the charge should be taken up by the Commission tomorrow, when a hearing will be given to the defendant.

Lively scenes are expected.

ATLANTA, Ga., Nov. 20.—Mrs. Mary Grant, a lady of great respectability, some time ago began to develop a passion for claiming the inside of the walk whenever she appeared on the street. Saturday morning she assaulted a gentleman on Whitehall street who didn't turn out. She pulled his whiskers and threw his hat into the street, while a large crowd enjoyed his astonishment as he tried to disengage himself from the woman's grasp. This morning she went down Decatur street, shoving every man into the ditch who would not give her the track. She was finally arrested and will go to an asylum.

Special to the Gazette.

AUSTIN, Tex, Oct. 11 — A large and threatening mob of indignant citizens now surround the jail at Crockett, Houston county, and at this time they are loudly demanding the negro prisoner, Young Johnson, who was yesterday convicted of attempting to outrage a respectable white girl, Miss Sims. The intention is to lynch the offender, and it is feared they will succeed. The Sheriff has barricaded the jail, and he and eleven men armed with Winchesters refuse to surrender the prisoner, and are ready to defend him to the last. They say the law must be respected and upheld at all cost, and to this end they have telegraphed the Governor for aid. In the meantime the mob is increasing in numbers and becoming more threatening and demonstrative and what the upshot of the trouble will be cannot be predicted. Governor Ross has ordered Adjutant General King to the scene. General King left on to-night's train for Crocket.

Mrs. Mollie Fry, widow of the late city marshal of Gonzales, who was killed in Booth's store a year ago, has filed a suit agafnst G. J. Booth, Geo. Booth and William Booth, whom she sues for $25,000 actual, and $50,000 exemplary damages for the killing of her husband.

A fire started in the gun store of A. Stert, on Main street, Fort Worth, yesterday morning. The gun store, the boot and shoe store of S. M. Fry, photograph gallery of G. C. Rhine, Knights of Labor hall, all in the same building, were completely destroyed, and several others were damaged. It is thought the fire was caused by burglars who tried to blow open the safe.

An historic building is built at Harrisburg, five miles south of Houston. The property was originally built by Jno. R. Harris, a pioneer in 1826, and has been in the family ever since. It was burned by Santa Anna's army in 1836, and rebuilt soon after the battle of San Jacinto. John Harris was one of the first American settlers in the county which was named after him.

A TEXAS HANGING.
John Andrew Johnson, a Colored Boy, Nineteen Years Old, the Victim.
He Pays the Death Penalty for Assaulting a Young White Girl Seventeen Years Old, of Good Family.
Special to the Gazette.
CROCKETT, TEX., Dec. 21.—John Andrew Johnson was executed to-day at 11 o'clock a.m. He was reticent to the last. A large crowd witnessed the hanging, estimated at 3000 persons, mostly colored. All approve the justice of the vindication of the law.

HISTORY OF THE CRIME.

On the 13th day of June, 1888, Miss Allie Simms was violently assaulted and a rape committed upon her about six miles from Crockett, near her father's residence. She was about seventeen years of age and of good family. Soon after, John Andrew Johnson, a colored youth of about nineteen years of age, was arrested, charged with the offense. He was brought to Crockett and placed in jail by the sheriff. The citizens were greatly incensed and excitement ran high and it was well known that many intended to take the law in their own hands and take the flend from jail and dispatch him upon the most convenient limb. The sheriff having learned of such intentions, took the prisoner, and, by stratagem, reached the jail of Harris county. There he remained until the fall term of our district court when he was brought back, and upon the return of an indictment he was placed upon his trial. He was defended by able counsel appointed by the court, and after a full and fair investigation, a jury of some of the best citizens returned a verdict of guilty, in forty-five minutes, and assessed the penalty of death. Upon the trial the injured party testified as to the perpetration of the offense, and fully identified the defendant as the party. One other witness, a colored boy, said that he was in sight of the parties at the time, and saw the assault made, and immediately afterwards the defendant came to him and gave him the particulars of the whole affair. The defense was not guilty and that the defendant was not seventeen years of age, both of which pleas totally failed. After sentence his case was appealed to the court of appeals and there argued by counsel, and the judgment affirmed. Up to the present time he claims to be innocent and says that the girl was mistaken in identifying him as the party, and that the colored boy who testified to having seen the assault made was not true. He has professed conversion and on the 18th inst. was baptised.
